知道	zhī dào	to know — The everyday verb for knowing a fact, and how it differs from 认识 (to be acquainted with) and 了解 (to understand deeply).
智慧	zhì huì	wisdom; prajna — 智慧 brings together Confucian moral discernment and Buddhist prajna under one compound: two traditions, one word, different objects of knowing.
中国	Zhōng guó	the Middle Kingdom; China — Two characters older than the country they now name. 中 (center) and 国 (state) joined three thousand years ago to mean "the central states"; the modern country took the phrase for itself only in the 19th century.
中国画	zhōng guó huà	Chinese painting — Brush and ink as philosophy: Chinese painting aims to capture the spirit of a subject and express the painter's inner cultivation rather than represent what the eye sees.
中文	zhōng wén	Chinese Language and Writing — 中文 names both the written script and the spoken language: the most common term among learners, but it sits alongside 汉语, 普通话, and 汉字 in a system of names that carries real distinctions.
中医	zhōng yī	Traditional Chinese Medicine — Two thousand years of systematic medical thought: qi, yin-yang, the Five Elements, acupuncture, and the living tradition that treats the person, not the disease.
终于	zhōng yú	finally, at last — The adverb for "finally, at last," used when something long-awaited or hard-won comes to pass, where it sits in a sentence, and how it differs from 最后, 总算, and 到底.
自然	zì rán	nature; natural; of course — Laozi placed 自然 at the center of his cosmology: the Way models itself on what is so of itself: no outside force required.
爱不释手	ài bù shì shǒu	love it so much you cannot put it down — Lit: love-not-release-hand. The standard phrase for something you cannot stop using, reading, or holding: so beloved that your hand refuses to let go. Used for books, gadgets, food, art. 这本小说写得太好了，让人爱不释手 "This novel is so well-written; you can't put it down."
爱美之心，人皆有之	ài měi zhī xīn , rén jiē yǒu zhī	the love of beauty is universal — everyone has a heart for beauty — Classical proverb affirming the universality of aesthetic appreciation. Often used to gently excuse vanity or the appreciation of beautiful people and things.
爱莫能助	ài mò néng zhù	willing but unable to help — Literally "to love but be unable to aid," used when you sympathize and would gladly help, but cannot. A gracious, slightly rueful way to decline: 我也想帮你，可惜爱莫能助 ("I'd like to help, but sadly it's beyond me"). The 助 again is the aid of 帮助.
爱屋及乌	ài wū jí wū	love me, love my dog — love extends to all connected with the beloved — Lit: love-house reach-crow. If you love the house, you even love the crow on the roof. Love spreads to everything associated with the beloved, even people or things that would otherwise seem unremarkable.
安步当车	ān bù dàng chē	to walk calmly in place of riding: to be content with a simple, unhurried life — Lit: walk at ease, treat it as a carriage. Here 当 takes the dàng reading, "to treat as." From a Warring-States anecdote: to stroll on foot and reckon it as good as riding, content without luxury.
安居乐业	ān jū lè yè	to live in peace and be content in one's work: a settled, secure life — Lit: peaceful-dwelling, joyful-work. 安居 is to live securely, 乐业 to take pleasure in one's occupation. The classic image of social well-being: a people housed, employed, and at ease. Often invoked as the aim of good governance.
按部就班	àn bù jiù bān	to follow the proper sequence: to do things step by step in due order — Lit: according-to-section, settle-into-rank. Originally a writer's image of arranging material into its right divisions and lines; now it means to proceed methodically by the established order, neither rushing nor skipping steps. Here 部 keeps its old sense of an ordered division.
傲慢无礼	ào màn wú lǐ	arrogant and rude; haughty and without manners — Lit: arrogant-rude-without-courtesy. The social-failure sense of 慢 crystallized into a four-character indictment.
八仙过海，各显神通	bā xiān guò hǎi , gè xiǎn shén tōng	"the Eight Immortals cross the sea, each showing their powers" — everyone uses their own talents — The Eight Immortals, crossing the sea, each rely on a different magical skill rather than a single method. The saying describes a group facing a shared task in which every member contributes through their own distinct ability, and is used to praise resourceful, varied teamwork.
把握时机	bǎ wò shí jī	to seize the moment; to grasp the opportunity at the right time — 把握 bǎwò (grip; certainty; grasp) + 时机 shíjī (the right moment). A common exhortation in business, speech, and motivational contexts. Also used as a noun: 有把握 yǒu bǎwò = "to be confident, certain" (lit. to have a grip on it). 没有把握 = "not sure, not confident."
白发苍苍	bái fà cāng cāng	hair gone hoary white: aged, in advanced old age — Lit: white-hair-grey-grey. A vivid picture of a head of grizzled white hair, used affectionately or respectfully of the elderly. Again the fà reading, since the phrase is literally about hair.
百发百中	bǎi fā bǎi zhòng	a hundred shots, a hundred hits — unerring accuracy — 百 (hundred) + 发 fā (to shoot, release) + 百 + 中 zhòng (to hit the mark). A perfect score: every arrow finds its target. From archery contexts in the Warring States period, now applied to any domain where one's predictions, arguments, or shots unfailingly land.
百感交集	bǎi gǎn jiāo jí	a hundred feelings converging — a complex rush of mixed emotions all at once — Lit: hundred-feelings-intersect-gather. For when emotions are too tangled and complex to name individually. 百 = figurative "many."
百家争鸣	bǎi jiā zhēng míng	a hundred schools contend — free intellectual debate; a golden age of ideas — Lit: "hundred schools contend and cry out." The standard Chinese phrase for the Warring States philosophical explosion. Still used today for any period of open intellectual competition.
百闻不如一见	bǎi wén bù rú yī jiàn	hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once — From the Han Shu (Book of Han), attributed to general Zhao Chongguo (赵充国), who when asked by Emperor Xuan to estimate how many troops would be needed for a campaign said: "Hearing about a situation a hundred times is not as good as seeing it once.
百折不挠	bǎi zhé bù náo	unbowed after a hundred setbacks — perseverance through repeated failure — 百 (hundred) + 折 zhé (to break, to bend; a setback) + 不 (not) + 挠 náo (to scratch; to give way, to yield). Literally: a hundred snappings, yet never yielding. The material image is bamboo or a sword repeatedly bent but not permanently deformed.
败坏门风	bài huài mén fēng	to ruin the family's good name: to disgrace one's household — 败坏 (to corrupt, ruin) acting on 门风, a family's reputation and moral tradition. Said of conduct shameful enough to stain the whole family, a phrase out of old domestic and clan morality.
班门弄斧	bān mén nòng fǔ	Showing Off Before the Master — Brandishing an axe at Lu Ban's door: the idiom for presuming to display skill before someone who has mastered it.
半部论语治天下	bàn bù Lún yǔ zhì tiān xià	half the Analects suffices to govern all under heaven — the centrality of the classics in governance — Attributed to the Song statesman 赵普 Zhào Pǔ, who supposedly told an emperor that he governed with only half his knowledge of the Analects and had the other half in reserve.
半懂不懂	bàn dǒng bù dǒng	half understanding, half not: imperfectly grasped — A colloquial set phrase built on the 半A不A frame (half-A, not-A). It marks shaky comprehension, the state of catching the gist of a lecture or a foreign language without truly mastering it.
半斤八两	bàn jīn bā liǎng	"half a catty, eight taels" — six of one, half a dozen of the other; much the same — Under the old measure of sixteen 两 to a 斤, half a catty was exactly eight taels: 半斤 and 八两 are the identical weight. The idiom says two things or two people are essentially the same despite appearing different, usually with a hint that neither is impressive.
半途而废	bàn tú ér fèi	to give up halfway: to abandon a task before it is finished — Lit: half-road-and-quit. 而 links the halfway point to the giving-up that follows. Said in reproach of someone who starts strong but lacks the resolve to see a thing through.
半信半疑	bàn xìn bàn yí	half believing, half doubting — skeptical; not fully convinced — 半 bàn (half) + 信 xìn (to believe; to trust) + 半 bàn (half) + 疑 yí (to doubt; to suspect). The state of being precisely between trust and doubt: believing something enough to entertain it, doubting it enough not to act on it. 我对他说的话半信半疑 = I'm not sure whether to believe what he said.
绑票勒索	bǎng piào lè suǒ	to kidnap and extort: to seize a hostage and demand ransom — 绑 bǎng = to tie up; to bind. 票 piào = here, a kidnapped person held for ransom (the slang 肉票 ròupiào, a human "ticket" to be cashed in). 勒索 lèsuǒ = to extort; to blackmail. A four-character description, not a classical chéngyǔ, but a fixed legal and news expression for kidnapping for ransom.
饱经风霜	bǎo jīng fēng shuāng	to have weathered wind and frost: hardened by hardship — 饱 here means having had a full share of something. The image is a face lined by years of exposure; used of people who have lived through long adversity. Common in literary and journalistic prose.
饱食终日	bǎo shí zhōng rì	to eat one's fill all day: to idle in comfort — From the Analects (论语), where Confucius reproaches those who eat their fill the whole day and apply their minds to nothing. A pointed criticism of idleness; carries a moral edge.
饱学之士	bǎo xu é zhī shì	a scholar full of learning: an erudite person — 饱 extends from a full stomach to a full mind. 饱学 means saturated with learning; a respectful term for a deeply read scholar. Formal register.
饱以老拳	bǎo yǐ lǎo quán	to treat to a full helping of fists: to give a sound beating — A grim joke on the eating sense: instead of a meal, the recipient gets a generous serving of punches. From the Jìn Shū (晋书). Vivid and slightly humorous in tone.
保家卫国	bǎo jiā wèi guó	"defend the family, guard the country" — patriotic sacrifice — 保家 (protect the family) + 卫国 (defend the country). The phrase that encodes the family-state bond as a call to military service: you fight for the country by fighting for your family; you fight for your family by defending the country.
报仇雪恨	bào chóu xu ě hèn	avenge a wrong and wipe out a grudge — 报仇 (take revenge) paired with 雪恨 (wash away the hatred). The standard four-character phrase for settling a blood debt, frequent in martial-arts fiction and historical drama.
暴风骤雨	bào fēng zhòu yǔ	violent wind and sudden rain — a sudden, overwhelming storm of events — Lit: violent-wind-sudden-rain. 暴 means violent, sudden, savage; 骤 means abrupt, arriving all at once. The idiom describes any sudden, overwhelming onslaught: a torrential crisis, a savage attack, a rapid political upheaval.
悲欢离合	bēi huān lí hé	sorrows and joys, partings and reunions — Literally "grief, joy, parting, union", the full arc of human fortune in four characters. 离 (parting) and 合 (reunion) form the pair at its heart, the comings and goings of a life. From a famous Song lyric by Su Shi on the moon and human separation.
北风怒号	běi fēng nù háo	"the north wind howls in fury" — biting cold; adversity — 北风 (north wind) + 怒 (furious) + 号 (to howl). A classical weather image used in poetry and prose to evoke bitter cold and desolation. Du Fu's famous poem 茅屋为秋风所破歌 uses the howling north wind as a metaphor for the hardships of his refugee years during the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763 CE).
本来面目	běn lái miàn mù	original face: a thing's true, unaltered nature — Lit: original-face-and-features. A Chan Buddhist phrase for one's true self before all conditioning, now used broadly for the real character of anything once the disguises are stripped away.
本末倒置	běn mò dào zhì	to put root and tip in the wrong order: to mistake the essential for the trivial — Lit: root-tip-upside-down. 本 (the root) and 末 (the branch-tips) are the two ends of the tree. To reverse them is to spend effort on the minor while neglecting what truly matters.
逼上梁山	bī shàng liáng shān	forced up Mount Liang — driven to a desperate course — From the heroes' repeated path of being pushed by injustice until they have no refuge but the outlaw stronghold of Liangshan. The chengyu now means being driven by circumstance to take a drastic step one would never have chosen freely, the very pattern by which the novel's decent men become rebels.
笔走龙蛇	bǐ zǒu lóng shé	the brush moves like dragons and snakes: bold, flowing, vigorous calligraphy — Lit: brush-runs-dragon-snake. The line of cursive writing twists and surges with the energy of a dragon and a snake in motion. High praise for a calligrapher whose hand is alive and free.
必由之路	bì yóu zhī lù	the road one must take; the only viable path forward — 必 (must) + 由 yóu (to pass through; to travel by way of) + 之路 (the road). The path through which one must pass, with no alternative route. Used when describing the single viable way forward in a difficult situation: 改革是必由之路 (Reform is the only path forward).
鞭长莫及	biān cháng mò jí	the whip is long but cannot reach — distance defeats even great strength or authority — Lit: whip-long-cannot-reach. From the Zuǒzhuàn (左传), a Spring and Autumn period chronicle. A ruler may have power, but he cannot govern what is too distant from him.
变本加厉	biàn běn jiā lì	to alter the base and pile on more: to grow worse than before, to intensify — Lit: change-base-add-severity. Said when behavior that was already bad escalates rather than improving, the original measure exceeded and then redoubled.
变化莫测	biàn huà mò cè	change beyond prediction — unpredictable; mercurial; always surprising — 莫 mò = no one can; impossible to. 测 cè = measure; fathom; predict. Lit: "the changes cannot be measured." Used to describe weather, markets, political situations, and people whose behavior cannot be anticipated.
辨方正位	biàn fāng zhèng wèi	"to discern direction and rectify position" — to orient oneself correctly before acting — From the Zhouli (周礼). The phrase belongs to the rituals of city-founding and palace-construction: before laying the foundations, the official must determine the cardinal directions and align the building correctly. By extension, in any major undertaking, one must first establish one's bearings.
彪形大汉	biāo xíng dà hàn	a burly, powerfully built man — Lit: tiger-bodied big fellow. 彪 (a young tiger) lends its image of muscular bulk, so the phrase paints a tall, broad, imposing man, the bodyguard or strongman of a scene.
表里如一	biǎo lǐ rú yī	outside and inside are as one: consistent in word and deed; the same within as without — 表 biǎo = the outside, the surface. 里 lǐ = the inside, the interior. 如一 rú yī = as if one; identical. A person whose outward conduct matches their inner thoughts, who is honest and undivided, with no gap between the surface they show and the substance underneath. A strong compliment to integrity.
别馆离宫	bié guǎn lí gōng	separate lodges and detached palaces: the same scattered residences, with the lodge named first — The attested inversion of 离宫别馆, listed as its own form in idiom dictionaries. Putting 馆 first foregrounds the lodging over the palace.
宾朋满座	bīn péng mǎn zuò	guests and friends fill the seats: a house full of company — Lit: guests-friends fill the seats. 宾朋 pairs guest with friend; the image is a hall packed with visitors. Close kin to 高朋满座, used of a lively, well-attended occasion where every seat is taken.
彬彬有礼	bīn bīn yǒu lǐ	refined and courteous in bearing; gracefully well-mannered — From the Lúnyǔ (论语·雍也): 文质彬彬，然后君子 ("when refinement and substance are in balance , only then is one a 君子"). 彬彬 bīn bīn names the quality of refined balance , neither rough nor showy.
冰天雪地	bīng tiān xu ě dì	ice in the sky, snow on the ground — a frozen, bitterly cold world — 冰 bīng (ice) + 天 tiān (sky) + 雪 xuě (snow) + 地 dì (ground). A vivid set phrase for a landscape locked in deep winter, ice above and snow below, everything frozen. Used to describe the far north, high mountains, or any scene of extreme cold. 探险队在冰天雪地里走了好几天。
兵临城下	bīng lín chéng xià	troops at the foot of the wall: the enemy at the gates — 兵 bīng = soldiers, troops; 临 lín = to arrive at, to overlook; 城下 = below the city wall. The enemy army has reached the base of the wall, the last moment before a siege becomes an assault.
兵马俑	bīng mǎ yǒng	soldier-and-horse figures — the terracotta army — The name breaks down as 兵 bīng (soldiers) + 马 mǎ (horses) + 俑 yǒng (tomb figures, funerary effigies). The key word is 俑: a sculpted human or animal figure made specifically to be buried with the dead in place of living sacrifices.
兵无常势，水无常形。	bīng wú cháng shì , shuǐ wú cháng xíng .	An army has no fixed configuration, as water has no fixed shape. — Sunzi's image for strategic adaptability, strikingly close to the water imagery of the Daodejing.
兵者，诡道也。	bīng zhě , guǐ dào yě .	Warfare is the way of deception. — A blunt rejection of chivalric ideals: success in conflict depends on shaping the enemy's perceptions, concealing one's own strength and intentions, and striking where one is not expected.
病急乱投医	bìng jí luàn tóu yī	when the illness is desperate, one runs to any doctor — A proverb rather than a classical chengyu: desperation abandons judgment. Used far beyond medicine, for panicked job hunts, failing companies grasping at consultants, or students trying every cram school at once. The tone is sympathetic but critical; the flailing rarely works.
病入膏肓	bìng rù gāo huāng	the illness has entered the vitals: beyond cure — From the Zuǒ Zhuàn: a duke dreams the disease hides in the 膏肓, the region between heart and diaphragm that no needle or medicine can reach. Used today for any situation, not only medical, that has decayed past saving.
博爱	bó ài	universal love; philanthropy — broad, impartial love for all — 博 bó = broad, extensive. Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles include 博爱 as a founding ideal. Also the Chinese word for philanthropy and humanitarian love. Related to the Mohist concept of 兼爱.
博采众长	bó cǎi zhòng cháng	"broadly gather the strengths of many" — to learn from many sources — 博 (broad) + 采 (to gather, to select) + 众 (many, the crowd) + 长 (strengths, advantages). A virtue in learning: drawing on the best from many teachers and traditions rather than following a single school. Used for scholarship, artistic development, and leadership style.
博大精深	bó dà jīng shēn	"broad, great, refined, and deep" — vast and profound — 博 (broad) + 大 (great) + 精 (refined, essential) + 深 (deep). The standard four-character formula for describing Chinese culture in formal contexts: 中华文化博大精深 is a set phrase appearing in textbooks, official speeches, and tourist literature.
博闻强记	bó wén qiáng jì	widely read and retentive: of broad learning and a powerful memory — Lit: broad-hearing-strong-memory. Praise for a person who has read and heard much and remembers it all. Also written 博闻强识, with 识 read zhì in the sense of "to retain."
不耻下问	bù chǐ xià wèn	"not ashamed to ask those below" — intellectual humility; willingness to learn from anyone regardless of status — From the 论语 (Analects) , Confucius praising the minister Kong Wenzi: 敏而好学，不耻下问，是以谓之'文'也 (Quick-minded and fond of learning, not ashamed to ask those of lower rank , this is why he was given the posthumous title 'Wen').
不到长城非好汉	bú dào cháng chéng fēi hǎo hàn	"he who has not reached the Great Wall is not a true hero" — From Mao Zedong's 1935 poem 清平乐·六盘山. Not technically a 成语 (it is seven characters), but functions as a fixed quotation. Often paired in modern usage with 越长城: to "cross the wall" is to prove oneself. The verb implied is 越 (to cross over) or 到 (to reach).
不分青红皂白	bù fēn qīng hóng zào bái	without distinguishing the colors — to act heedlessly, without regard for right and wrong — 不分 bù fēn (not distinguishing) + 青红皂白 (blue, red, black, white). 皂 zào is an old word for black. To plunge into action without bothering to tell the colors apart, that is, without finding out who is actually at fault. 他不分青红皂白就把孩子骂了一顿。
不欢而散	bù huān ér sàn	to part on bad terms: to break up unhappily, the gathering souring — Lit: not-joyful-and-scatter. The mirror image of the joyful idioms: a meeting or meal that ends in discord, everyone leaving displeased. 两人话不投机，不欢而散 "the two could not agree, and parted on bad terms."
不慌不忙	bù huāng bù máng	neither panicked nor rushed — composed and unhurried — Lit: not-panic-not-hurry. Does not contain 慢 but is its most important semantic companion. Where 慢 can carry a negative charge (negligence, arrogance), 不慌不忙 frames the same unhurriedness as mastery: the person who is slow because they are in control, not because they are lazy or contemptuous.
不计其数	bú jì qí shù	countless; too many to count — Literally "not to reckon their number," so many that counting is hopeless. Used for vast, uncountable quantities, the far end of the scale that 多少 stretches toward. The answer to 多少 when the true reply is "beyond counting."
不教而诛	bú jiào ér zhū	to punish without having taught: to penalize people never instructed in the rule — Lit: not-teach-yet-punish. From the Analects, a criticism of the ruler who punishes failings the people were never taught to avoid. To hold someone to a standard you never showed them.
不解之缘	bù jiě zhī yuán	a bond that cannot be untied: an indissoluble tie — Lit: a connection 缘 that cannot 不 be untied 解. An unbreakable bond or lifelong affinity, often with a person, a place, or a pursuit. 他和音乐结下了不解之缘 = he formed a lifelong bond with music. Here 解 is "to untie," and the negation makes the tie permanent.
不紧不慢	bù jǐn bù màn	neither tight nor slow: unhurried, even-paced — A steady, measured tempo with no rush and no dawdling. Often admiring, describing someone who keeps composure under pressure.
不胫而走	bù jìng ér zǒu	"to travel without legs" — (of news) to spread rapidly on its own — A classical chengyu (using 走 in its classical "to run" sense, before 跑 took over). 胫 jìng = the lower leg; the image is of news that has no legs but somehow runs everywhere by itself. Used today for rumors, viral information, and news that spreads without effort.
不可估量	bù kě gū liàng	cannot be estimated: immeasurable, beyond reckoning — 不可 bù kě (cannot) + 估 gū (to estimate) + 量 liàng (to measure, to gauge). So vast or so consequential that no estimate can capture it. Used for losses, impact, or value too large to quantify: 损失不可估量 (the losses are immeasurable), 意义不可估量 (the significance is beyond reckoning).
不可思议	bù kě sī yì	inconceivable; unimaginable — Literally "cannot be thought or discussed," beyond comprehension, originally a Buddhist term for the ineffable. Here 可 ("can / possible"), the first character of 可能, takes its sense of "able to be": what cannot possibly be grasped by thought.
不可一世	bù kě yī shì	insufferably arrogant: to think no one in the whole age is one's equal — Lit: cannot be matched by anyone of the age. Said of someone so overweeningly proud that they look down on everyone alive, behaving as though the entire era holds no rival worthy of them. Strongly critical in tone.
不了了之	bù liǎo liǎo zhī	to let a matter fade away unresolved; to end without proper conclusion — Lit: not-conclude-conclude-it. Uses 了 liǎo as a verb twice , "to not conclude [a matter], to conclude [it anyway]." A set phrase for when a problem or investigation is allowed to dissolve without resolution , bureaucratic negligence, diplomatic evasion, quiet abandonment. 这件事就这样不了了之了。
不立文字	bù lì wén zì	not relying on written words — the foundational Chan stance on language — One of the four Chan axioms: 教外别传，不立文字，直指人心，见性成佛 , "Special transmission outside the scriptures; not relying on written words; directly pointing to the human mind; seeing the nature, becoming Buddha." 不立文字 does not mean Chan rejected literacy , monks studied extensively.
不谋而合	bù móu ér hé	to agree without prior consultation: to coincide spontaneously — Lit: without-conferring yet-agree. Said when two people arrive at the same view or plan independently, their thoughts fitting together though they never discussed it.
不求甚解	bù qiú shèn jiě	not seeking deep understanding — reading for pleasure, not to dissect — From Tao Yuanming's self-portrait Mr. Five Willows (五柳先生传): 好读书，不求甚解 "He loved to read, but did not press for fine-grained interpretation." The classical defense of reading widely and lightly rather than scholastically.
不容置疑	bù róng zhì yí	leaving no room for doubt: beyond question; indisputable — 不容 = leaves no room for; 置疑 = to cast doubt. A fact or conclusion so certain that no doubt can be entertained. The same 不容 pattern as 义不容辞: there is simply no space for the doubt to enter. 这个事实不容置疑。(This fact is beyond dispute.)
不三不四	bù sān bù sì	neither one thing nor another — shady, dubious, not upright — Lit: not-three not-four. Three and four are "middle" numbers: something that is neither here nor there, neither proper nor improper. Used for shady people or behavior that doesn't conform to standards.
不忘初心	bù wàng chū xīn	never forget the original aspiration — keep faith with founding ideals — A phrase with pre-revolutionary Buddhist origins (初心 = the first aspiration toward enlightenment) now central to Xi Jinping-era CCP rhetoric. Used in the context of the Cultural Revolution to mean: remember what the revolution was supposed to achieve, and do not let it be corrupted.
不违农时	bù wéi nóng shí	do not violate the farming seasons: act in step with the right time — From the Mencius (孟子). The ruler who does not drag farmers off to other work during planting and harvest will have grain enough to feed the realm. Now a general caution against wrong timing.
不闻不问	bù wén bù wèn	neither hear nor ask: to pay no attention to a matter at all — Lit: not-hear-not-ask. To stay wholly indifferent, neither listening for news nor inquiring after it. Often a reproach for someone who ignores what should concern them.
不言而喻	bù yán ér yù	without words, it is understood — self-evident; goes without saying — Lit: not-speak-yet-understand. What goes without saying: a truth so obvious that to speak it would be redundant. Contrasts with the power attributed to 语 elsewhere: here, the deepest understanding transcends the need for words.
不要脸	bú yào liǎn	to want no face: shameless, brazen — Not a classical four-character chengyu but a fixed colloquial phrase: to want no face is to discard all sense of shame. A sharp insult, stronger than it looks in English.
不翼而飞	bù yì ér fēi	to fly off without wings: to vanish suddenly — Used of objects that disappear inexplicably, as if something with no wings had taken to the air. Also of news that spreads everywhere overnight.
不约而同	bù yu ē ér tóng	to agree without prior arrangement: to coincide as if by plan — Lit: not-agreed-yet-alike. Without having arranged it (不约), people 而 nonetheless act alike (同). Used when several act or think the same way by sheer coincidence.
不着边际	bù zháo biān jì	wide of the mark; irrelevant; rambling without getting to the point — 不 + 着 zháo (achieve, land) + 边际 (edge, boundary). Literally "not landing on any boundary" , the talk or argument fails to touch the relevant point. Said of speech, writing, or proposals that circle around without engaging the actual issue.
不知所措	bù zhī suǒ cuò	at a loss what to do — Literally "not knowing what to set one's hands to", thrown into confusion and unable to act. It is the inner state behind a panicked 怎么办, the moment when you cannot even begin to choose a course of action.
部署周密	bù shǔ zhōu mì	deployed with careful thoroughness: arranged in close and complete order — 部署 bùshǔ is to lay out forces or tasks in their assigned positions, the military sense of 部; 周密 zhōumì means thorough and tightly planned. Said of a plan or operation set up with every detail in place.
才华横溢	cái huá héng yì	talent brimming over: overflowing with brilliance — Lit: talent-brilliance-spilling-overflowing. 才华 is creative or literary brilliance, and 横溢 paints it as water flooding past its banks. Said of someone whose gifts are too abundant to contain.
才能出众	cái néng chū zhòng	outstandingly talented — ability that stands above the crowd — 才能 cáinéng (talent and ability) + 出众 chūzhòng (to stand out from the crowd). 能 here combines with 才 (talent, capacity) to form the compound 才能. Used in recommendations, eulogies, and formal praise. 她才能出众，前途无量 "Her talents are exceptional; her future is limitless."
才思敏捷	cái sī mǐn jié	quick-witted; rapid and agile in thought and creative expression — 才思 cáisī = literary talent and flow of ideas (才 here is the noun "talent," not the adverb). 敏捷 = swift and agile. A high compliment for writers, poets, and scholars who produce brilliant work quickly.
沧海桑田	cāng hǎi sāng tiān	the blue sea becomes mulberry fields — dramatic change over time; the world transformed beyond recognition — From a Daoist tale recorded in 神仙传 (Biographies of Immortals, attributed to Ge Hong, 4th century CE): the immortal Magu tells of having seen the eastern sea turn to mulberry fields three times. 沧海 cānghǎi = the dark blue sea (沧 = cold, dark; vast).
操之过急	cāo zhī guò jí	to act on it too hastily: to rush a matter — A gentle warning that someone moved too fast and forced a result before its time. Often used to advise patience: 这件事不能操之过急 (don't rush this).
草草了事	cǎo cǎo liǎo shì	to finish a matter hastily and carelessly — The doubled 草草 means hurriedly and roughly, borrowing the haste of fast-growing grass. To 草草了事 is to wrap something up sloppily just to be rid of it, the opposite of thorough work.
草菅人命	cǎo jiān rén mìng	to treat human life as cheap as grass: to kill or harm people without regard — From the Hanshu account of Jia Yi. 菅 jiān is a coarse wild grass; to regard a person's life as no more than a weed is to be utterly callous about killing. Used of tyrants and reckless rulers.
草木皆兵	cǎo mù jiē bīng	grass and trees all look like soldiers: to be so jumpy that every shadow seems a threat — From the Battle of Fei River (淝水之战, 383 CE) in the Jin Shu: the routed Former Qin emperor Fú Jiān, in panic, mistook the grass and trees on Mount Bagong for enemy troops. Now describes nervous, paranoid fear that sees danger everywhere.
恻隐之心，人皆有之。	cè yǐn zhī xīn , rén jiē yǒu zhī .	The heart of compassion — every person has it. — Mencius 6A:6. The full passage lists all four hearts (恻隐、羞恶、恭敬、是非之心) and asserts that all four are universal: "every person has them." This is the foundation of the 性善论 argument: if the moral emotions are universal, they are innate, not learned.
茶馆酒肆	chá guǎn jiǔ sì	teahouses and wine-shops: the everyday public houses of a town — A four-character set phrase pairing 茶馆 with 酒肆 (the wine-shop) to stand for the street-level places where ordinary people gathered, drank, and talked.
察言观色	chá yán guān sè	to weigh words and read faces: to gauge a person's mood and intent — Lit: examine-words-observe-expression. The skill of watching what someone says and how they look in order to sense their true feelings, a prized social sensitivity in Chinese life.
唱独角戏	chàng dú jiǎo xì	to sing a one-man show: to carry the whole thing alone — From opera, where a 独角戏 is a one-actor play. Used when someone is left doing all the talking or all the work while no one else joins in.
朝令夕改	zhāo lìng xī gǎi	issue an order at dawn and change it by dusk — From debates on Han fiscal policy. A sharp criticism of fickle, unstable rule whose constant reversals leave people unable to plan.
朝气蓬勃	zhāo qì péng bó	full of youthful vigor: brimming with life and energy — Lit: morning-vigor, luxuriant-thriving. 朝气 is the spirit of a new day, 蓬勃 the look of growth in full flush. Said of people, teams, or whole societies that are young and full of drive.
朝秦暮楚	zhāo Qín mù Chǔ	Qin in the morning, Chu at night — serving different masters; inconsistency and opportunism — From the reality of Warring States advisors who moved between states as circumstances changed. The phrase originally described border regions whose allegiance shifted with the military tide. Now a common idiom for fickleness, opportunism, or having no fixed loyalties.
朝三暮四	zhāo sān mù sì	three in the morning, four at dusk: fickle, forever changing one's mind — From a fable in which a keeper offers his monkeys three nuts in the morning and four at night; they protest, so he swaps it to four and three, and they are content though the total is the same. Now it names someone fickle, who keeps switching with no real difference.
朝思暮想	zhāo sī mù xiǎng	to think of morning and night; to long for ceaselessly — 朝 zhāo (morning; dawn) + 思 sī (to think of; to long for) + 暮 mù (dusk; evening) + 想 xiǎng (to think of; to miss). Thinking at dawn and thinking at dusk: longing that fills the entire arc of a day. Used for intense, sustained yearning: romantic longing, homesickness, or grief for the absent.
尘埃落定	chén āi luò dìng	the dust has settled; a situation has finally reached resolution — Lit: dust-settle-fixed. Evokes the moment after turmoil when everything finally comes to rest and the outcome is clear. Title of Alai's celebrated Tibetan novel.
沉鱼落雁	chén yú luò yàn	"sinking fish and falling geese" — describing a woman so beautiful that fish dive and birds fall when she passes — From the Zhuangzi, originally a wry critique of relativism in beauty (the fish do not actually find her beautiful , they hide because they are afraid of humans).
趁热打铁	chèn rè dǎ tiě	strike the iron while it's hot: seize the moment — 趁 while, 热 hot, 打铁 to forge iron. The blacksmith's wisdom, identical to the English proverb. Used to urge acting on momentum before it cools.
称心如意	chèn xīn rú yì	to suit the heart and match the wish: perfectly satisfactory — Lit: fitting-the-heart-as-the-wish. Everything turning out exactly as one hoped, in feeling and in fact alike. A warm phrase for contentment, and a common blessing for someone's plans or new beginnings.
成家立业	chéng jiā lì yè	start a family and establish a career — the two milestones of adult life — 立业 = to establish one's career or livelihood. The traditional sequence of adult life goals: first you build a home; then you build a livelihood. 他终于成家立业了。(He has finally started a family and established himself.) The phrase encodes a whole theory of the proper human life cycle.
成千上万	chéng qiān shàng wàn	thousands upon thousands: a vast, countless number — Lit: amounting-to-thousands-up-to-ten-thousands. A vivid way to say a great many, used of crowds, stars, raindrops, anything too numerous to count. Here 成 carries the sense of reaching a quantity.
成群结队	chéng qún jié duì	to form crowds and bands: in droves, in flocks — The most common 队 idiom in daily speech. Pictures people or animals gathering thick enough to clump into groups and lines. Used for crowds streaming somewhere: 游客成群结队地涌入古镇.
成也萧何，败也萧何	chéng yě Xiāo Hé , bài yě Xiāo Hé	rise by Xiao He, fall by Xiao He — the same hand that made you can unmake you — Xiao He recommended Han Xin for command (making him); later lured Han Xin into the trap that got him executed (destroying him). Now: a person or factor that is simultaneously the source of your rise and your ruin. Often used in business for a single decision or relationship that cuts both ways.
承前启后	chéng qián qǐ hòu	carry on the past and open the way for the future — To inherit what came before and pass it on, serving as the bridge between earlier and later generations, a 代 to 代 handing-on. Said of a person, work, or era that links what preceded it to what follows, the connective role between ages.
城隍爷	Chéng huáng yé	City God (respectful address) — The suffix 爷 yé is an honorific for senior male figures, divine and human: 土地爷, 老天爷. It conveys respectful familiarity rather than formal distance. Worshippers address the City God as 城隍爷 in prayer and casual speech; formal temple documents may use the full title with rank designation.
吃喝玩乐	chī hē wán lè	eat, drink, play, be merry: a life of indulgence — Four verbs of pleasure strung together, with 喝 as the drinking. Usually mildly disapproving, said of someone who does nothing but enjoy themselves.
吃苦耐劳	chī kǔ nài láo	to endure hardship and persevere in labor — a core work-ethic virtue — The defining work-ethic phrase in Chinese culture. Applied to individuals, generations, and national character. Eating bitterness + tolerating labor = the formula for achievement.
吃亏是福	chī kuī shì fú	suffering loss is a blessing — short-term disadvantage leads to long-term benefit — A proverb attributed to Zheng Banqiao (Qing dynasty). The Daoist-inflected wisdom: accepting being at a disadvantage cultivates humility and patience, which eventually bring greater good. Widely quoted in Chinese business and parenting contexts.
充耳不闻	chōng ěr bù wén	"stuff the ear and not hear" — deliberately ignoring what is said — 充 (to fill, to stuff) + 耳 (ear) + 不闻 (not listening). Plugging the ear on purpose , willful deafness to advice, complaint, or truth. From the Shijing (詩經, Classic of Poetry): the earliest citation describes a ruler who stopped his ears to his ministers' counsel.
愁眉苦脸	chóu méi kǔ liǎn	knitted brows and a bitter face: a picture of gloom and worry — 愁 (worry) eyebrows over a 苦 (bitter) face. The whole head sags with anxiety. A vivid, everyday way to say someone looks miserable.
出乎意料	chū hū yì liào	to come out beyond expectation: contrary to what anyone anticipated — Lit: come-out-of-reckoning. 意料 is what the mind reckons in advance; to fall 出乎意料 is to land outside it. Its mirror is 不出所料, "just as expected."
出类拔萃	chū lèi bá cuì	to stand out from the class and rise above the finest — exceptional; head and shoulders above — From Mencius (孟子): 出于其类，拔乎其萃. 类 lèi = category; type; peers. 拔 bá = to pull up; to surpass. 萃 cuì = the finest, the gathered best. To emerge beyond one's category and surpass even the finest specimens within it. Classical Confucian praise for moral and intellectual excellence.
出其不意	chū qí bù yì	emerge from its unexpectedness — to catch someone off guard; to act when least expected — 出 chū (emerge; go out) + 其 qí (their; its) + 不意 bù yì (not anticipated; unexpected).
出其不意，攻其无备。	chū qí bù yì , gōng qí wú bèi .	Emerge where unexpected; attack where unprepared. — From the first chapter, now the standard chengyu 出其不意 ("catch off guard"). The principle is to direct one's effort at the point and moment the opponent has not anticipated and cannot defend, turning surprise itself into a decisive advantage.
出奇制胜	chū qí zhì shèng	to achieve victory through surprise — to win by doing the unexpected — 出奇 = to deploy the unusual, to emerge with something unexpected. 制胜 = to achieve victory; to control the outcome.
出人意料	chū rén yì liào	"beyond people's expectation" — unexpected; surprising; contrary to what was anticipated — Lit: exceed-people-intention-anticipate. One of the most common ways to say "surprisingly" or "unexpectedly" in formal Chinese. 这个结果出人意料，没有人预测到。"This result was unexpected , no one had predicted it." Also appears in the variant 出乎意料 chū hū yìliào with identical meaning.
出神入化	chū shén rù huà	to leave the mundane and enter the magical: superb; consummate; masterly — 出 chū = to leave, 神 shén = the divine, 入 rù = to enter, 化 huà = the transformed, transcendent state.
除旧布新	chú jiù bù xīn	"remove the old, spread the new" — ritual clearing and renewal — 除 (chú, to remove, to clear away) + 旧 (old) + 布 (bù, to spread, to lay out) + 新 (new). The ritual logic of the Spring Festival: the house is swept, old paper charms are replaced with new ones, debts are settled, quarrels patched over.
穿针引线	chuān zhēn yǐn xiàn	thread the needle and lead the thread: to act as go-between — Literally the seamstress's first move. Figuratively, to broker a connection between two parties, matchmaking a deal, a marriage, a meeting.
传宗接代	chuán zōng jiē dài	to carry on the family line: to continue the ancestral lineage through descendants — Lit: pass on the clan, link the generations. The traditional duty of producing heirs so that the family line does not end. 宗 is the ancestral lineage and 代 the generations; 传 and 接 are the passing-on and the picking-up that keep the chain unbroken.
船坚炮利	chuán jiān pào lì	sturdy ships and sharp guns: overwhelming naval and military might — A late-Qing phrase for the foreign gunboats whose strength forced the treaty ports open. Now shorthand for raw technological force.
闯南走北	chuǎng nán zǒu běi	"boldly moving through south and north" — widely traveled; experienced in the world — 闯 (to push through boldly) + 南 (south) + 走 (to travel) + 北 (north). A person who has made their way through the whole country, acquiring experience and resilience. The verb 闯 suggests the travel was not comfortable or planned but forced through obstacles.
春风得意	chūn fēng dé yì	riding the spring wind, full of pride: flush with success — From Mèng Jiāo's Tang poem on passing the imperial exam. Describes someone on a winning streak, often with a hint that the pride may be premature.
春暖花开	chūn nuǎn huā kāi	spring is warm and flowers bloom: the good season has come — The stock image of spring at its best. Used literally for the season and figuratively for the right moment, a turn for the better after hardship.
词不达意	cí bù dá yì	the words fail to convey the meaning: to express oneself poorly — Lit: words-not-reach-meaning. Said when the language a speaker or writer chooses does not match what they meant, so the point comes across muddled or wrong. A common way to apologize for an unclear remark.
此心光明，亦复何言	cǐ xīn guāng míng , yì fù hé yán	this mind is bright and clear — what more is there to say? — Wang Yangming's last words, spoken on his deathbed in 1529 when a student asked if he had any final instructions. His response , that his mind was luminous (光明 guāngmíng), and that this was sufficient , encapsulates his entire philosophy.
从容不迫	cóng róng bù pò	calm and unhurried: composed under pressure — 从容 = calm, leisurely; 不迫 = not pressed, not rushed. To act with poise and no sign of haste even when stakes are high. Here 容 sits in 从容, the word for unflustered composure: someone with room inside to spare. 他从容不迫地回答了所有问题。(He answered every question calmly and without haste.)
存天理，灭人欲	cún tiān lǐ , miè rén yù	preserve Heavenly Principle, eliminate human desire — Zhu Xi's formulation of moral cultivation — Perhaps the most quoted and most criticized phrase in Neo-Confucianism. 天理 tiānlǐ = Heavenly Principle (the universal moral norm); 人欲 rén yù = human desires (not all desires but those that conflict with Heavenly Principle: excessive appetite, selfishness).
错综复杂	cuò zōng fù zá	crisscrossed and tangled: intricate and complicated — Lit: interlaced-gathered-doubled-mixed. Keeps the "crossing" sense of 错: relationships or situations so interwoven and layered that they are hard to untangle. 错综复杂的关系 "a web of tangled relationships."
答非所问	dá fēi suǒ wèn	the answer is not what was asked: to give a reply beside the question — Lit: answer-not-what-asked. A reply that fails to address the actual question, whether from evasion or misunderstanding. A near neighbor of 文不对题, but about spoken answers rather than written work.
打抱不平	dǎ bào bù píng	to stand up for the wronged; to right injustices — 打 (to strike at) + 抱 (to hold) + 不平 (unfairness). To beat back unfairness, to intervene on behalf of someone being treated unjustly. The righteous stranger who steps in. A heroic frame common in wuxia literature.
打草惊蛇	dǎ cǎo jīng shé	to beat the grass and startle the snake — to tip off the target through careless action — One of the 36 Stratagems (三十六计). The grass is struck and the snake hiding inside is alerted. Used to warn against premature or clumsy action that reveals your intentions and lets the target escape or prepare. Common in military, political, and business contexts.
大材小用	dà cái xiǎo yòng	great timber put to small use — talent wasted on a trivial task — Lit: great-timber small-use. A large structural beam cut down for use as a chopstick. The standard expression for overqualification or talent misallocation. Said politely of others, rarely of oneself. The 小 here measures not the person but the scope of the task assigned to them.
大吃大喝	dà chī dà hē	to eat and drink lavishly: feast extravagantly — The doubled 大 stresses excess. Modern usage often flags wasteful banqueting or living beyond one's means.
大错特错	dà cuò tè cuò	greatly and especially wrong: utterly, completely mistaken — Lit: big-error-particularly-error. An emphatic doubling that drives home how badly someone has misjudged: 你这样想就大错特错了 "if you think that, you are gravely mistaken."
大大方方	dà dà fāng fāng	generous and unaffected; poised and at ease in manner — The reduplicated form of 大方 dàfang (generous; gracious; not stingy or awkward). Said in praise of someone whose bearing is relaxed and dignified rather than petty or self-conscious.
大哥别说二哥	dà gē bié shuō èr gē	the eldest shouldn't mock the second: pot calling the kettle black — A proverb on shared flaws: 大哥 and 二哥 are equally at fault, so neither has standing to criticize the other. The Mandarin take on glass houses.
大公无私	dà gōng wú sī	utterly fair and selfless: putting the common good above all private interest — Lit: great-public-without-private. The highest praise for an official or leader who holds to the public good and lets no personal interest sway the judgment. 公 and 私 stand at the two poles of the phrase.
大功告成	dà gōng gào chéng	the great work is accomplished — mission complete — Lit: great-achievement-announce-accomplished. A formal declaration that a major undertaking (a construction project, a campaign, a long creative work) has been completed. Often used with a tone of proud announcement: 大功告成！(We did it!).
大好河山	dà hǎo hé shān	the great and beautiful rivers and mountains; the magnificent homeland — The near-synonym of 大好江山, using 河山 héshān (Yellow River and mountains) instead of 江山 (Yangtze and mountains). 河 hé specifically refers to the Yellow River , 黄河 Huáng Hé , the cradle of northern Chinese civilization.
大喝一声	dà hè yī shēng	to give a great shout: bellow once, loudly — Here 喝 takes its hè reading, "to shout". A stock phrase in classical fiction and storytelling, the warrior or judge who freezes a room with a single roar.
大江东去	dà jiāng dōng qù	the great river flows east — time and history flow on; the brilliant figures of the past are gone — From Su Shi's 苏轼 famous ci poem "Niannujiao · Red Cliff Nostalgia" (念奴娇·赤壁怀古): 大江东去，浪淘尽，千古风流人物. "The great river flows east; its waves wash away the brilliant figures of a thousand ages." Invoked for historical grandeur and the irreversible passage of time.
大街小巷	dà jiē xiǎo xiàng	big streets and small lanes: everywhere in town — The standard way to say all over the city, every street and back alley. Neutral register, extremely common in news and speech: 大街小巷都挂满了灯笼, lanterns hung all over the streets.
大姐大	dà jiě dà	top sister: a commanding, dominant woman — A colloquial trigram, not a classical idiom, for the female leader of a group or a forceful, authoritative woman. Carries a half-admiring, half-wary tone.
大惊小怪	dà jīng xiǎo guài	to make a big fuss over nothing — overreacting to small things — Lit: big-shock small-wonder. To be shocked and amazed by things that are actually trivial. A mild criticism of someone who overreacts or lacks perspective.
大开眼界	dà kāi yǎn jiè	to greatly open one's horizons — to have one's eyes opened — Lit: greatly-open-eye-boundary. The standard phrase for the experience of suddenly seeing something new and broadening one's outlook. Said after a trip, a museum visit, a striking piece of work.
大快人心	dà kuài rén xīn	greatly satisfying to the people's hearts — a righteous outcome that pleases everyone — Lit: greatly-fast/free-people's-hearts. Used when a wrongdoer receives punishment, a long-overdue verdict is handed down, or a corrupt official is finally removed. The 快 here is squarely in the "heart released from obstruction" sense: justice has cleared away what was blocking everyone.
大闹天宫	dà nào tiān gōng	havoc in Heaven — the Monkey King's great rebellion — The celebrated early episode in which Sun Wukong storms the celestial palace, defeats Heaven's armies, and helps himself to the food and treasures of the gods.
大起大落	dà qǐ dà luò	dramatic rises and falls — extreme volatility and turbulence — Lit: great-rise great-fall. For lives, markets, or dynasties marked by dramatic swings: the roller-coaster image. Common in financial commentary and biographical writing.
大失所望	dà shī suǒ wàng	to be greatly let down: bitterly disappointed in what one had hoped for — Literally "greatly to lose what one hoped for." Used when reality falls far short of expectation and the disappointment is severe, as when an eagerly awaited result turns out badly. The intensified form of plain 失望.
大手大脚	dà shǒu dà jiǎo	big hands and big feet — extravagant; throwing money around — Lit: big-hand-big-foot. Said of someone who spends lavishly without thinking, makes large gestures, lives beyond their means. Mildly disapproving, the opposite of 节俭 jiéjiǎn (frugal).
大义凛然	dà yì lǐn rán	full of the greatest righteousness — awe-inspiring moral authority; unshakeable in the face of evil — 大义 dàyì (the greater righteousness; overriding moral principle) + 凛然 lǐnrán (awe-inspiring; commanding; cool and stern; the quality of moral authority that makes others straighten up).
大有希望	dà yǒu xī wàng	very promising; full of hope — Literally "to greatly have hope," said of a person or prospect with bright chances: 这个项目大有希望 ("this project is very promising"). A warm, encouraging phrase built directly on 希望, the bright mirror of 大失所望.
大运河	dà yùn hé	the Grand Canal — The Sui's enduring monument: 运 yùn (to transport) + 河 hé (river), a man-made transport river. Built at terrible human cost under Emperor Yang, it linked the rice-rich south to the political north and remained the backbone of Chinese internal trade for over a millennium.
大智若愚	dà zhì ruò yú	great wisdom appears foolish; the truly wise seem simple — 大 dà (great; profound) + 智 zhì (wisdom; discernment) + 若 ruò (appears like; seems as if) + 愚 yú (foolish; simple-minded). The phrase appears in its classical form in the 老子 Laozi, Chapter 45: 大直若屈，大巧若拙，大辩若讷 , and in the later formulation 大智若愚 that crystallizes the pattern.
待人接物	dài rén jiē wù	to treat people and handle affairs: the way one conducts oneself with others — Lit: treat-people-engage-things. The whole manner of dealing with others and managing matters; said in praise of someone whose conduct is gracious and well judged.
当机立断	dāng jī lì duàn	to decide decisively at the right moment; not to hesitate when the time comes — Lit: facing-the-opportunity-immediately-decide. The complement of 把握时机 , not just grasping the moment but acting on it decisively. 断 here means to cut through, to decide without wavering. The virtuous counterpart to 犹豫不决 (hesitating and unable to decide).
当局者迷，旁观者清	dāng jú zhě mí , páng guān zhě qīng	those involved are confused; bystanders see clearly — 当局者 = the one who is in the situation; the person directly involved + 旁观者 = the one standing to the side watching. 迷 = confused, lost / 清 = clear, perceptive. Two contrasting 者 nominalizings set in opposition: the agent inside the situation vs. the observer outside it.
当头棒喝	dāng tóu bàng hè	a staff-blow and a shout to the head — a jolt that wakes someone up — From Chan pedagogy at its most physical: Master Deshan was famous for the staff, Master Linji for the shout, both deployed to shatter a student's conceptual dithering. Now any sharp warning that snaps a person out of a bad course: a failed audit, a doctor's blunt sentence.
荡气回肠	dàng qì huí cháng	stirring the breath and coiling the gut: deeply moving, soul-stirring — Lit: surging-breath-coiling-innards. Said of music, writing, or a story so moving that it seems to turn one's very insides. 回 keeps its coiling sense here.
道不同不相为谋	dào bù tóng bù xiāng wéi móu	"those who follow different ways cannot work together" — fundamental value divergence ends cooperation — From the Analects: when the fundamental principles (道) that govern a person's life diverge, strategic cooperation becomes impossible. Used when parting ways with a colleague, organization, or ally over principle , not personal dislike but incompatible directions.
道可道，非常道。	dào kě dào , fēi cháng dào .	The Way that can be spoken is not the constant Way. — The opening line of chapter 1, and the most famous sentence in the entire text. It establishes at once that the 道 lies beyond the reach of fixed language: any 道 that can be fully captured in words is already a limited, conditioned thing, not the constant, nameless source.
道听途说	dào tīng tú shuō	"heard on the road, told on the path" — hearsay; rumor; unverified gossip — 途 tú = road; path (in transit). Things overheard on the road, passed on without verification. The road is a place of unfiltered information, strangers, and half-truths. 不要相信道听途说。(Don't believe hearsay.) Used to dismiss rumors or unverified claims.
得道多助	dé dào duō zhù	"the righteous have many helpers" — moral legitimacy generates real-world support — From Mencius (孟子). Full phrase: 得道多助，失道寡助 (Those who have the Way have many helpers; those without the Way have few). Moral legitimacy is not merely symbolic , it creates tangible coalitions. Those who govern well attract support; those who govern badly find themselves isolated.
得心应手	dé xīn yìng shǒu	handy and skillful: to do something with effortless mastery — Lit: the hand answers the heart. What the mind intends, the hand at once carries out. Praise for a skill so practiced it feels automatic. Here 应 takes the yìng reading, "to respond."
得意忘形	dé yì wàng xíng	so pleased with oneself that one forgets propriety — overweening pride — Lit: obtain-pleasure-forget-form/shape. 得意 = satisfied, pleased (here 得 is the full verb "to get/obtain," not the particle). 忘形 = to forget one's bearing/form. Used for someone carried away by success or compliments.
德才兼备	dé cái jiān bèi	to have both virtue and talent; the ideal of the capable and morally upright person — 德 dé (virtue; moral character) + 才 cái (talent; ability; practical capability) + 兼 jiān (simultaneously; to combine) + 备 bèi (to possess; to be equipped with). The ideal of the complete person , someone who is not only capable and skilled (才) but also genuinely good (德).
德高望重	dé gāo wàng zhòng	of lofty virtue and weighty reputation — a venerable elder — Lit: virtue-high, reputation-heavy. The standard four-character honorific for a respected senior figure , a teacher, a scholar, a community elder. Used at retirement banquets, in obituaries, and in introductions of distinguished guests.
地大物博	dì dà wù bó	vast land, abundant resources — used of China's territory — Lit: land-great-things-abundant. The 地 here is the full noun "land, earth" (dì, 4th tone), not the adverbial particle de. Appears frequently in descriptions of China's natural endowment. A reminder: 地 has a full semantic life beyond its particle function.
灯红酒绿	dēng hóng jiǔ lǜ	red lamps and green wine: gaudy nightlife — The glow of pleasure quarters, often tinged with disapproval. Describes a city of bars and neon, sometimes implying decadence or excess.
灯火辉煌	dēng huǒ huī huáng	lamps blazing splendidly: brilliantly lit — A hall or street ablaze with light, suggesting wealth, festivity, or grandeur. A common way to paint a banquet or a lit skyline.
灯火通明	dēng huǒ tōng míng	lamps lit all through: every light blazing — A house, street, or ship lit up from end to end, not one window dark. Plainer than 灯火辉煌: it stresses that everything is lit rather than that the light is splendid.
登科及第	dēng kē jí dì	to ascend the rolls and place in the rankings: to succeed in the civil-service exam — Lit: mount-the-roster-reach-rank. 登科 is to have one's name posted on the pass list, 及第 to be ranked within it. A set phrase of congratulation for examination success.
低声下气	dī shēng xià qì	"lower the voice, lower the breath" — to speak with extreme humility; to be submissive in order to placate someone — 低声 (lower the voice) + 下气 (bring down one's breath/spirit). The physical image is precise: a person who speaks quietly and exhales slowly is physiologically in a submissive, de-escalated state.
滴水穿石	dī shuǐ chuān shí	dripping water bores through stone: persistence wins — The image of a single drip, repeated for years, drilling a hole in rock. The standard idiom for patient, steady effort overcoming a hard obstacle.
颠倒黑白	diān dǎo hēi bái	to invert black and white — to deliberately confuse right and wrong — 颠倒 diāndǎo (to turn upside down) + 黑白 hēibái (black and white). To knowingly call wrong right and right wrong, twisting the truth for one's own ends. Stronger and more accusatory than simply lying: it charges the speaker with corrupting the very standard of judgment. 他为了脱罪，竟然颠倒黑白。
颠倒是非	diān dào shì fēi	to invert right and wrong; to call black white and white black — Lit: overturn-invert-right-wrong. A severe accusation: to deliberately misrepresent the facts, to claim something wrong is right and vice versa. The logical extreme of a bad-faith 是…的 , not just correcting a focus, but inverting the entire reality. Common in political rhetoric and moral arguments.
点石成金	diǎn shí chéng jīn	to touch stone and turn it to gold: to transform the ordinary into the priceless — Lit: touch-stone-become-gold. From Daoist immortal lore, the touch that turns base rock to gold. Now used of an editor, teacher, or craftsman who makes something dull suddenly shine.
凋零	diāo líng	"to wither and fall" — to fade and drop away; (of people) to pass away — 凋 (to wither) + 零 (to fall in drops). Strictly a two-character word rather than a four-character chengyu, but a fixed literary expression worth knowing.
顶天立地	dǐng tiān lì dì	head touching heaven, feet on earth — a person of complete integrity and heroic stature — 顶 dǐng = to stand at the top of; to press against from below. 立 lì = to stand; to be upright. The image is of a person so morally complete that they fill the entire vertical axis of the universe , feet firmly planted on earth, head pressing against heaven.
鼎力相助	dǐng lì xiāng zhù	to render great help: a respectful thanks for another's strong assistance — Lit: with-tripod-strength-to-help. 鼎 is the massive bronze ritual tripod, so 鼎力 is great strength. A polite phrase used to acknowledge or request another person's powerful support.
丢人现眼	diū rén xiàn yǎn	"lose people, show eyes" — to make a spectacle of oneself; disgraceful public behavior — Lit: lose-person-expose-eyes. A stronger and more colorful version of 丢脸 , specifically about embarrassing public display. 现眼 (to expose one's eyes to public ridicule) adds the dimension of being stared at and judged.
东奔西跑	dōng bēn xī pǎo	"running east and dashing west" — to rush around in every direction — A four-character formula combining 奔 and 跑 across the directional pair 东 dōng / 西 xī. Used for someone constantly on the move, often in service of obligations or in pursuit of a livelihood.
东奔西走	dōng bēn xī zǒu	"rushing east, running west" — frantically busy everywhere; constantly in motion — Lit: east-rush-west-walk. Describes someone perpetually in motion, always somewhere else, never settled. Often implies exhausting, stressful busyness with little to show for it. 他为了这件事东奔西走了好几年。"He spent years running all over the place trying to make this happen."
东拼西凑	dōng pīn xī còu	"pieced together from east and west" — cobbled together from miscellaneous sources — 东拼 (stitched from the east) + 西凑 (gathered from the west). Something assembled by scraping together bits and pieces from wherever they could be found. Used for a speech that draws from random sources, a meal made from leftovers, or a budget patched together with emergency measures.
东山再起	dōng shān zài qǐ	"rise again from the Eastern Mountain" — to make a comeback after defeat — From the biography of Xiè Ān (謝安, 320–385 CE), a Jin dynasty statesman who retired to 东山 (Eastern Mountain, in present-day Zhejiang) and refused office for years. When the court fell into crisis, he was recalled and restored Jin to stability.
东施效颦	Dōng Shī xiào pín	to imitate blindly without understanding, and make things worse — A homely woman copies Xi Shi's famous frown and clears the street: Zhuangzi's parable about form without essence.
东张西望	dōng zhāng xī wàng	"looking east and west" — glancing around nervously or curiously; gawking — Lit: east-look-west-gaze. Used for someone whose eyes dart around, whether out of nervousness, suspicion, or simple distraction. The four-character structure vividly enacts the scanning motion itself. 他在街上东张西望，好像在找人。"He was looking all around the street as if searching for someone."
动手动脚	dòng shǒu dòng jiǎo	to move hands and feet: to get physical, to grope or rough up — Lit: move-hand-move-foot. To put one's hands on someone, either to start a fight or to touch improperly. The doubled 动 spreads the action across hands and feet alike.
洞房花烛	dòng fáng huā zhú	bridal chamber and wedding candles: the wedding night — 洞房 is the bridal chamber, the deep inner 房 of the house; 花烛 are the red wedding candles. The set phrase stands for a marriage celebration, often paired as 洞房花烛夜, the night of the wedding.
独门绝技	dú mén ju é jì	a unique school's matchless skill: a signature technique known to no one else — Lit: sole-school-unmatched-skill. 门 here is a school or lineage of practice. A 独门绝技 is the secret art that belongs to one tradition or master alone.
独占鳌头	dú zhàn áo tóu	to come in first; to stand at the apex — Lit: to stand alone on the giant turtle's head. 鳌 áo is the mythical sea turtle whose head is the highest point, corresponding to the top of the imperial examination standings. Metaphor: to take first place.
读书破万卷	dú shū pò wàn juàn	read until ten thousand scrolls are worn through — saturate yourself in reading — From Du Fu's "Twenty-Two Rhymes Presented to Vice-Director Wei" (奉赠韦左丞丈二十二韵): 读书破万卷，下笔如有神 "Read until ten thousand scrolls are worn through, and your pen will move as if inspired." The classical statement of how literary skill is built.
读万卷书，行万里路	dú wàn juàn shū , xíng wàn lǐ lù	read ten thousand scrolls of books, walk ten thousand li of road — learn from text and from travel both — A Ming-dynasty saying attributed to the painter and theorist Dong Qichang. The pairing of 读 and 行 as the two halves of an educated life: book-knowledge and lived experience as equally necessary, neither sufficient alone.
短兵相接	duǎn bīng xiāng jiē	short weapons meet: close-quarters combat, a fierce face-to-face clash — From the Chu Ci. Now applied figuratively to any direct, intense confrontation, including debate and competition.
短命王朝	duǎn mìng wáng cháo	a short-lived dynasty — The standard description of the Sui, paired in Chinese historical thinking with the 秦朝 Qin: brilliant, transformative, and brief, doing the hard work of unification and building before collapsing and yielding to a long, glorious successor.
对牛弹琴	duì niú tán qín	playing the qin to a cow — speaking to someone incapable of understanding — From a Han dynasty text attributed to 牟融 Móu Róng. A musician plays the most refined music for a cow; the cow goes on eating grass. The problem is not the cow's intelligence but the category mismatch: the music is addressed to the wrong kind of listener.
对症下药	duì zhèng xià yào	prescribe according to the symptoms; tailor the remedy to the problem — 对 (match) + 症 (symptoms) + 下药 (administer medicine). From the case lore of the Han physician Hua Tuo, who gave two patients with identical headaches different prescriptions because the causes differed.
多才多艺	duō cái duō yì	of many talents and many skills: versatile, multitalented — Lit: much-talent-much-skill. High praise for a person gifted in several arts at once, the painter who also writes and plays music. 艺 yì is craft or art, the paired half of 才.
多此一举	duō cǐ yī jǔ	"one unnecessary action too many" — to do something superfluous — 多 (extra, unnecessary) + 此 (this) + 一举 (one action). An extra action that wasn't needed , wasted effort that doesn't improve the result. A gentle criticism of overcaution or unnecessary elaboration: 你不用解释，多此一举 ("you don't need to explain , that's unnecessary").
多多益善	duō duō yì shàn	the more the better — Literally "more and more is the more beneficial," the more the merrier. From a remark attributed to the general Han Xin, who said that as a commander he could lead troops 多多益善 ("the more the better"). Built on the 多 ("many") of 多少.
多事之秋	duō shì zhī qiū	an eventful autumn: a troubled time, full of upheavals — Lit: many-matters' autumn. Autumn was the season of harvest reckoning and of war, so a "many-matters autumn" came to mean a period crowded with crises and disturbances, a turbulent, eventful time for a state or a person.
恩将仇报	ēn jiāng chóu bào	to repay kindness with enmity: to bite the hand that feeds you — 恩 (kindness) is met with 仇 (enmity) as its 报 (return). A sharp condemnation of ingratitude, common in everyday speech to call out a betrayer.
耳目一新	ěr mù yī xīn	"ears and eyes completely renewed" — a refreshingly new impression — 耳 (ear) + 目 (eye) + 一 (completely) + 新 (new). All your senses reset , everything seems fresh and surprising. Used for places recently renovated, new presentations, or any experience that resets one's perception. The compound treats ears and eyes as a pair, the full perceptual system.
耳濡目染	ěr rú mù rǎn	"ears soaked, eyes stained" — influenced by constant exposure — 耳濡 (ear soaked/wetted) + 目染 (eye stained). The effect of growing up surrounded by something , gradually absorbing it through the senses without formal instruction. Often used for children who learn by immersion: 耳濡目染，自然就会了 ("soaked by ears and eyes, one naturally learns").
耳听八方	ěr tīng bā fāng	"ears listening in all eight directions" — alert and perceptive to everything around — 耳 (ears) + 听 (listening) + 八方 (the eight directions , north, south, east, west, and the four diagonals; by extension, all sides).
耳闻目睹	ěr wén mù dǔ	"heard with the ear, seen with the eye" — witnessed firsthand — 耳 (ear) + 闻 (heard) + 目 (eye) + 睹 (seen). Both the ear and the eye were present and active. A marker of direct personal testimony, as opposed to hearsay. Used in legal testimony, journalism, memoir, and any context where the authority of a claim depends on personal presence.
二虎相争	èr hǔ xiāng zhēng	two tigers fight — when two powerful forces clash, both suffer — The full form is often 两虎相争，必有一伤 liǎng hǔ xiāng zhēng, bì yǒu yī shāng: "when two tigers fight, one is certain to be wounded." Used to counsel against unnecessary conflict between equals, and to describe political or commercial battles where both sides bleed.
二话不说	èr huà bù shuō	without a second word: at once, without hesitation or argument — Lit: a-second-word-not-said. Said of someone who acts immediately, raising no objection and wasting no breath: 他二话不说就答应了 "he agreed without a moment's hesitation."
发扬光大	fā yáng guāng dà	to carry forward and make flourish: to develop a good thing to its fullest — Lit: send-forth-raise-bright-great. Said of carrying on a tradition, virtue, or fine quality and making it grow even greater. The fā reading: to bring something forth and develop it. 把好传统发扬光大 "to carry a good tradition forward."
法不阿贵	fǎ bù ē guì	the law shows no favor to the noble — law applies equally regardless of rank — From Han Feizi. 阿 ē = to show favoritism, to bend. 贵 guì = the noble, the powerful. The complete saying continues: 绳不绕曲 shéng bù rào qū , "the carpenter's line does not bend around curves." Law, like a measuring line, must be straight.
法不容情	fǎ bù róng qíng	the law allows no room for sentiment: justice must not bend to feeling — Lit: law-not-tolerate-feeling. The principle that the law must be applied evenly, without softening for personal ties or sympathy. The level standard of the water radical made into a maxim.
翻江倒海	fān jiāng dǎo hǎi	to overturn rivers and upend seas: overwhelming, world-shaking force — Lit: overturn-river topple-sea. Said of a power great enough to churn the waters of the world, and by extension of turbulent emotion or upheaval: 心里翻江倒海 "the heart in utter turmoil."
翻山越岭	fān shān yu è lǐng	"to cross mountain ridge after mountain ridge" — to traverse difficult terrain, by extension, to overcome great obstacles — A four-character compound combining 翻越 (to climb over) split across 山 (mountain) and 岭 (ridge). Used both literally (an arduous mountain journey) and figuratively (overcoming a series of difficulties to reach a goal). Frequent in war-history and biographical writing. 他翻山越岭，终于来到了家乡。
反复无常	fǎn fù wú cháng	to flip back and forth with no constancy: fickle and unpredictable — Lit: repeatedly-without-constancy. A criticism of someone whose moods, promises, or positions keep changing, so that no one can rely on them.
反客为主	fǎn kè wéi zhǔ	turn from guest to host: to seize the initiative and take control — Lit: reverse-guest-become-host. Once a stratagem of war: the side that arrives in a weaker, guest-like position turns the tables and takes command. Now used of anyone who flips a passive role into a controlling one.
返璞归真	fǎn pú guī zhēn	return to the unpolished, restore the authentic — strip away ornament for plain truth — Lit: return-uncarved-restore-real. Daoist in spirit. 璞 = uncarved jade. The aesthetic and ethical movement back from elaboration to unworked simplicity.
方寸之地	fāng cùn zhī dì	a space of mere inches; a tiny place — also: one's heart and mind — Lit: square-inch-of-ground. 方寸 = one square cun (about an inch). Used literally for extremely small physical spaces, and metaphorically for the heart/mind (one's inner space).
房谋杜断	fáng móu dù duàn	Fáng plans, Dù decides: a perfect pairing of complementary talents — From the Tang statesmen Fáng Xuánlíng, famed for strategy, and Dù Rúhuì, famed for decisiveness. Here 房 is the surname Fáng; the idiom praises two people whose strengths complete each other.
放下屠刀，立地成佛	fàng xià tú dāo , lì dì chéng fó	lay down the butcher's knife and become a Buddha on the spot — radical redemption is always possible — The full form of 立地成佛. Rooted in the Chan teaching that Buddha nature is present in all beings, even the most hardened. Used both seriously (in discussions of rehabilitation, forgiveness, religious conversion) and ironically (with skepticism about a villain's sudden change of heart). 只要放下屠刀，立地成佛.
放眼天下	fàng yǎn tiān xià	cast one's eyes across all-under-heaven — to think broadly; to have a global perspective — 放眼 fàng yǎn (to let one's gaze range freely; to look far) + 天下. To look beyond one's immediate circumstances, neighborhood, or nation and think on a civilizational or global scale. The opposite of 鼠目寸光 (shǔ mù cùn guāng , mouse-eyes seeing only an inch; short-sightedness). 要放眼天下，不能只看眼前。
飞黄腾达	fēi huáng téng dá	Feihuang gallops upward: to rise rapidly in rank — 飞黄 (Fēihuáng) is a legendary divine steed; the phrase pictures a career rising as if riding it skyward. The standard idiom for a meteoric rise in office or fortune.
非同小可	fēi tóng xiǎo kě	no small matter: serious, of great importance — Lit: not-the-same-as-trivial. 小可 means a small or trivial thing, and 非同 negates it: this is not on a par with the trivial, so treat it with weight. 这件事非同小可 "this is no small matter."
非我族类	fēi wǒ zú lèi	those not of our kin; those outside our group
分久必合，合久必分。	fēn jiǔ bì hé , hé jiǔ bì fēn .	What is long divided must unite; what is long united must divide. — The opening philosophy of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, stating the cyclical rhythm of Chinese political history between unity and fragmentation. It is one of the most quoted sentences about Chinese history as a whole, used to frame any long swing between consolidation and breakup.
分秒必争	fēn miǎo bì zhēng	to fight for every minute and second: to lose not a moment — Lit: minute-second-must-contend. Said when time is so pressing that each unit counts, in a race, an emergency, a deadline. 争分夺秒 is the common variant.
焚书坑儒	fén shū kēng rú	burn the books and bury the Confucians — state censorship and intellectual repression — The four-character condemnation of the Qin cultural purges of 213–212 BCE. Still the standard Chinese phrase for any government suppression of thought or culture. Note that 坑 kēng (pit) also functions in modern colloquial Chinese as a verb meaning "to trap" or "to screw over someone" , e.g.
风调雨顺	fēng tiáo yǔ shùn	favorable weather: good conditions for a harvest — Lit: the wind is well-tuned and the rain comes in due course. A set wish for a year of mild, timely weather and a good harvest, often paired with 国泰民安 (the country at peace and the people content). Here 调 takes the tiáo reading, "to harmonize," the weather brought into balance.
风平浪静	fēng píng làng jìng	the wind is calm and the waves are still: calm seas, a tranquil situation — Lit: wind-level-waves-quiet. The sea at perfect rest, used both literally and for any situation that has settled into calm after trouble has passed.
风水轮流转	fēng shuǐ lún liú zhuǎn	feng shui rotates in turn — fortunes change; cycles of luck; the wheel keeps turning — The most common figurative use of 风水. Used to express acceptance of change, comfort in adversity, or (more pointedly) schadenfreude when an opponent's luck runs out. 三十年河东，三十年河西，风水轮流转 (thirty years east of the river, thirty years west , the wheel of fortune keeps turning).
风雨同舟	fēng yǔ tóng zhōu	to weather a storm in the same boat — Literally "wind and rain, the same boat", to stand together through hardship, sharing the danger. From the Sunzi Bingfa, which notes that even old enemies in one storm-tossed boat will help each other. The deepest form of being 在一起, bound by shared trial.
封官许愿	fēng guān xǔ yuàn	to dole out titles and make promises: to buy support with offers of office
封妻荫子	fēng qī yìn zǐ	titles for the wife, privilege for the sons: rank and honor extended to one's family — The reward of high office under the empire: a man's success earned a title for his wife and protected status for his sons. Evokes the prestige of the old examination-and-rank system.
烽火连三月，家书抵万金	fēng huǒ lián sān yu è , jiā shū dǐ wàn jīn	beacon fires for three months; a letter from home worth ten thousand gold — Du Fu's couplet from 春望 (Spring View), written during the An Lushan Rebellion while imprisoned in rebel-held Chang'an (756 CE). Among the most quoted lines in Chinese literature: a complete world of wartime separation compressed into fourteen characters.
烽火戏诸侯	fēng huǒ xì zhū hóu	lighting the beacon fires to toy with the lords — crying wolf at the cost of a dynasty — From the story of King You and Bao Si: the beacon fires lit for entertainment, the vassal lords who stopped responding, and the Quanrong attack that ended Western Zhou. Used to describe any deception that destroys the credibility needed in a real crisis.
否极泰来	pǐ jí tài lái	after extreme obstruction (yin) comes peace (yang) — when things hit rock bottom, improvement follows — From the Yijing hexagrams 否 pǐ (stagnation; obstruction , a yin hexagram) and 泰 tài (peace; harmony , a yang hexagram). The cosmological law: forces cycle, yin cannot dominate forever, the turn of yang is inevitable. A comforting phrase in hard times: 否极泰来，好日子还在后面。
夫唱妇随	fū chàng fù suí	the husband sings and the wife follows: a harmonious married couple — Literally "the husband leads, the wife accompanies." A traditional image of marital harmony in which the couple act in accord, one taking the lead and the other in step.
福无双至，祸不单行	fú wú shuāng zhì , huò bù dān xíng	blessings don't come in pairs; misfortunes never come alone — The Chinese equivalent of "when it rains it pours," and its optimistic inverse. Fortune is rare and singular; misfortune clusters. A paired proverb that encodes Chinese realism about luck.
福星高照	fú xīng gāo zhào	the star of fortune shines from above — to be under a lucky star — 福星 fúxīng = the star of fortune (one of the three auspicious stars 福禄寿). 高照 = shining from on high. A blessing used at New Year, weddings, and new ventures.
父慈子孝	fù cí zǐ xiào	the father kind, the son filial: the reciprocal duty between generations — A Confucian formula for the father-son relationship, paired in the classics with 兄友弟恭 (elder brother caring, younger respectful). Authority and obedience are framed as mutual obligations, not one-way command.
父债子还	fù zhài zǐ huán	the father's debt, the son repays: a debt or wrong passes down the line — Once a literal expectation in family law, now used figuratively for any burden inherited from a previous generation. Carries a tone of grim inevitability.
富国强兵	fù guó qiáng bīng	"enrich the country, strengthen the army" — national power as a policy goal — 富国 (enrich the state) + 强兵 (strengthen the army). The paired goals of realist statecraft, traceable to the Legalist ministers of the Warring States period (especially Shāng Yāng of Qin, died 338 BCE).
富甲一方	fù jiǎ yī fāng	wealthiest in the whole region: the richest man around — 甲 here means "to rank first." Said of a local magnate whose fortune tops everyone in the district. Admiring, slightly old-fashioned register.
富可敌国	fù kě dí guó	wealth that can rival a state: fabulously rich — 敌 means "to match." A private fortune so vast it equals a kingdom's treasury, applied to tycoons past and present.
富丽堂皇	fù lì táng huáng	rich, beautiful, grand and imposing: sumptuous and magnificent — Describes a palace, mansion, or banquet hall dazzling with luxury. Common in travel writing and architecture description today.
改朝换代	gǎi cháo huàn dài	to change dynasty and era: a change of regime — Lit: change-dynasty, swap-era. 朝 and 代 are the dynasty and its age. The phrase names the fall of one ruling house and the rise of another, and by extension any sweeping change of who holds power.
改头换面	gǎi tóu huàn miàn	change the head, swap the face: a superficial makeover — Originally Buddhist, on the soul taking a new body. Now usually pejorative: the form is redone but the substance is unchanged, like a rebranded scam.
改弦更张	gǎi xián gēng zhāng	change the string and retune — fundamental reform, not adjustment — 改弦 = to change the string (of a stringed instrument); 更张 = to restring and retune. The 更 is gēng, first tone. A musician who only retunes (改弦) is making incremental adjustments; one who also rerestrings (更张) is starting fresh.
改弦易辙	gǎi xián yì zhé	"change the bowstring, switch the wheel-rut" — to change direction; to take a new approach — 改 (change) + 弦 (xián, bowstring) + 易 (change) + 辙 (zhé, wheel-rut). The two halves are parallel images of changing tools and changing track. Used for any decisive shift in policy, method, or life-direction.
改邪归正	gǎi xié guī zhèng	to abandon the crooked and return to the straight: to mend one's ways — Lit: change-evil-return-upright. Said of someone who gives up wrongdoing and comes back to honest living. 邪 (crooked, evil) is the standing opposite of 正.
敢作敢为	gǎn zuò gǎn wéi	"dare to do, dare to act" — bold and decisive; willing to take initiative and responsibility — 敢 (to dare) + 作 (to do) + 敢 (to dare) + 为 (to act). The positive image of 为 as confident, owned action , the opposite pole from 无为. Where 无为 counsels releasing the forcing quality of striving, 敢作敢为 describes the quality of someone who acts decisively and stands behind what they do. 这个领导敢作敢为，大家都很佩服。
敢做敢当	gǎn zuò gǎn dāng	to dare to act and dare to answer for it — to own one's actions — 敢 gǎn (to dare) + 做 + 敢 + 当 dāng (to bear, to take responsibility). The mark of a person of integrity: bold enough to act, and equally willing to shoulder the consequences. The phrase praises moral courage paired with accountability, the refusal to act and then duck the blame.
感激涕零	gǎn jī tì líng	"so grateful the tears fall" — moved to tears by gratitude; deeply thankful — 感激 (deep gratitude) + 涕 (tears) + 零 (to fall in drops). Here 零 returns to its literal verb sense, "to fall in drops," applied not to rain but to tears: gratitude so overwhelming that the tears come down. The phrase describes being moved to weeping by another's kindness or favor.
感慨万千	gǎn kǎi wàn qiān	ten thousand emotions surging — overwhelmed by bittersweet feeling at life's passage — Go-to phrase for homecomings, reunions, and witnessing great change. Appears constantly in memoirs and personal essays.
