两败俱伤	liǎng bài jù shāng	"both defeated, both hurt" — a mutually destructive outcome; both sides lose — 两败 (both defeated) + 俱伤 (both injured). A conflict in which neither side wins and both come away damaged, the lose-lose result of a fight pushed too far: 这样争下去只会两败俱伤 (going on fighting like this will only hurt both sides).
两情相悦	liǎng qíng xiāng yu è	two hearts delighting in each other — mutual affection — A classical phrase for mutual romantic fondness, where 悦 yuè (to delight in, akin to 喜欢) is shared by both sides. It names the ideal of love that is returned, two people who like and are gladdened by each other, and is often quoted in the context of relationships and marriage.
两全其美	liǎng quán qí měi	"complete the good of both" — a solution good for both sides; the best of both worlds — 两全 (keep both whole, satisfy both) + 其美 (their goodness). A way of handling things that serves both parties or both goals without sacrificing either, the win-win outcome: 找一个两全其美的办法 (to find a solution good for both sides).
量力而行	liàng lì ér xíng	measure your strength, then act: do only what you can manage — 量 liàng (to assess, here in the assessing sense) + 力 lì (strength) + 而 ér (and then) + 行 xíng (to act). Gauge how much you are capable of, and act within that limit. A counsel of prudence: take on what your resources, ability, and circumstances can actually support, rather than overreaching.
量入为出	liàng rù wéi chū	measure income to set spending: live within your means — 量 liàng (to gauge) + 入 rù (income, what comes in) + 为 wéi (to make, to determine) + 出 chū (expenditure, what goes out). Let the size of your income decide the size of your spending.
寥寥无几	liáo liáo wú jǐ	very few; scarcely any — Literally "sparse, sparse, not even a few," describing something so scarce it can almost be counted on one hand. Here 几 ("a few") takes its statement sense rather than its question sense. The mirror image of 多多益善.
邻里之间	lín lǐ zhī jiān	"between neighbors and the neighborhood" — community bonds; relations among people living nearby — 邻 (lín, neighbor) + 里 (the neighborhood unit) + 之间 (between). Uses 里 in its oldest sense , the bounded residential community of the Zhou system.
临时抱佛脚	lín shí bào fó jiǎo	clasping the Buddha's feet at the last minute — cramming — From a proverb about neglecting incense in ordinary times and embracing the statue's feet only when disaster looms (平时不烧香，临时抱佛脚). The universal student condition, named without mercy. Usable for any deferred preparation: visas, taxes, wedding speeches.
零零星星	líng líng xīng xīng	"scattered like stray stars" — sparse and scattered; bits and pieces here and there — A reduplication of 零星 (scattered, sporadic), itself 零 (scattered drops) plus 星 (stars, scattered points of light).
流连忘返	liú lián wàng fǎn	so enthralled as to forget to leave: lingering, reluctant to go home — 流连 liúlián = to linger, to be unable to tear oneself away; 忘返 wàng fǎn = to forget to return.
六亲不认	liù qīn bù rèn	to disown all six kinships — utterly cold-blooded, recognizing no family bond — Lit: six-relatives-not-recognize. The classical six kinships are father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, child. Said of someone who in the pursuit of power or self-interest will not even acknowledge their own kin.
六神无主	liù shén wú zhǔ	"the six spirits have no master" — panic-stricken; at a total loss — 六神 (the six spirits) are the guardian spirits believed in Daoist physiology to govern the vital organs (heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, spleen, gallbladder). When they are 无主 (without a master, leaderless), the person loses all composure.
六十而耳顺	liù shí ér ěr shùn	at sixty, the ear follows — one can hear without resistance
六月飞霜	liù yu è fēi shuāng	"frost flies in the sixth month" — a sign of grievous injustice — 六月 (the sixth lunar month, high summer) plus 飞霜 (flying frost). Frost in midsummer is an impossibility that heaven produces only in response to a wrong so great it disturbs the natural order.
龙飞凤舞	lóng fēi fèng wǔ	dragon flying, phoenix dancing — describes bold, unrestrained calligraphy — Lit: dragon-fly phoenix-dance. Originally a description of grand, sweeping calligraphy where the strokes move with the energy of mythic creatures. Now used both admiringly (fluid, powerful brushwork) and ironically (illegible scrawl that only the writer understands).
龙争虎斗	lóng zhēng hǔ dòu	dragon and tiger fighting — two powerful forces in fierce competition — 龙 lóng + 争 zhēng (to contend; to compete) + 虎 hǔ (tiger) + 斗 dòu (to fight; to contend). Used when two equally formidable opponents , companies, athletes, armies, political factions , clash with serious intensity. Neither side is diminished; both are worthy adversaries. 这场决赛简直是龙争虎斗，双方势均力敌。
路不拾遗	lù bù shí yí	"on the road no one picks up what others have dropped": the mark of a well-governed society — From the Hánfēizǐ (Legalist text, 3rd century BCE), describing the ideal state under good rule. Paired with 夜不闭户 yè bù bì hù ("at night doors are not bolted").
率性而为	shuài xìng ér wéi	to act following ones nature: to do as one's disposition prompts — Literally "to follow nature and act." To behave according to one's true temperament rather than calculation or constraint. It can praise an honest, unaffected spirit or, in a cooler reading, describe someone who simply acts on impulse without weighing the consequences.
绿树成阴	lǜ shù chéng yīn	green trees forming shade — lush, leafy, and cool — 绿树 lǜshù (green trees) + 成 chéng (to form) + 阴 yīn (shade). Trees grown so full that their crowns join into continuous shade, a picture of a flourishing, well-grown garden or avenue in high summer. Here 阴 is the welcome, cooling shadow, the same positive sense as 阴凉. 几十年过去，当年的小树苗如今已绿树成阴。
乱七八糟	luàn qī bā zāo	"chaotic seven, messy eight" — in complete disorder; a total mess — 乱 (chaotic) + 七八 (seven-eight) + 糟 (rotten, spoiled). One of the most common expressions in spoken Mandarin for utter disorder, whether of a messy room, a tangled situation, or muddled thinking. The embedded 七八 again uses the clashing seven-and-eight to mean jumbled, every-which-way.
落后就要挨打	luò hòu jiù yào ái dǎ	if you fall behind, you will be beaten — the fundamental lesson of the century of humiliation — The defining phrase of modern Chinese nationalist historiography. Attributed to various leaders; popularized by Deng Xiaoping. The phrase frames national development not as aspiration but as existential necessity: weakness invites predation, therefore modernization is survival.
落花流水	luò huā liú shuǐ	fallen blossoms and flowing water — spring's end; utter defeat — Lit: falling-flowers flowing-water. A classical image from Tang and Song poetry for the beauty of spring's end. Also used for utter defeat: 打得落花流水 "beaten to pieces."
落井下石	luò jǐng xià shí	to throw stones at someone who has fallen in a well — to kick someone when they're down — Lit: fall-well-down-stone. The act of throwing rocks on top of someone already trapped in a well. Vivid idiom for betrayal or cruelty toward someone already in misfortune.
落叶归根	luò yè guī gēn	fallen leaves return to the root — everyone returns to their origins — Lit: fallen-leaves-return-root. The universal Chinese sentiment about homeland: no matter how far one has traveled or how long one has been away, the natural ending is to return to one's place of origin.
麻木不仁	má mù bù rén	numb and inhumane; deadened to feeling — both physical and moral — 麻木 mámù (numb; without sensation , 麻 hemp, suggesting the prickling of nerves; 木 wood, suggesting deadness) + 不仁 bùrén (without humaneness; without feeling). Originally a medical term for physical numbness , limbs that have lost sensation.
马到成功	mǎ dào chéng gōng	immediate success upon arrival — "when the cavalry arrives, victory follows" — Lit: horse-arrive-success. Originally a wish for military campaigns, deeply resonant with the Mongol cavalry tradition that shook the known world. Used today as a congratulatory phrase for new endeavors. 祝你马到成功！ "Wishing you swift success!"
马马虎虎	mǎ mǎ hū hū	horse-horse tiger-tiger: so-so, careless, passable — The doubled form of 马虎. Used both for sloppy work and, self-deprecatingly, to answer "how are you?" with a shrugging "just so-so."
埋头苦干	mái tóu kǔ gàn	to bury the head and toil hard: to work diligently without distraction — Lit: bury-head-bitter-work. To lower one's head and labor away, absorbed in the task and indifferent to praise or notice. The picture is of someone bent over their work, head down.
满街都是圣人	mǎn jiē dōu shì shèng rén	saints fill the streets — everyone already has the innate moral knowledge to be a sage — Said to have been uttered by Wang Yangming after a student asked skeptically whether ordinary people could really possess 良知. His response: walk out onto any busy street and observe; anyone who acts from their innate moral sense in that moment is a sage.
满面春风	mǎn miàn chūn fēng	a face full of spring breeze: beaming, radiant with joy — Lit: full-face-spring-wind. The whole face glowing like a warm spring day, said of someone visibly pleased, content, or flush with good fortune.
满腔热血	mǎn qiāng rè xu è	a chest full of hot blood: brimming with fervor — 满腔 a full chest, 热血 hot blood. Describes youthful idealism and the will to throw oneself into a cause. Warm and slightly literary in tone.
满室生辉	mǎn shì shēng huī	the whole room glows — a radiant, welcoming presence fills the space — Lit: room-full-give-off-radiance. Used for a beautiful person or a remarkable guest whose presence lights up a room. A formal compliment in social and literary contexts.
满载而归	mǎn zài ér guī	to return fully laden — to come home with rich gains — 满载 (loaded full) + 而归 (and return). The image of Xuanzang re-entering Chang'an with 657 manuscripts after sixteen years abroad. Now a common phrase for any return rich in results , from a successful trip, a fruitful search, or a profitable venture. The opposite is 一无所获 "to come back empty-handed."
满纸荒唐言，一把辛酸泪。	mǎn zhǐ huāng táng yán , yī bǎ xīn suān lèi .	A whole page of absurd words, a fistful of bitter tears. — From Cao Xueqin's own opening verse, his description of the book and of the grief that went into it. The pairing of seeming absurdity (a tale of stones and dreams) with real suffering captures the novel's double nature as fantasy and as a wound from the author's own ruined life.
慢工出细活	màn gōng chū xì huó	slow work produces fine goods — Lit: slow-work-produce-fine-goods. The Chinese counterpart to "haste makes waste." A proverb rather than a classical four-character 成语 in the strict sense, but widely used and culturally important. Invoked to defend careful, unhurried craftsmanship against pressure for speed.
慢条斯理	màn tiáo sī lǐ	slow and methodical; unhurried and in proper order — Lit: slow-stitch-this-manage. Describes someone who does everything at an unhurried, measured pace and in proper sequence. Can be neutral (a composed, methodical person) or slightly pejorative (someone frustratingly slow to act).
漫不经心	màn bù jīng xīn	careless and inattentive: with no thought passing through the mind — Lit: idly not passing-through the heart. 经心 means to take to heart, to attend to. To do something 漫不经心 is to do it absent-mindedly, paying it no real attention.
美不胜收	měi bù shèng shōu	beauty beyond what the eye can take in — overwhelmingly beautiful — Lit: beauty-not-able-to-receive/contain. Used for spectacular natural scenery, festivals, or exhibitions where there is simply too much beauty to absorb at once.
门当户对	mén dāng hù duì	matched gates and doors: of equal social standing (for a marriage) — Lit: gate-matching-door-matching. The old principle that the two families in a marriage should be of comparable rank and wealth. Still used, sometimes critically, of pairing by status.
门庭若市	mén tíng ruò shì	the gateway like a marketplace: thronged with visitors — Lit: gate-courtyard-like-market. Said of a household or office so busy with callers that the entrance resembles a crowded market. Its opposite is 门可罗雀, a gate so deserted you could net sparrows in it.
扪心自问	mén xīn zì wèn	"to press one's hand to the heart and question oneself" — honest self-examination; to look inward without flinching — 扪 mén (to press or feel with the hand) + 心 + 自 (self) + 问 (to question). The gesture of placing one's hand over one's heart and asking honestly: what do I know? what did I actually do? It is the physical enactment of consulting 良心 directly, without evasion.
懵懵懂懂	měng měng dǒng dǒng	muddled and only half-aware: in a fog — A vivid reduplication pairing 懵 (měng, dazed) with 懂 (dǒng, understand) to describe a hazy, half-comprehending state, like a child too young to grasp what is happening or a person fresh out of sleep.
孟姜女哭长城	Mèng Jiāng nü kū Cháng chéng	"Meng Jiangnu weeping at the Great Wall" — grief strong enough to move stone — One of China's four great folk legends (四大民间故事 sì dà mínjiān gùshì). Meng Jiangnu's husband Fan Xiliang was conscripted to build the Qin wall and died of exhaustion.
孟母三迁	Mèng mǔ sān qiān	Mencius's mother moves three times — the importance of environment in education — Not from the Mencius text itself but from the Lienüzhuan 列女传 (Biographies of Exemplary Women), attributed to Liu Xiang 刘向 (77–6 BCE).
迷途知返	mí tú zhī fǎn	To Realise You Are Lost and Turn Back — Four characters that describe one of the most human experiences: taking a wrong road, recognising it, and finding the way home. The Chinese idiom for course-correction done with dignity.
靡靡之音	mǐ mǐ zhī yīn	enervating music: sounds thought to soften the will and sap the spirit — Lit: dispirited music. A classical term of disapproval for music seen as decadent and weakening, the kind moralists blamed for a ruler's downfall. Still used, half-seriously, of overly sentimental songs.
面不改色	miàn bù gǎi sè	"face doesn't change color" — unruffled; keeping composure under pressure; poker-faced — Lit: face-not-change-color. The mark of composure under pressure , your face doesn't betray fear, surprise, or discomfort. 他面不改色地接受了批评，继续进行演讲。"He received the criticism without changing expression and continued his speech." Often admired as a sign of courage or self-discipline.
面红耳赤	miàn hóng ěr chì	face red, ears crimson — flushed with anger, embarrassment, or the heat of argument — 面 miàn (face) + 红 hóng (red) + 耳 ěr (ears) + 赤 chì (the deeper crimson). The face and ears flush red from a surge of emotion, most often a heated argument or acute embarrassment. 两个人争得面红耳赤，谁也不让谁。
面面俱到	miàn miàn jù dào	every aspect covered; thorough in all directions — 面 miàn (face; surface; aspect) + 面 + 俱 jù (all; together) + 到 (arrived at). Arrival has reached every face, every surface, every angle of the matter. Used to praise comprehensive coverage , a plan that misses nothing, a speech that addresses every concern, an analysis that leaves no gap.
面有菜色	miàn yǒu cài sè	a face with the color of greens: gaunt and sallow from hunger — Lit: face-has-vegetable-color. 菜色 is the wan, greenish pallor of someone who has eaten nothing but wild greens, with no grain or meat. The phrase paints a face worn down by famine or hardship.
妙笔生花	miào bǐ shēng huā	a wondrous brush gives birth to flowers — gifted writing that makes words bloom — Lit: wondrous-brush-give birth-flowers. From a Tang dynasty story about the poet Li Bai dreaming that his brush sprouted flowers, foretelling his literary gifts. Used to praise writing of exceptional beauty or imagination , prose or verse that transforms language into something alive.
妙手回春	miào shǒu huí chūn	miraculous hands bring back the spring; masterly healing — 妙手 (wondrous hands) + 回春 (return spring, restore life's season). The stock phrase of gratitude to a doctor, embroidered on the silk banners (锦旗 jǐnqí) that patients present to hospital departments, a living custom: the walls of a respected clinic hang red with them.
民不聊生	mín bù liáo shēng	the people can scarcely survive: a populace plunged into misery — Literally "the people have no means to make a living." A grim phrase for times of misrule, war, or disaster when ordinary people cannot even keep themselves alive. 聊 liáo here is the classical sense "to rely on, to depend on for," so 不聊生 means having nothing to depend on for life.
民以食为天	mín yǐ shí wéi tiān	to the people, food is heaven: nothing matters more than feeding the people — Literally "the people take food as heaven." An ancient maxim of statecraft: the first and highest concern of any ruler is that the people have enough to eat. Still quoted constantly in everyday life, often half-jokingly, to defend the seriousness of a good meal.
名不副实	míng bù fù shí	name does not match reality — the condition 正名 diagnoses — 名 (name) + 不 (does not) + 副 (match, correspond to) + 实 (reality). The set phrase for the gap that 正名 targets.
名不虚传	míng bù xū chuán	the reputation is not falsely spread: to live up to one's name; to be as good as people say — Lit: the name is not emptily passed around. Said of a person or thing whose fame turns out to be well deserved, the praise that circulated was no exaggeration. Here 传 keeps the chuán reading, the spreading of a reputation.
名存实亡	míng cún shí wáng	existing in name but not in reality — Literally "the name survives, the reality is dead," describing something that keeps its title or form while its substance has vanished, an alliance, a rule, or an institution that is hollow inside. The 名 versus 实 contrast, the gap between what is called and what truly is, that 其实 itself points to.
名副其实	míng fù qí shí	the name matches the reality — Literally "the name fits its reality," said of someone or something that truly lives up to its reputation or title. 名 (name) and 实 (reality) match. The opposite is 名不副实 ("the name does not match the reality"), all show, no substance. Note the shared 其实 morphemes 其 and 实.
名落孙山	míng luò Sūn Shān	one's name fell behind Sun Shan's — to fail an examination — Sun Shan, a Song-dynasty wit, passed the provincial exam in last place. Asked by a neighbor whether the neighbor's son had passed, he answered in verse: "The last name on the list was Sun Shan; your worthy son came after Sun Shan." The gentlest failure notice in the language, still the standard lite…
名实相符	míng shí xiāng fú	name and reality correspond — the goal of 正名 — 名 (name) + 实 (reality) + 相符 (mutually correspond, match). The affirmative formulation of what 正名 aims to restore. Where 名不副实 names the problem and 名正言顺 names the condition of legitimacy in action, 名实相符 states the standard of alignment itself.
名正言顺	míng zhèng yán shùn	the name is right and the speech follows smoothly — acting with proper authority and justification — Lit: name-correct speech-flows. Directly from the Analects 13.3 argument: when the name is rectified, speech follows naturally, and what follows from speech can be accomplished. Used today when someone has the proper credentials or title to do something , "now that you have the title, you can act."
明察秋毫	míng chá qiū háo	to perceive the finest detail — exceptional discernment — Lit: bright-observe-autumn-hair-tip. 秋毫 = the impossibly fine tip of an animal's autumn coat. Used of leaders and judges who miss nothing. Its opposite: 不见舆薪 bùjiàn yú xīn "unable to see a cartload of firewood", missing what's obvious.
明日黄花	míng rì huáng huā	yesterday's news — past its prime, no longer relevant — Lit: tomorrow's chrysanthemum. Chrysanthemums peak at the Double Ninth Festival (重阳节); by tomorrow they are wilted and past. Used of news, opportunities, or people who are no longer timely.
明月几时有？把酒问青天。	míng yu è jǐ shí yǒu ? bǎ jiǔ wèn qīng tiān .	When did the bright moon first appear? Cup in hand, I ask the blue sky. — Opening of Su Shi's 水调歌头 (Prelude to Water Melody), written on the Mid-Autumn Festival while missing his younger brother Su Zhe.
明哲保身	míng zhé bǎo shēn	the wise protect themselves; prudent self-preservation — From the Book of Odes, where it praised wise self-conduct. Two millennia of court politics turned it ambivalent: today it usually criticizes the colleague who sees the problem and says nothing, keeping their own 身 safe. A compliment in the Zhou dynasty, a workplace accusation now.
明知故犯	míng zhī gù fàn	to knowingly do wrong: to break a rule while fully aware it is wrong — 明 (míng, clearly) + 知 (zhī, to know) + 故 (deliberately, the willed-action sense) + 犯 (fàn, to violate, to offend). To commit an offense while clearly knowing it is forbidden, the opposite of an honest mistake.
明知故问	míng zhī gù wèn	to ask knowing the answer — a rhetorical or teasing question — Lit: clearly-know-yet-ask. For when someone already knows the answer but asks anyway, either to tease, to confirm, or to draw out a confession. 你明知故问！"You already know the answer; why are you asking?"
命中注定	mìng zhōng zhù dìng	written in one's fate — destined; predestined — Lit: in-one's-fate written-and-fixed. The classic phrase for fatalism: this was always going to happen. Extremely common in romantic narratives, films, and everyday speech when reflecting on life's significant turns.
摸着石头过河	mō zhe shí tou guò hé	crossing the river by feeling for stones — Deng's gradualist pragmatism — The most important political metaphor of the reform era. 摸 (to grope, to feel one's way) + 着 (progressive aspect) + 石头 (stones) + 过河 (cross the river).
莫须有	mò xū yǒu	perhaps he did — a charge without evidence; judicial murder by innuendo — Chancellor Qin Hui's response when asked what evidence existed for Yue Fei's treason charge: 莫须有, variously translated as "perhaps," "maybe there was a reason," or "need it necessarily be?" The phrase captures the essence of political show-trial logic: the accusation is sufficient; evidence is irrel…
墨守成规	mò shǒu chéng guī	to stick rigidly to established rules — The natural antonym of 与时俱进. 墨守 refers to Mozi's legendary skill at defensive warfare: holding a position without yielding. The phrase criticizes inflexibility and mechanical adherence to convention.
目不转睛	mù bù zhuǎn jīng	"eyes not turning from the pupil" — to stare fixedly, riveted — 目 (eye) + 不转 (not turning) + 睛 (pupil). Eyes so fixed on something that even the pupils don't move. Used for complete absorption in watching a performance, a fight, or any gripping sight.
目中无人	mù zhōng wú rén	"no people in the eye" — arrogant; treating no one as worthy of notice — 目 (eye) + 中 (within) + 无 (without) + 人 (people). Looking out from one's eye and seeing no one worth registering , arrogance so total that others become invisible. A criticism of conceit and contempt. 目空一切 (eye-empty-everything) intensifies this further: not even things are worth looking at.
南腔北调	nán qiāng běi diào	a jumble of accents: speech mixing many regional tongues — Lit: southern resonance and northern tones. Said of speech that mixes accents from all over, or of a gathering where many dialects are heard at once. Here 调 takes the diào reading, "accent, manner of speech."
南辕北辙	nán yuán běi zhé	"going south in the shafts, tracks heading north" — completely self-contradictory — From the Zhànguó Cè: a man in the state of Wèi claimed he was going to the state of Chǔ (which lies south) but pointed his carriage north. When told he was heading the wrong way, he replied that his horse was fast, his driver skilled, and he had plenty of provisions, all the wrong justifications.
难分难解	nán fēn nán jiě	hard to divide and hard to untangle: locked together, evenly matched — Lit: hard-to-separate-hard-to-loosen. Of a contest too close to call, or of people so entwined, whether fighting or in love, that they cannot be pulled apart.
难解难分	nán jiě nán fēn	hard to untie, hard to part: locked together — Lit: hard 难 to untie 解, hard 难 to separate 分. Two sides so entangled they cannot be pulled apart: a deadlocked contest, a fierce struggle, or two people inseparably close. 双方打得难解难分 = the two sides fought to a standstill.
内外有别	nèi wài yǒu bié	inside and outside are distinct: insiders and outsiders are treated differently — Lit: inside-outside-have-distinction. The principle that there is a proper line between those within a family, group, or nation and those without, and that the two are not handled the same way.
内忧外困	nèi yōu wài kùn	troubles within, pressures without: beset on every side — A state or organization squeezed simultaneously by internal worry and external pressure. Common in political and business commentary; a near twin of 内忧外患.
能者多劳	néng zhě duō láo	the capable bear the heavier burden; the able do more work — 能者 = the capable one; one who can + 多劳 = works more, bears more labor. A maxim that can be used approvingly (the talented should take on more responsibility) or ironically (the competent get punished with extra tasks).
泥菩萨过河	ní pú sà guò hé	a clay Bodhisattva crossing a river — unable to save even oneself — Lit: clay-bodhisattva-cross-river. 菩萨 púsà (Bodhisattva) is made of clay , crossing water would destroy it. Used to say someone is in no position to help others when they can barely save themselves. 泥菩萨过河，自身难保。
你觉得呢？	nǐ ju é de ne ?	What do you think? — An extremely common conversational turn, throwing the question back to the other person. The particle 呢 ne softens it and invites their view. One of the most natural ways to ask for an opinion in spoken Chinese, and a good phrase to keep a conversation going.
拈花微笑	niān huā wēi xiào	holding up a flower, smiling faintly — wordless understanding — Chan's founding legend, recorded in Song-era lamp histories: the Buddha silently held up a flower before the assembly, and only Mahākāśyapa smiled, receiving the transmission outside words. Cited for any perfect unspoken communication between two people who need no explanation.
年富力强	nián fù lì qiáng	rich in years and strong in force — in the prime of life — Lit: year-rich-strength-strong. Used to describe someone in their prime: still young enough to have full physical and mental energy, experienced enough to have skill and judgment. The ideal working age. 他正值年富力强之时 "He is at the prime of his powers." A compliment to someone in their 30s–50s.
念念不忘	niàn niàn bù wàng	to keep thinking of without ever forgetting — to hold something constantly in mind — Lit: thought-after-thought, never forgetting. 念念 doubles the character to mean "moment after moment of mind." Used for an attachment, a wish, or a person one cannot let go of: 他对故乡念念不忘 (he never stops thinking of his hometown).
念念有词	niàn niàn yǒu cí	to mutter words under one breath: to chant or murmur incantations — Lit: muttering-and-having-words. Originally of a priest or sorcerer murmuring a spell, now of anyone muttering steadily to themselves, whether praying, reciting, or grumbling.
念兹在兹	niàn zī zài zī	to think of it and dwell on it — to keep a matter constantly before the mind — A classical phrase from the Book of Documents (书经): 兹 zī means "this." To think of this and be present to this , to give a duty or concern unbroken attention. More literary than the others, used in formal or written contexts to describe devotion to a cause or responsibility one never sets aside.
鸟语花香	niǎo yǔ huā xiāng	birds singing, flowers fragrant: a beautiful spring scene — A stock phrase for an idyllic countryside in spring, the birds talking and the blossoms in scent. Warm and common in description.
宁为玉碎，不为瓦全	níng wéi yù suì , bù wéi wǎ quán	Better to be shattered jade than intact tile — choose integrity over ignoble survival — Lit: rather be jade-shattered, not be tile-whole. The contrast is between two kinds of material: jade, which is rare, beautiful, and breaks rather than bends; and roof tile (瓦 wǎ), which is common, dull, and merely functional.
牛刀小试	niú dāo xiǎo shì	a small test of the ox-cleaver: great talent on a minor task — From the cook Páo Dīng of the Zhuāngzǐ, whose ox-carving blade glides through every joint. A heavy cleaver lightly tried, said when a capable person handles an easy job and shows the skill in reserve.
弄假成真	nòng jiǎ chéng zhēn	a pretense becomes real — what was performed turns out to be true — Lit: do-fake-become-real. For situations where pretending leads to the actual outcome: fake engagement turns into a real one, a play-acted role becomes the person's real life.
排兵布队	pái bīng bù duì	to arrange soldiers and deploy units: to marshal forces — A military set phrase, sibling to 排兵布阵. Describes a commander laying out troops in formation; now applied to organizing a team or lineup before a contest or launch.
庖丁解牛	Pāo dīng jiě niú	Cook Ding carves the ox; acting in perfect accord with natural structure — 庖丁 Pāodīng (Cook Ding , 庖 páo = kitchen, cook; 丁 Dīng = a name/title) + 解 jiě (to separate; to cut apart; to resolve; to understand , the character shows a horn + knife + cow) + 牛 niú (ox; cattle). Zhuangzi's most celebrated parable, from the third chapter (养生主 , The Secret of Caring for Life).
跑了和尚跑不了庙	pǎo le hé shàng pǎo bu liǎo miào	"the monk may run, but the temple cannot run" — even if the person flees, the institution stays put — A folk saying, not a classical chengyu, but functionally fixed. The proverb captures a specific reasoning about accountability: a debtor or wrongdoer may try to flee, but the property, family, or institution they are tied to will remain, and can be held responsible.
跑龙套	pǎo lóng tào	"to run the dragon costume" — to play a minor role; to be a bit-part player — From traditional Chinese opera. 龙套 lóngtào is the costume worn by the chorus of attendants (soldiers, servants, courtiers) who fill out a scene without lines. To 跑龙套 is to be one of these background figures: present, busy, but never central.
朋比为奸	péng bǐ wéi jiān	to band together for evil: to collude in wrongdoing — Lit: friends-allying to-do evil. 朋比 is to band together as a clique, 为奸 to commit villainy. A sharply negative idiom for cronies who join forces for corrupt or treacherous ends, the dark side of company kept on a level footing.
朋友遍天下	péng you biàn tiān xià	to have friends all over the world — A warm saying praising someone with a wide circle of friends everywhere. 遍 biàn means "all over," 天下 "under heaven, the whole world." Often paired with the encouraging proverb 在家靠父母，出门靠朋友 ("at home you rely on parents; away from home you rely on friends"), which captures the practical importance of…
披星戴月	pī xīng dài yu è	cloaked in stars, capped with the moon — toiling from before dawn until after dark — To wear the stars as a cape and the moon as a hat is to be outdoors working while they are up. Said admiringly of farmers, delivery riders, and anyone on the early-and-late grind: 他披星戴月地工作，就为了孩子上大学。He works from starlight to moonlight, all so his child can attend university.
劈头盖脸	pī tóu gài liǎn	splitting the head and covering the face: full in the face, without holding back — Describes a torrent that lands straight on you, a downpour of rain or a barrage of scolding, leaving no chance to dodge.
匹夫之勇	pǐ fū zhī yǒng	the courage of a common man: reckless bravery without strategy — 匹夫 pǐfū is an ordinary fellow of no rank. The phrase names the brute, headlong courage of one who rushes in to fight without thought or plan, contrasted with the cool, calculated valor of a true leader. It is a gentle put-down: brave, but foolishly so.
平安无事	píng ān wú shì	safe and sound, nothing amiss: all is calm and well — Lit: peaceful-safe-no-matter. A reassuring summary that nothing has gone wrong: a journey passed without incident, a household at peace. The 无事 here is the formal cousin of colloquial 没事.
平分秋色	píng fēn qiū sè	to split the autumn colors evenly: to share equally, to be evenly matched — Lit: evenly-divide-autumn-scenery. Two sides each take half, as if dividing the beauty of autumn. Used when rivals are so closely matched that neither comes out ahead.
平心静气	píng xīn jìng qì	a level heart and quiet breath: calm and composed — Lit: level-heart-quiet-breath. To approach something with a settled mind and even temper, neither agitated nor hasty. 平心静气地谈 "to talk it over calmly."
平易近人	píng yì jìn rén	"level and easy, close to people" — approachable; unpretentious; accessible — 平易 (flat and easy , without obstacles or pretension) + 近 (close to; approachable) + 人 (people). A person who is 平易近人 does not stand on ceremony, does not use their position as a barrier, and can be approached by ordinary people without formality or anxiety.
评头论足	píng tóu lùn zú	to judge the head and discuss the feet: to nitpick and find fault — Lit: appraise-head-discuss-feet. Originally about appraising a person's looks head to toe; now it means to carp over trifles and make petty, unwanted criticisms of others.
萍水相逢	píng shuǐ xiāng féng	to meet by chance: like duckweed drifting together on water — Lit: duckweed-water mutually-meet. Floating duckweed has no fixed place, so the phrase describes strangers who meet briefly by accident and then drift apart again.
破四旧	pò sì jiù	smash the Four Olds — destroy old ideas, culture, customs, and habits — The central slogan of the Cultural Revolution's attack on traditional Chinese civilization. 破 (smash, break) + 四旧 (the Four Olds).
普度众生	pǔ dù zhòng shēng	to universally deliver all sentient beings from suffering — A Buddhist phrase (from Guanyin's vow) applied also to Mazu, who is often assimilated with the Goddess of Mercy in folk practice. 普度 pǔdù = universally deliver; 众生 zhòngshēng = all living beings.
七零八落	qī líng bā luò	"seven scattered, eight fallen" — scattered and broken up; in pieces — 七零 (sevens scattered) and 八落 (eights fallen): things strewn about, broken apart, no longer whole. Used of an army routed and dispersed, of belongings scattered, or of a once-unified group now fragmented.
七上八下	qī shàng bā xià	"seven up, eight down" — nervous and unsettled; anxious about the outcome — Seven and eight are the neighbors of ten who cannot agree on direction. Seven goes up, eight goes down: the image is of something that cannot find rest, oscillating without resolution. The idiom describes the feeling of anxiety before a result, the inner turbulence of waiting without knowing.
七十二变	qī shí èr biàn	seventy-two transformations — endless versatility — Sun Wukong's power to transform himself into seventy-two different forms, from a fly to a temple. Used as a chengyu for boundless adaptability and resourcefulness, the capacity to change shape to fit any situation, and applied admiringly to anyone strikingly versatile or quick to adapt.
七嘴八舌	qī zuǐ bā shé	"seven mouths, eight tongues" — everyone talking at once; a clamor of voices — 七嘴 (seven mouths) and 八舌 (eight tongues): so many people speaking at the same time that no single voice can be made out. Describes a crowd all offering opinions at once, a noisy discussion where everyone interrupts everyone.
齐心协力	qí xīn xié lì	to make a concerted effort — Literally "aligned hearts, joined strength", everyone striving together as one. A close cousin of 同心协力, stressing that all hearts are lined up in the same direction. The collective togetherness that 一起 points toward when a group acts as a team.
其貌不扬	qí mào bù yáng	its appearance not outstanding — plain-featured; ordinary-looking — 其 qí (its) + 貌 mào (appearance; face) + 不扬 bù yáng (not elevated; not distinguished). Used of people with unremarkable physical appearance, often with an implied "but capable": the phrase sets up the contrast between appearance and substance.
起死回生	qǐ sǐ huí shēng	to bring back from the dead — to revive a desperate situation — Lit: raise-dead-return-life. Originally medical (miraculous cures); now used for companies, projects, and relationships revived against all odds.
气急败坏	qì jí bài huài	breath urgent, composure ruined: flustered and furious, beside oneself with rage — Pictures someone so panicked or enraged that their composure has fallen apart. 败坏 doubles "defeated" and "ruined." Common in narration for a person who has lost their cool and is lashing out.
气吞山河	qì tūn shān hé	spirit that could swallow mountains and rivers — magnificent, all-encompassing force — Lit: qi-swallow-mountain-river. A classical idiom for heroic grandeur: the qi of a great army, a historical figure, or a piece of calligraphy or poetry so powerful it seems to contain all of nature within it. Often used in literary and historical commentary.
气壮山河	qì zhuàng shān hé	magnificent spirit that fills the mountains and rivers — Lit: qi-strong-mountain-river. Similar to 气吞山河 but with a sense of steadiness rather than swallowing, the qi standing as firm and vast as mountains and rivers. Used for patriotic spirit, heroic resolve, or great art. A phrase from Wen Tianxiang's 正气歌 tradition.
恰到好处	qià dào hǎo chù	just right; arriving at exactly the right point — 恰 qià (just; exactly) + 到 dào (arrive at) + 好 hǎo (good; right) + 处 chù (place; point). Arriving at precisely the right place: the perfectly calibrated amount, the perfectly timed remark, the execution that is neither too much nor too little.
恰如其分	qià rú qí fèn	exactly to its measure: just right, neither too much nor too little — Lit: precisely-matching-its-portion. Praise for words or actions pitched at exactly the right degree. Here 分 takes the fèn reading, the proper allotted measure.
千变万化	qiān biàn wàn huà	a thousand changes, ten thousand transformations: endlessly changing; protean — 千 qiān = thousand, 万 wàn = ten thousand, the two largest round numbers paired for the sense of "countless." Lit: "a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations." Describes anything in ceaseless, dazzling flux: clouds, markets, a magician's tricks, the moves of a skilled fighter. 舞台上的灯光千变万化。
千方百计	qiān fāng bǎi jì	a thousand methods and a hundred schemes: by every conceivable means — Lit: thousand-methods-hundred-plans. Stronger than 想方设法, often with a hint that the effort is dogged or even scheming. 千方百计地想办法 "to try every trick in the book."
千夫所指	qiān fū suǒ zhǐ	pointed at by a thousand men: condemned by everyone — Literally "what a thousand men point their fingers at." It describes a person reviled by the whole public, the target of universal blame and reproach. To be 千夫所指 is to stand utterly condemned in the eyes of the crowd, a heavy figure for public disgrace.
千古绝唱	qiān gǔ ju é chàng	a peerless masterpiece: a work unmatched through the ages — Literally "a song unmatched in a thousand ages." Here 千古 means all the ages, and 绝唱 the supreme, unrepeatable performance. Reserved for a poem, song, or work of art so fine that nothing across the centuries can equal it.
千军万马	qiān jūn wàn mǎ	"a thousand armies, ten thousand horses" — an overwhelming force; a vast host — 千军 (a thousand armies) and 万马 (ten thousand horses): a military host so large it cannot be counted. The phrase pictures an unstoppable onrush of force and is applied to any overwhelming mass, an army, a flood of competitors, a tide of demand.
千钧一发	qiān jūn yī fà	"a thousand jun hanging by one hair" — a moment of extreme peril; hanging by a thread — 千钧 (a thousand jun, an enormous weight, the 钧 being an ancient heavy measure) suspended by 一发 (a single hair). The image is of a crushing weight held by the thinnest possible thread, an instant of utmost danger in which the slightest thing decides catastrophe or escape.
千里之行，始于足下	qiān lǐ zhī xíng , shǐ yú zú xià	"a thousand-li journey begins beneath the feet" — every great endeavor starts with a single step — From the Daodejing, chapter 64. 千里 (a thousand li) + 之 (connecting particle) + 行 (journey, travel) + 始 (to begin) + 于 (at, from) + 足下 (beneath the feet).
千里之行，始于足下。	qiān lǐ zhī xíng , shǐ yú zú xià .	A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet. — From chapter 64, now a chengyu used worldwide. The surrounding passage teaches that great things grow from small beginnings and that the wise act early, while problems are still tiny and easy to handle: the tree that fills an armspan grew from a sprout, the nine-storey tower rose from a heap of eart…
千人千面	qiān rén qiān miàn	a thousand people, a thousand faces — each one different — Often used to describe the terracotta warriors, whose faces are all individual. As a general chengyu it means that every person (or every case, or every product) is distinct, with no two alike, and it can praise rich variety or warn against treating different things as the same.
千丝万缕	qiān sī wàn lǚ	a thousand threads and ten thousand strands: countless intricate connections — Lit: thousand-silk-ten-thousand-threads. Used of relationships or matters knit together by innumerable fine ties: 千丝万缕的联系 "connections beyond counting." The literal silk threads behind every abstract 系.
千辛万苦	qiān xīn wàn kǔ	"a thousand pains, ten thousand toils" — untold hardships; every kind of suffering — 千辛 (a thousand bitternesses) and 万苦 (ten thousand toils): hardship piled on hardship beyond counting. Used to describe the immense effort and suffering endured to reach a goal: 历尽千辛万苦 (to have gone through every kind of hardship).
谦谦君子	qiān qiān jūn zǐ	"the humbly modest exemplary person" — the junzi whose modesty is doubled and genuine — From the 易经 (Yijing), first line of hexagram 15 谦 Qiān: 谦谦君子，用涉大川，吉 (The humbly modest exemplary person , it is advantageous to cross the great river. Good fortune). The doubling of 谦谦 marks the quality as thorough and genuine rather than surface-level.
前车之鉴	qián chē zhī jiàn	"the lesson of the overturned cart ahead" — learn from the mistakes of those who came before — 前 (in front) + 车 (cart) + 之 (possessive) + 鉴 (mirror; lesson; to take as a warning). A cart that has already overturned lies visible on the road ahead of you , it is the past made legible, a warning you can see precisely because the past stands in front.
前仆后继	qián pū hòu jì	"the front one falls, the next one follows" — wave after wave of sacrifice; undeterred succession — 前 (front; those ahead) + 仆 pū (to fall forward, to fall face-down) + 后 (back; those behind) + 继 jì (to continue; to succeed). Those in the front ranks fall; those behind step up to continue.
前因后果	qián yīn hòu guǒ	the full cause and effect — Literally "the prior cause and the later result", the whole chain from why to what-happened. To know the 前因后果 is to understand a matter completely, from the reason a 为什么 seeks to the outcome it explains. 因 (cause) and 果 (effect, "fruit") are the two poles of explanation.
钱可通神	qián kě tōng shén	money can reach the gods — money can accomplish anything — A cynical proverb about the power of money to overcome any obstacle. 通神 = to reach the divine, suggesting even the sacred can be bought. The Tang-dynasty origin makes this one of the oldest commentaries on corruption in Chinese literature.
潜移默化	qián yí mò huà	to shift unseen and transform in silence: to influence imperceptibly over time — 潜 qián = hidden, submerged, 移 yí = to shift, 默 mò = silent, 化 huà = to transform. Lit: "shifting while submerged, transforming in silence." Describes the slow, unnoticed way an environment, a teacher, or a habit gradually changes a person's character or thinking without any single dramatic moment.
锲而不舍，金石可镂	qiè ér bù shě , jīn shí kě lòu	Persevere without giving up, and you can engrave even metal and stone — From 劝学. The full passage contrasts: if you chisel but give up, you cannot even cut rotten wood; if you persevere without stopping, you can engrave metal and stone.
亲密无间	qīn mì wú jiàn	close with no gap between: utterly intimate, inseparable — Lit: intimate-close-without-gap. Of a friendship or bond so tight that no space, no estrangement, divides the two. Here 间 takes the jiàn reading, the gap as separation.
亲贤臣，远小人	qīn xián chén , yuǎn xiǎo rén	keep worthy ministers close and petty men far — From Zhuge Liang's Chushibiao (出师表), the memorial he submitted before the northern campaigns, diagnosing why the Former Han rose and the Later Han fell.
琴瑟和鸣	qín sè hé míng	qin and se playing in harmony — a happy and loving marriage — 琴 qín (seven-string zither) and 瑟 sè (larger twenty-five string zither) are the classical paired instruments. When they sound together in harmony, they are the image of a couple in accord. A literary idiom for marital happiness, used in wedding toasts and poetry.
青出于蓝	qīng chū yú lán	The Student Surpasses the Teacher — Indigo is made from the indigo plant, yet it is bluer than the plant itself. Xunzi's image for the student who surpasses the teacher through sustained effort.
青出于蓝而胜于蓝	qīng chū yú lán ér shèng yú lán	Blue comes from indigo but surpasses indigo — the student surpasses the teacher — From 劝学 (Encouraging Learning), the opening chapter of the Xunzi. The original context is an argument about the power of education to transform: the product (blue dye) surpasses its source (the indigo plant) through processing.
轻举妄动	qīng jǔ wàng dòng	to act rashly and recklessly: to move without due thought — Lit: light-lifting-reckless-moving. A warning against hasty, ill-considered action, often 不要轻举妄动 "do not act rashly," said when caution and patience are called for.
倾国倾城	qīng guó qīng chéng	to topple states and cities: a woman of overwhelming beauty — 倾 qīng = to overturn, to topple; 国 guó = state; 城 chéng = city. The image is hyperbolic: a beauty so dazzling that rulers neglect their duties and whole cities and states fall because of her.
清真	qīng zhēn	pure and true — the Chinese term for halal and for Islam's monotheism — 清 qīng (pure, clear) + 真 zhēn (true, genuine). The standard Chinese translation of the Islamic concept of divine purity and absolute transcendence. Applied in Chinese to: halal food (清真饮食), mosques (清真寺 , "pure truth temple"), and informally to Islamic identity.
情不自禁	qíng bù zì jīn	unable to restrain one's feelings: cannot help oneself — Lit: feeling-not-self-restrain. When emotion wells up too strongly to hold back: 她情不自禁地哭了 "she could not help crying." 禁 here is jīn, "to bear; to restrain."
穷兵黩武	qióng bīng dú wǔ	to exhaust the troops in endless war: reckless militarism — Literally "drain the soldiers, abuse the martial." A sharp condemnation of a ruler who wages war without end, squandering lives and resources in aggression for its own sake. 黩 dú means to defile or abuse, so 黩武 is the abuse of military force.
穷途末路	qióng tú mò lù	"the road's end, the last stretch": at the end of one's resources; cornered, no way forward — 穷 qióng (exhausted) + 途 tú (way) + 末 mò (final) + 路 lù (road). Used for someone whose options have run out: a bankrupt business, a defeated army, a person at the end of their rope. Slightly literary in register.
求同存异	qiú tóng cún yì	seek common ground while keeping differences: agree where you can, set the rest aside — Lit: seek-sameness-preserve-difference. A principle of diplomacy and negotiation: build on what is shared without forcing every disagreement to be resolved first.
曲则全	qū zé quán	yield and you will be preserved — the paradox of strength through softness — Daodejing 22: 曲则全，枉则直，洼则盈. "Yield and you will be preserved; bend and you will be straightened; hollow and you will be filled." The full paradoxical sequence of Daoist counterintuition.
屈指可数	qū zhǐ kě shǔ	countable on bent fingers, a mere handful — 屈指 (bend the fingers) + 可数 (can be counted). The vivid opposite of 不计其数: so few you can tally them on one hand. 像他这样的人才屈指可数 "Talents like him can be counted on one hand." Note 数 here is shǔ (to count), the verb reading, against shù (number) in 不计其数.
取而代之	qǔ ér dài zhī	to take over and replace it: to supplant another and assume their place — Lit: take it, and replace it. From the Records of the Grand Historian, where the young Xiang Yu, seeing the First Emperor's procession, vows that he could take the emperor's place. Now used for any decisive supplanting of one thing by another.
取经	qǔ jīng	to fetch the scriptures — to go and learn from a master source — Literally "to obtain the sutras," from Xuanzang's mission and its retelling in 西游记.
取长补短	qǔ cháng bǔ duǎn	take strengths to補 compensate weaknesses — learn from others — Lit: take-long-补-short. The standard phrase for learning from others to compensate for one's own deficiencies. 互相取长补短 "learn from each other's strengths to make up for each other's weaknesses" is the common collaborative formulation.
去而复返	qù ér fù fǎn	"to go and then come back again" — to depart and return unexpectedly — 去 qù (to leave) + 而 ér (but; and then) + 复 fù (again; to return) + 返 fǎn (to turn back). Someone who had departed comes back, often unexpectedly or after a significant interval.
去留无意	qù liú wú yì	indifferent to going or staying — free of attachment to outcome — From the famous couplet: 宠辱不惊，去留无意 , "Undisturbed by honor or disgrace; indifferent to going or staying." A Daoist attitude of equanimity and non-attachment. 去 (go/leave) contrasts with 留 (stay/remain). The phrase captures the ideal of acting without being determined by results.
去伪存真	qù wěi cún zhēn	"remove the false, preserve the true" — to sift out falsehood and keep what is genuine — 去 wěi = send away the false. 存 cún = preserve; 真 zhēn = the true. The epistemological program of discernment: not just believing what you are told but actively removing the counterfeit to preserve what is real.
全力以赴	quán lì yǐ fù	to go all out: to throw one's full strength at a task — Lit: with-full-strength-to-go-toward. To commit every ounce of effort to something, holding nothing back. The everyday phrase for total commitment, whether to a contest, a project, or a rescue.
全神贯注	quán shén guàn zhù	fully absorbed: to concentrate every bit of attention on one thing — Lit: whole-spirit-pour-into. With one's entire mind poured into a single focus, oblivious to all else. The phrase for deep, undivided concentration.
全心全意	quán xīn quán yì	with whole heart and whole mind: wholeheartedly, with total devotion — Lit: whole-heart-whole-intent. The 心 (heart) and 意 (intent) doubled to mean nothing held back: 全心全意为人民服务 "to serve the people wholeheartedly." The strongest everyday way to say one is fully committed.
群龙无首	qún lóng wú shǒu	a flock of dragons with no head: a leaderless, directionless group — Lit: flock-dragons-without-head. A phrase from the Book of Changes: many capable members but no one to lead them, so the group drifts. Used of an organization left rudderless after its leader is gone.
热火朝天	rè huǒ cháo tiān	heat and fire toward the sky: a buzzing, full-tilt scene — The image is a fire roaring up at the heavens. Used for a worksite, campaign, or rehearsal humming with energy. Common in news and everyday speech.
热泪盈眶	rè lèi yíng kuàng	hot tears filling the eye sockets: moved to tears — 热泪 hot tears, 盈眶 brimming the eye rims. For the moment emotion wells up and the eyes flood. Used for reunions, awards, and stirring speeches.
人定胜天	rén dìng shèng tiān	human will can overcome heaven — perseverance defeats fate — The Maoist rejoinder to classical fatalism. 人定 = human resolution and determination; 胜 = to overcome; 天 = heaven/fate. Against the traditional acceptance of 天命, this phrase asserts that collective human effort can reshape nature and destiny.
人尽其才	rén jìn qí cái	every person fully uses their talents; no talent is wasted — Lit: person-exhaust-their-talent. A governance and organizational ideal: the right people in the right roles, fully realizing their abilities. Often paired with 物尽其用 wù jìn qí yòng (every object fully utilized).
人困马乏	rén kùn mǎ fá	men worn out and horses spent: an army exhausted — The classic picture of a column at the end of a long march, fighters and mounts alike drained. Frequent in historical novels such as the Sānguó Yǎnyì.
人面兽心	rén miàn shòu xīn	a human face with the heart of a beast: a cruel person behind a civil mask — Not built on 社 itself, but a classic measure of how a person fits or fails the bonds of human society: someone who looks like one of us yet behaves with brute cruelty. A reminder that belonging to a 社会 is judged by conduct, not appearance.
人命关天	rén mìng guān tiān	a human life is a matter of Heaven; "lives are at stake," used to underscore extreme gravity — 人命 "human life" plus 关天 "concerns Heaven." The phrase invoked when human lives are on the line in medical, legal, or rescue contexts, to communicate that ordinary calculations no longer apply. The implicit logic: a life belongs to Heaven; touching it is a cosmic, not merely human, matter.
人山人海	rén shān rén hǎi	a mountain of people, a sea of people — an enormous crowd — Lit: person-mountain-person-sea. The go-to phrase for describing massive crowds: national holidays, concerts, train stations during Spring Festival rush. Pairing 山 (mountain) with 海 (sea), the two largest natural forms, captures the sense of scale without irony.
人神相通	rén shén xiāng tōng	humans and spirits communing — the fundamental premise of shamanism — Lit: human-spirit-mutually-communicate. The cosmological axiom that makes shamanism possible: the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is permeable, and certain human specialists can cross it.
人算不如天算	rén suàn bù rú tiān suàn	human plans yield to Heaven's plans — fate overrides strategy — Lit: human calculations are no match for Heaven's calculations. A fatalist proverb at the heart of folk cosmology: 谋事在人，成事在天 (planning is human, success is Heaven's). Used when the best-laid plans go awry.
人往高处走，水往低处流	rén wǎng gāo chù zǒu , shuǐ wǎng dī chù liú	"people move toward high places; water flows to low places" — the natural human drive for self-improvement; ambition as gravity — A folk proverb rather than a classical four-character chengyu, but one of the most widely cited sayings about ambition and social mobility in Mandarin. Water follows physical gravity downward; people follow social gravity upward.
人为财死，鸟为食亡	rén wèi cái sǐ , niǎo wèi shí wáng	people die for money; birds die for food — 财 cái = wealth, property. One of the most widely quoted Chinese proverbs about greed and human nature, a parallel structure comparing human ambition to animal survival instinct. Sobering, not condemnatory; an observation about the force of desire.
人心向背	rén xīn xiàng bèi	whether hearts face toward or turn away: popular support or opposition — Lit: people's-hearts, facing-or-backing. 向 is to face toward (support), 背 to turn one's back (oppose). The phrase names the balance of public sentiment that decides whether a cause or a ruler will stand.
人言可畏	rén yán kě wèi	what people say is to be feared — A shorter, more colloquial formulation of the same truth: public opinion is a force that should not be underestimated. Less analytical than 三人成虎, more emotionally immediate. Often used in the context of reputation and social pressure.
人在曹营心在汉	rén zài Cáo yíng xīn zài Hàn	body in Cao's camp, heart in Han — physically present but mentally elsewhere; loyalty divided — From Romance of the Three Kingdoms: Guan Yu was held in Cao Cao's camp but his heart remained loyal to Liu Bei's Han cause. The 在…在 parallel structure contrasts physical location (body) with emotional location (heart).
人在江湖身不由己	rén zài jiāng hú shēn bù yóu jǐ	in the rivers-and-lakes world, one's body is not one's own — once entered, you are bound by its rules — The defining 江湖 saying. Used seriously to explain why one cannot simply walk away from obligations , and humorously to explain why you have to attend yet another obligatory dinner, meeting, or social engagement.
仁义道德	rén yì dào dé	humaneness, righteousness, the Way, and virtue — the full Confucian moral vocabulary — The four great concepts of Confucian ethics strung together: 仁 rén (humaneness), 义 yì (righteousness), 道 dào (the Way , the correct path of conduct), 德 dé (virtue , moral power accumulated through right conduct). Together they describe the ideal moral life.
仁者爱人	rén zhě ài rén	the benevolent person loves others — the most concise definition of 仁 — From Mencius (4B:28). The simplest, most direct statement of the first virtue. 仁 is not an abstract principle but an orientation toward actual people. Love here (爱 ài) means caring about the genuine wellbeing of others, not sentimental attachment.
仁者乐山，智者乐水	rén zhě yào shān , zhì zhě yào shuǐ	"the benevolent love mountains, the wise love water" — The companion form of the Analects couplet, often quoted with the order reversed. 仁 (benevolence) and 智 (wisdom) are matched to mountain (immobile, supporting) and water (mobile, responsive) respectively.
仁者无敌	rén zhě wú dí	the humane have no enemies — From Mencius (孟子). The political claim that follows from 仁 as a virtue of rule: a ruler who genuinely cares for the people will have no one willing to make war against them, because no one wants to fight a benefactor.
仁至义尽	rén zhì yì jìn	humaneness to the utmost, righteousness to its limit — to do everything one possibly can — Said of someone who has discharged every moral obligation, exhausted every avenue of help or forgiveness, usually before walking away. Often used right before delivering a hard refusal: "I have done everything humanly possible; the rest is not on me."
认贼作父	rèn zéi zuò fù	to take a thief for a father: to serve one's enemy as a benefactor — A harsh condemnation, aimed at a traitor or collaborator who submits to the very people who wronged him. The image inverts the sacred father-son bond into betrayal.
认祖归宗	rèn zǔ guī zōng	to acknowledge one's ancestors and return to the lineage — Lit: recognize-ancestor-return-lineage. Used for those who were separated from their family (by adoption, diaspora, or historical disruption) and formally reconnect with their ancestral line. A profoundly significant act in Chinese social life.
任人宰割	rèn rén zǎi gē	to be at the mercy of others; to be slaughtered at will by whoever wants to — Lit: let-people-slaughter-carve. The extreme end of the 被 spectrum , not just being acted upon but being vulnerable to anyone who chooses to exploit you. 宰割 = to slaughter and carve up (animals, and by extension, the weak).
任重道远	rèn zhòng dào yuǎn	"the burden is heavy, the road is far" — great responsibility with a long journey ahead — From the Analects of Confucius (论语): 仁以为己任，不亦重乎？死而后已，不亦远乎？(Is taking benevolence as one's charge not heavy? Does the journey end only at death , is that not far?) Used to describe serious long-term undertakings: social reform, academic work, national development. Conveys gravitas without complaint.
日积月累	rì jī yu è lěi	accumulate day by day, build up month by month — the power of small consistent effort — Lit: day-accumulate-month-build. The Chinese formulation of compounding: small daily efforts accumulate into transformative results over time. Used to encourage consistent study, practice, and work. 日积月累，功到自然成 "accumulate consistently and success will naturally follow."
日新月异	rì xīn yu è yì	changing by the day and the month — rapid, ceaseless progress — Literally "new each day, different each month," for change so fast it is visible from one stretch of time to the next. The standard phrase for the breakneck pace of modern development, especially technology and the transformation of cities, the felt texture of living in the 现代 age.
荣华富贵	róng huá fù guì	glory and splendor, wealth and rank: a life of luxury and high station — Four near-synonyms stacked for weight. Often used wistfully or critically, the worldly prize that classical heroes are urged to see through.
融会贯通	róng huì guàn tōng	"melt together, thread through": to master a subject by integrating all its parts — 融 róng (to melt; to merge) + 会 huì (to come together) + 贯 guàn (to thread through; to run a string through) + 通 (to penetrate fully).
如火如荼	rú huǒ rú tú	like fire and like white reeds: in full, blazing swing — Lit: like-fire-like-white-flowers. 荼 is the white flower of a reed. From an account of an army arrayed in red and white, the phrase now describes a movement or campaign surging ahead at full intensity.
如雷贯耳	rú léi guàn ěr	"like thunder piercing the ear" — a name of thunderous fame — 如 (like) + 雷 (thunder) + 贯 (to pierce, to pass through) + 耳 (ear). A famous name entering the ear with the force of thunder.
如日中天	rú rì zhōng tiān	like the sun at its zenith — at the height of power or fame — Lit: like-sun-middle-sky. Used to describe someone or something at the apex of their power, influence, or popularity. 他的事业如日中天 "his career is at its zenith." Can refer to a person, a dynasty, a company, or a cultural trend.
如释重负	rú shì zhòng fù	as if a heavy load were set down: deeply relieved — Lit: as-if-releasing-a-heavy-burden. The feeling of relief once a worry or duty is finally over, the body lightening as the weight comes off. 长舒一口气 "to let out a long breath" is its companion image.
如鱼得水	rú yú dé shuǐ	like a fish that has found water — to be in one's element; perfectly suited to one's environment — A fish out of water dies; a fish in water is entirely itself. This chengyu describes the state of someone who has found the exact environment where they thrive , a new job that suits them perfectly, a community where they feel at home. 他在新公司如鱼得水，如虎添翼。
如愿以偿	rú yuàn yǐ cháng	to achieve one's wish; things went as hoped — The positive counterpart: wishes fulfilled, intention and outcome aligned. 如愿以偿 and 事与愿违 are natural antonyms: the same structure (relation of wish to outcome) with opposite results. Pairing them in commentary about uncertain situations (whether things went well or not) is a common rhetorical move.
入土为安	rù tǔ wéi ān	entering the earth brings peace — may they rest in peace — Lit: enter-earth-become-peaceful. The traditional Chinese expression for the peace of burial: entering the earth is how the deceased find rest. Used in discussions of funerary customs and in consoling the bereaved.
锐不可当	ruì bù kě dāng	too sharp to be withstood: an irresistible force — Lit: so sharp it cannot be matched. Here 当 means to stand against or block. Said of an advance, an army, or a momentum that nothing can stop.
瑞雪兆丰年	ruì xu ě zhào fēng nián	a timely snow foretells a good harvest — 瑞 ruì (auspicious) + 雪 xuě (snow) + 兆 zhào (to portend) + 丰年 fēngnián (a year of abundance). A farmer's proverb with real agronomy behind it: a heavy winter snow insulates the wheat from killing cold, kills overwintering pests, and melts into spring soil moisture.
塞翁失马	sài wēng shī mǎ	The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse — His horse ran off. His neighbours grieved. He shrugged. The Daoist parable that became China's word for the unknowability of fortune.
三代之治	sān dài zhī zhì	the governance of the Three Dynasties — the Confucian golden age — The Three Dynasties (Xia, Shang, Zhou) collectively were idealized by Confucians as the golden age of moral government, a standard against which all later dynasties were measured and found wanting. 三代 remains a byword for ideal antiquity in Chinese intellectual discourse.
三更半夜	sāng ēng bàn yè	the dead of night — the third watch, past midnight — 三更 (third night watch, 11 pm to 1 am) + 半夜 (middle of the night). The 更 is gēng, first tone. A fixed phrase for any unreasonably late hour. 你三更半夜打电话干什么? "What are you calling at this hour for?" Still in active everyday use; most speakers do not connect it to the premodern watch system.
三顾茅庐	sān gù máo lú	"three visits to the thatched cottage" — to seek out a person of talent with great persistence and sincerity — The most celebrated episode from Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Liu Bei, ruler of Shu, visits the hermit Zhuge Liang three times at his remote thatched cottage before Zhuge Liang agrees to leave seclusion and serve as his strategist.
三民主义	Sān mín Zhǔ yì	the Three Principles of the People — nationalism, democracy, livelihood — Sun Yat-sen's political program, still the official ideology of the Republic of China (Taiwan). The phrase is so embedded in Chinese political vocabulary that it functions almost as a set term.
三人成虎	sān rén chéng hǔ	three people make a tiger — A minister warns his king: if three people all claim there is a tiger in the marketplace, even the skeptical will believe it. The Zhanguo Ce parable of rumor that outlasts the warning against it.
三人行，必有我师	sān rén xíng , bì yǒu wǒ shī	where three walk together, one of them is sure to be my teacher — From the Analects (论语). Confucius's most-quoted statement on learning: in any company of three people, there will be something to learn , from the better among them by emulation, from the worse by avoidance.
三头六臂	sān tóu liù bì	"three heads and six arms" — superhuman ability; able to do many things at once — 三头 (three heads) and 六臂 (six arms), the form of certain fierce Buddhist and Daoist deities such as Nezha, who can fight and act on many fronts at once.
三心二意	sān xīn èr yì	"three hearts, two intentions" — indecisive; half-hearted; wavering — Three hearts pulling in different directions, two sets of intentions competing: the image is of someone who cannot commit. Used to criticize a lack of decisiveness or sincerity in a relationship, a task, or a position. 做事不能三心二意 (You can't do things half-heartedly).
三言两语	sān yán liǎng yǔ	"three words, two phrases" — in a few words; briefly — 三言 (three words) and 两语 (two phrases): just a handful of words, said briefly. Used to mean something can be (or cannot be) explained in a sentence or two: 三言两语说不清 (it can't be explained in a few words).
三阳开泰	sān yáng kāi tài	three yang lines open into prosperity: an auspicious fresh start, a New Year blessing — From the hexagram 泰 (peace) in the Book of Changes, whose lower three lines are 阳, marking yang rising as winter turns to spring. A traditional New Year greeting wishing renewal and good fortune for the year ahead.
色厉内荏	sè lì nèi rěn	fierce in appearance but cowardly within — all bark and no bite — Lit: color-fierce-inside-timid. A Confucian observation from the Analects: those who appear stern and imposing externally (色厉) but are weak-willed inside (内荏). The opposite of the virtuous person, whose outer bearing matches inner substance.
僧多粥少	sēng duō zhōu shǎo	many monks, little porridge — too many claimants for scarce resources — The monastery breakfast as economic model. Used for job markets (百个人抢一个岗位，僧多粥少), housing, research funding, and concert tickets. The pictorial economy of the phrase, one queue and one pot, is why it beats the abstract word for scarcity in daily speech.
杀鸡儆猴	shā jī jǐng hóu	kill the chicken to warn the monkey: punish one to frighten the rest — Make an example of a minor offender so the watching crowd falls into line. Common in talk of office discipline and political crackdowns.
歃血为盟	shà xu è wéi méng	to smear blood on the lips as an oath — to seal a solemn covenant — The ritual procedure of the Spring and Autumn covenant assembly (盟会 ménghuì): participants touched their lips with the blood of a sacrificial animal , usually a bull or horse , while swearing the covenant terms. The act bound the parties through ritual sanction, not just political agreement.
山高水长	shān gāo shuǐ cháng	"mountains high, water long" — virtue or reputation that endures across time — From a Northern Song memorial by Fan Zhongyan (范仲淹) describing the legacy of a virtuous official: 云山苍苍，江水泱泱；先生之风，山高水长 ("the cloudy mountains stretch dark; the rivers run wide; the master's spirit , high as the mountains, long as the rivers").
山清水秀	shān qīng shuǐ xiù	Mountains Clear, Waters Lovely — Clear mountains, lovely waters. The standard Chinese phrase for a picturesque landscape: four characters that compress the whole aesthetic vocabulary of natural beauty.
山穷水尽	shān qióng shuǐ jìn	"the mountains are exhausted, the waters are at their end" — at the end of one's resources — From Lu You (陆游, Song dynasty), 游山西村: 山穷水尽疑无路，柳暗花明又一村 ("when the mountains are spent and the waters are done and there seems to be no road , there, beyond the dim willows and bright flowers, is another village").
山重水复	shān chóng shuǐ fù	mountains piled on mountains, waters winding through waters — a seemingly hopeless impasse — From a poem by Lu You 陆游. Full line: 山重水复疑无路，柳暗花明又一村, "Mountain on mountain, water on water, seemingly no path; then through dark willows and bright flowers, a village appears." The proverb for finding hope when all seems lost.
删繁就简	shān fán jiù jiǎn	cut the complex and move toward the simple: prune the excess — 删 to delete, 繁 the complicated, 就 to go toward, 简 the simple. An editor's motto, applied to prose, procedures, and design alike.
善恶有报	shàn è yǒu bào	good and evil are rewarded accordingly — karmic accounting — The foundational moral logic of the City God's record-keeping function. 善 shàn = virtue; 恶 è = evil; 有报 yǒu bào = has retribution/reward. The phrase asserts that no deed escapes accounting, even if human courts miss it, because the City God has the complete ledger.
善始善终	shàn shǐ shàn zhōng	good beginning, good ending; to see something through properly from start to finish — Lit: good-start-good-end. The virtue of completing what one begins, and completing it well. 终 zhōng (end, conclusion) is the Classical Chinese counterpart to the grammatical 了 , both mark the reaching of an end. This idiom captures the moral weight of completion.
伤天害理	shāng tiān hài lǐ	to wound heaven and harm reason: utterly immoral — An act so cruel it offends both heaven and natural law. Strong condemnation of conscienceless deeds.
上善若水	shàng shàn ruò shuǐ	the highest good is like water — effortless giving that sustains without striving — Daodejing, Chapter 8. Functions as a classical four-character literary phrase rather than an everyday idiom. Cited in calligraphy, philosophy, and any context invoking the Daoist ideal of natural, uncontending benefit.
上善若水。	shàng shàn ruò shuǐ .	The highest good is like water. — From chapter 8. Water is the master image of the Daodejing: it benefits all things without contending, it seeks the low places that everyone else disdains, and in this very humility it comes closest to the 道.
上下其手	shàng xià qí shǒu	"hands moving up and down" — to manipulate facts; to connive — From the Zuǒzhuàn (左传), Spring and Autumn period. A general signaled with his hand upward or downward to indicate whether a captured soldier was high-ranking (ransom-worthy) or low-ranking (irrelevant) , the signal determined the truth, not the facts.
上行下效	shàng xíng xià xiào	"what the top does, the bottom imitates" — those in power set the moral tone — A foundational principle of Confucian political thought: the ruler's virtue or vice flows downward through society. If the one above is corrupt, those below will follow. If the one above is upright, the people will follow that too. 上 and 下 carry the full social hierarchy in two strokes.
少见多怪	shǎo jiàn duō guài	"seen little, amazed by much" — making a fuss about ordinary things — 少见 (having seen few things) + 多怪 (finding much to be strange/surprising). When you haven't seen much of the world, ordinary things seem remarkable. A mild criticism of provinciality or naïvety: someone who marvels at things a more experienced person takes for granted.
舍己为人	shě jǐ wèi rén	to sacrifice oneself for others: selfless devotion to others' good — Lit: give-up-self-for-others. The highest praise for selflessness, setting one's own interests aside for the sake of other people. The 己 here is exactly the self that 舍 (to give up) renounces.
舍生忘死	shě shēng wàng sǐ	to give up one's life and forget death; to face danger without thought of self — A standard high-register chengyu for selfless courage, used for soldiers, rescue workers, doctors during epidemics. The phrase doesn't contain 命 directly but belongs to its semantic field: it names the willingness to set down the command-to-live for something larger.
舍我其谁	shě wǒ qí shuí	if not I, then who? — the burden falls to me
身不由己	shēn bù yóu jǐ	the body is not controlled by oneself — driven by circumstances beyond one's will — 身 shēn (body; self) + 不 bù (not) + 由 yóu (controlled by; following from) + 己 jǐ (oneself). One's own body belongs to external forces , obligation, circumstance, social pressure, or fate. The counterpart to agency: when 他 (the other, external) overrides 己 (the self).
身体力行	shēn tǐ lì xíng	to practice with one's own body and strength; to live what one preaches — 身 and 体 here are both verbs in the classical grammar: to embody personally (身) and to enact (体力行, carry out with strength). The Confucian ideal of the teacher whose conduct is the curriculum. Modern usage praises leaders who do rather than direct: 环保不能只喊口号，要身体力行。
深思熟虑	shēn sī shú lǜ	deep thought, mature deliberation — to think long and carefully before acting — 深 shēn (deep) + 思 sī (think) + 熟 shú (mature; thoroughly cooked) + 虑 lǜ (to deliberate; to consider). A four-character description of the deliberative ideal: thought that has gone deep and has been given time to mature, like food that has cooked through completely.
慎终追远	shèn zhōng zhuī yuǎn	careful attention to death rites and honoring distant ancestors — From the Analects (论语): 慎终追远，民德归厚矣. "When the people are careful about death rites and diligently honor distant ancestors, the virtue of the people will return to richness." Confucius's most concise statement of why ancestor veneration matters: it cultivates moral seriousness in the living.
生龙活虎	shēng lóng huó hǔ	living dragon, active tiger — bursting with energy and vitality — 生 shēng (alive; living) + 龙 lóng + 活 huó (active; lively) + 虎 hǔ (tiger). Used to describe a person , especially a child, an athlete, or anyone at the peak of their physical vitality , who radiates robust, irrepressible energy. 这些孩子个个生龙活虎，根本停不下来。
生生不息	shēng shēng bù xī	life generating life without ceasing — the endless renewal of existence — A Daoist cosmological phrase: life perpetually generating more life. Used in nature writing, philosophical prose, and speeches about cultural continuity.
生死与共	shēng sǐ yǔ gòng	to share life and death together — a bond through the deepest adversity — Lit: life-death-with-together. Used for close comrades, soldiers, and couples who have endured extreme hardship. The deepest statement of loyalty.
生于忧患，死于安乐。	shēng yú yōu huàn , sǐ yú ān lè .	One lives through hardship and worry; one dies from comfort and pleasure. — Mencius 6B:15. The full passage argues this through historical examples: great figures of the past were all tempered through adversity before they could accomplish anything.
声东击西	shēng dōng jī xī	"feign east, strike west" — strategic deception; misdirection before attacking — Lit: declare-east-strike-west. A classic military stratagem from the Sun Tzu tradition , make noise in the east to draw attention, then attack from the west. Used broadly for any deceptive misdirection tactic in business, politics, or argument. 他用声东击西的策略迷惑了对手。
十年寒窗	shí nián hán chuāng	ten years at a cold window — long, austere years of study — The image of the exam candidate reading through winters without heat. The full couplet adds the payoff: ten years at the cold window unknown, one exam success and the world knows your name (十年寒窗无人问，一举成名天下知). Modern parents invoke it during gaokao season with full sincerity.
十年树木，百年树人	shí nián shù mù , bǎi nián shù rén	"ten years to grow a tree, a hundred years to cultivate a person" — education takes far longer than any other cultivation — From the classical text 管子 Guǎnzi. Growing a tree requires ten years of patience: planting, watering, waiting. Cultivating a human being , educating, civilizing, forming character , requires ten times longer. The century-scale horizon is a deliberate rebuke to impatience.
十全十美	shí quán shí měi	perfect in every way — ten-complete and ten-beautiful, with nothing lacking — The most-used idiom of perfection in Chinese. The doubling of 十 means completeness is measured twice , in wholeness and in beauty , so that neither a technical nor an aesthetic standard is left unmet.
时不我待	shí bù wǒ dài	time will not wait for me — seize the moment; there is no time to lose — Lit: time-not-me-wait. A classical inversion , the subject (时, time) is placed before the negation, with "me" as object, producing the archaic feel of a proverb. The phrase frames time as an agent with no personal loyalty: it moves whether you are ready or not.
时过境迁	shí guò jìng qiān	time passes, circumstances change — things are different now; that was then — 时过 (time has passed) + 境迁 (the situation has shifted , 境 jìng: circumstances, context; 迁 qiān: to move, to change). Used to acknowledge that what was true, appropriate, or possible in the past no longer applies , without judgment, simply as a statement of temporal fact.
时候不早	shí hou bù zǎo	the hour is not early: it is getting late — A common set expression rather than a classical chengyu. Used to signal politely that time has slipped on, often as a cue to wrap up or take one's leave: 时候不早了，我该走了 "it is getting late, I should go."
时来运转	shí lái yùn zhuǎn	when the time comes, fortune turns — one's luck changes for the better — Lit: time-comes fortune-turns. Fortune is not fixed; it turns like a wheel. Used when someone's luck dramatically improves after a period of misfortune. The Daoist wheel of fortune encoded in a four-character phrase.
时势造英雄	shí shì zào yīng xióng	the times produce their heroes — Great figures are made by the conditions of their age, not by innate destiny alone, the circumstances create the opportunity for greatness.
实事求是	shí shì qiú shì	to seek truth from facts — address problems realistically — A classical phrase, later a famous modern slogan, meaning to approach a 问题 on the basis of facts rather than wishful thinking or ideology. 实事 (real matters) + 求是 (seek what is so). The standard expression for a pragmatic, evidence-based way of analysing and solving problems.
使坏心眼	shǐ huài xīn yǎn	to harbor a wicked scheme: to act with malicious intent — A colloquial set phrase, 使坏 (to scheme) plus 心眼 (mind, intention). Describes someone secretly plotting harm rather than acting openly. Everyday spoken register, not classical.
士农工商	shì nóng gōng shāng	scholar, farmer, artisan, merchant: the four classes of old society — The traditional ranking of occupations, with the farmer placed second only to the scholar and above the merchant, a clue to how high agriculture stood in the Confucian moral order.
世界第八大奇迹	shì jiè dì bā dà qí jì	the eighth wonder of the world — The popular epithet attached to the terracotta army since foreign dignitaries applied it after the discovery.
世世代代	shì shì dài dài	generation after generation: for all the generations to come — A doubling of 世 (age) and 代 (generation), each repeated for emphasis. Describes something passed down or continuing without break across every generation, as in a craft, a duty, or a family living on the same land.
世外桃源	shì wài táo yuán	a haven of peace: an idyllic refuge cut off from the troubled world — Lit: a peach-blossom spring beyond the world. From Tao Yuanming's fable of a fisherman who stumbles on a hidden valley untouched by war and time. Now any tranquil place sheltered from the strife and bustle of ordinary life.
事半功倍	shì bàn gōng bèi	half the work, double the result: maximum output from minimum effort — Lit: work-half-achievement-double. The ideal of efficiency: accomplishing more by working smarter. From Mencius (孟子). Its mirror image is 事倍功半 shì bèi gōng bàn (double the work, half the result), wasted, inefficient effort.
事倍功半	shì bèi gōng bàn	double the effort, half the result — A related but distinct phrase: where 事与愿违 says the outcome diverged from the wish without specifying the ratio, 事倍功半 specifically describes disproportionate effort yielding inadequate results.
事不过三	shì bù guò sān	"nothing happens more than three times" — the third time is the last; do not push beyond three — A folk saying rather than a classical text quotation: three is the outer limit of tolerance or recurrence.
事出有因	shì chū yǒu yīn	everything happens for a reason — Literally "when a matter arises, there is a cause", nothing comes out of nowhere. It is the quiet conviction behind every 为什么: ask the question and there will be a 因 (cause) to find. The 因 here is the same one in 因为 ("because").
事到如今	shì dào rú jīn	now that things have come to this — Literally "matters have arrived at the present," a set opener used when a situation has reached its current, often difficult, point and one must face it: 事到如今，只能这样了 ("now that it's come to this, this is all we can do"). Built on 如今 (nowadays, the present).
