凶多吉少	xiōng duō jí shǎo	much ill fortune, little good — the outlook is grim — 多 and 少 as a probability report: on the scale of outcomes, the bad end is heavy. The stock phrase of thriller narration and worried families when someone has gone missing; expect it in every wuxia novel's darkest chapter.
兄弟姐妹	xiōng dì jiě mèi	brothers and sisters; siblings — The full set of siblings named in birth-order pairs: 兄 (elder brother), 弟 (younger brother), 姐 (elder sister), 妹 (younger sister). A staple four-character phrase, and one of the few common ones to carry 姐 directly.
休戚相关	xiū qī xiāng guān	sharing joys and sorrows: bound together by a common fate — Lit: joy-sorrow-mutually-connected. Two parties so closely tied that whatever befalls one befalls the other, the deep 关系 in which fortunes rise and fall as one.
袖手旁观	xiù shǒu páng guān	to watch from the sidelines with folded arms: to look on without lifting a finger — Lit: sleeve-hands-aside-watch. With hands tucked in the sleeves, the onlooker stands by and does nothing while others struggle. A reproach for passivity and refusal to help.
虚有其表	xū yǒu qí biǎo	to have only its surface: impressive on the outside but hollow within; all show and no substance — 虚 xū = empty; hollow; in vain. 有其表 yǒu qí biǎo = to have (only) its outer appearance. The phrase describes something or someone that looks fine on the surface but lacks real worth underneath. 这家公司虚有其表，其实早就负债累累。
喧宾夺主	xuān bīn duó zhǔ	the noisy guest usurps the host: a secondary thing overshadows the main one — Lit: clamoring-guest-seizes-host. Said when something minor draws all the attention away from what should be central, like a sideshow that swallows the main event or a flashy detail that buries the point.
削尖脑袋往里钻	xu ē jiān nǎo dai wǎng lǐ zuān	to sharpen one's head and bore in: to push to the front of the queue — A colloquial saying, not a classical 成语, paired here with 加塞儿 (jiāsāir, to cut the line). Mentioned to contrast the orderly 排队 ideal with the elbows-out reality of a crowded queue.
学不可以已	xu é bù kě yǐ yǐ	Learning cannot stop — the process of cultivation has no natural endpoint — Opening line of the Xunzi and of the 劝学 chapter, the programmatic statement of Xunzi's entire educational philosophy. 已 yǐ: to stop, to cease. The philosophical force follows from the 性恶论: if goodness is not innate but must be cultivated, then the cultivation is never complete by its own logic.
学而时习之	xu é ér shí xí zhī	to study and constantly practice what one has learned — the joy of learning — The opening phrase of the Analects (1.1). 时 shí means "at the right times" or "constantly/regularly"; Confucius is describing not cramming but sustained, rhythmic practice. 习 xí originally depicted a young bird practicing flight: iteration until mastery.
学而时习之，不亦说乎？	xu é ér shí xí zhī , bù yì yu è hū ?	Is it not a pleasure to learn and repeatedly practice what you have learned? — Opening line of the Analects (1.1). The word 说 here is read yuè, an archaic form of 悦 "pleased, delighted." The passage continues: "Is it not a joy to have friends come from afar? Is it not a mark of the noble person not to be resentful when others do not recognize him?" Three questions that establi…
学而优则仕	xu é ér yōu zé shì	excel in learning, then enter officialdom — From the Analects (子张 chapter): the formulation attributed to Confucius's disciple Zixia establishing the connection between scholarly achievement and public service. 优 (yōu) means to excel, to have surplus capacity; 仕 (shì) means to serve in office.
学富五车	xu é fù wǔ chē	"learning fills five carts" — immensely learned; erudite — 学 (learning) is 富 (rich enough) to fill 五车 (five cartloads of books). The image comes from an age when books were bamboo strips, so that a serious library was measured by the cartload. Originally said of the philosopher Hui Shi, whose writings were said to fill five carts.
学无止境	xu é wú zhǐ jìng	learning has no boundary — there is always more to know — Lit: learning-has-no-stopping-point. The classical formulation of intellectual humility , no matter how much one has learned, the frontier of knowledge remains inexhaustible. Used to encourage continued study and to discourage complacency.
学以致用	xu é yǐ zhì yòng	learn in order to apply — practical application of knowledge — Lit: learn-by-means-of-reach-use. The Confucian insistence that learning is not ornamental but practical: knowledge must be applied in action to have value. The opposite of empty book-learning (书呆子 shū dāizi, "bookworm" in the pejorative sense).
雪上加霜	xu ě shàng jiā shuāng	frost on top of snow — to make a bad situation even worse — 雪 xuě (snow) + 上 shàng (on top of) + 加 jiā (to add) + 霜 shuāng (frost). Frost piled on snow already covering the ground: one hardship stacked on another. The everyday equivalent of "to rub salt in the wound" or "when it rains, it pours." 他刚失业，妻子又生病了，真是雪上加霜。
雪中送炭	xu ě zhōng sòng tàn	to send charcoal in the snow: timely help when it is needed most — The image is bringing fuel to someone freezing in a blizzard. Praises aid that arrives at the moment of real need, the warm counterpart of 锦上添花 (adding flowers to brocade), which only embellishes what is already fine. Still in everyday use.
血肉相连	xu è ròu xiāng lián	blood and flesh linked: tied as closely as flesh to blood — A near-twin of 骨肉相连, stressing the living, circulating closeness between people, or between an individual and a cause they cannot separate from.
循序渐进	xún xù jiàn jìn	to advance step by step in order — Literally "following the sequence, advancing gradually", to progress in proper order without rushing. It is the principle behind any 先…然后…最后 plan: each step in its turn, the next only after the last. A watchword in learning and training.
训练有素	xùn liàn yǒu sù	trained to a standard: well-drilled, disciplined — 素 here means a long-cultivated grounding. Praises a team, unit, or staff whose competence is visibly the product of systematic 训练 rather than luck.
鸦雀无声	yā qu è wú shēng	not a crow or sparrow to be heard — dead silence — The silence so complete even the loudest birds have stopped. The stock description of a classroom after a hard question, a courtroom before a verdict, a banquet after an unwise toast. Its cousin 悄无声息 describes stealth rather than hush.
严于律己	yán yú lǜ jǐ	strict in disciplining oneself: hold yourself to a high standard — Lit: strict-toward-disciplining-self. Often paired with 宽以待人, "lenient toward others," to describe the admired character who is hard on the self and gentle with everyone else.
言必有中	yán bì yǒu zhòng	words that always hit the mark; speech that is measured and unfailingly accurate — From Analects XI.14: Confucius describes a man who rarely speaks , 不言则已，一言必中: but when he does, always hits the target. 中 zhòng here means "center; bull's-eye," not "middle." The standard for speech that earns its right to be heard: few words, each one aimed and landing.
言不尽意	yán bù jìn yì	"words cannot exhaust meaning" — the inadequacy of language; what remains unsaid — Lit: words-not-exhaust-meaning. A classical lament about the limits of language , that what one truly means always exceeds what words can carry. Found in literary correspondence, essays, and poetry. Often appears at the end of letters: 语言有限，言不尽意。
言传身教	yán chuán shēn jiào	to teach by word and by example: to instruct both through speech and through one's own conduct — Lit: words pass it on, the body teaches it. Describes the ideal of a teacher or parent who not only explains in words (言传) but also models the lesson through their own actions (身教). The deeper teaching is the one carried by example.
言而有信	yán ér yǒu xìn	to speak and be trustworthy — to be as good as one's word — 言 yán (to speak; words) + 而 ér (and; then; connecting two qualities) + 有 yǒu (to have; to possess) + 信 xìn (trustworthiness).
言归正传	yán guī zhèng zhuàn	let the words return to the main story: to get back to the main topic — Lit: words return to the proper narrative. A storyteller's phrase, after a digression, for steering back to the central thread. Notably 传 takes the zhuàn reading here, since 正传 means the main body of the tale, the narrative proper, not a casual transmission.
言简意赅	yán jiǎn yì gāi	brief words, complete meaning — concise and comprehensive — 简 jiǎn = brief, few; 意 yì = meaning, intention; 赅 gāi = complete, thorough (a relatively rare character used almost exclusively in this idiom). The highest praise for a piece of writing or a speaker: nothing wasted, nothing missing.
言听计从	yán tīng jì cóng	"words heard, plans followed" — to comply with every word and plan — 言 (words) + 听 (heeded) + 计 (plans, strategies) + 从 (followed). Whatever someone says is accepted; whatever they plan is implemented. Used to describe a relationship of complete compliance , a ruler who accepts all counsel from a trusted advisor, or a person who follows another uncritically.
言行一致	yán xíng yī zhì	words and actions align — to practice what you preach — 言 yán (words) + 行 xíng (actions) + 一致 yīzhì (consistent; in agreement). The Confucian virtue of correspondence between speech and conduct. Used as a positive description of trustworthy, reliable people, and as a standard against which behaviour is measured.
掩耳盗铃	yǎn ěr dào líng	covering one's ears to steal the bell — self-deception — From the Lüshi Chunqiu: a thief found the great bell of the fallen Fan clan too heavy to carry, decided to break it up, and covered his own ears against the clang so no one would hear.
眼花缭乱	yǎn huā liáo luàn	eyes blurring, vision tangling — dazzled, overwhelmed by abundance — Lit: eye-flower-tangle-disorder. Used for the sensory overload of a busy market, a fireworks display, a dazzling performance: too much beauty or activity to take in at once. Almost always positive in tone (the overload of richness, not chaos).
扬眉吐气	yáng méi tǔ qì	to feel proud and elated; to finally breathe out after long suffering — Lit: raise-eyebrows-exhale-qi. The physical sensation of relief and pride after enduring hardship or injustice. The eyebrows lift, the breath that was held in tension is finally released. Used for vindication, promotion after years of struggle, or national pride after historical humiliation.
扬长避短	yáng cháng bì duǎn	play up strengths, avoid weaknesses: lean into what you do well — Common in advice and strategy contexts; the practical companion to 取长补短.
阳奉阴违	yáng fèng yīn wéi	obey openly, defy in secret — to comply in appearance while resisting in private — 阳 yáng (openly) + 奉 fèng (to obey; to comply) + 阴 yīn (covertly) + 违 wéi (to disobey). To nod and agree to someone's face while quietly doing the opposite behind their back. The phrase turns on the 阴 / 阳 contrast of overt and covert: the visible compliance is 阳, the hidden defiance is 阴.
养家活口	yǎng jiā huó kǒu	to support the family and feed its mouths: to provide for one's household — Lit: support-family-keep-alive-mouths. Here 活 is causative, to keep alive by feeding. The duty of the breadwinner to put food on the table and sustain everyone under the roof.
咬文嚼字	yǎo wén jiáo zì	to chew and gnaw on words — nitpicking at wording; pedantic attention to phrasing — 咬 = to bite; 嚼 = to chew. Vividly imagines someone masticating language rather than simply reading it. Can be used approvingly (careful, attentive reading) or critically (pedantry, missing the point). Context determines the register.
药到病除	yào dào bìng chú	the medicine arrives, the illness is gone: an instant, effective cure — A praise phrase for a skilled doctor or a decisive remedy. Extended to any solution that fixes a problem cleanly and at once.
要风得风，要雨得雨	yào fēng dé fēng , yào yǔ dé yǔ	want wind, get wind; want rain, get rain — getting whatever one wishes — Used to describe someone who gets everything they ask for: a pampered child, a powerful person, someone in a position where nothing is refused. The parallelism of 要…得… (want…obtain…) is the construction backbone. Can be admiring or envious. 他在家里要风得风，要雨得雨，什么都不缺。
业精于勤	yè jīng yú qín	mastery of one's work comes from diligence: skill is born of effort — Lit: work, refined-through, diligence. From Han Yu's essay on study: 业精于勤，荒于嬉, "mastery comes from diligence and is ruined by play." A maxim that one's craft or learning is perfected only through steady, hard application.
叶公好龙	Yè gōng hào lóng	Lord Ye Loves Dragons — He decorated his palace with dragons, until a real one appeared. The idiom for loving what you only love in the abstract.
一笔勾销	yī bǐ gōu xiāo	to cancel with one stroke of the pen: to write off entirely — Lit: one-stroke-cross-out. With a single line drawn through the ledger, a debt or a past grievance is wiped clean. Used of forgiving a debt or letting an old matter be settled and forgotten.
一步跨过	yī bù kuà guò	"to cross over in a single step" — to clear an obstacle in one move — Not a classical 成语 but a fixed conversational formula. Often used in development and policy rhetoric: 一步跨过工业化 "to leap past industrialization in a single step." Carries a faint flavor of skipping stages: sometimes admiring (decisive progress), sometimes ironic (rushing through what should have been…
一步一个脚印	yī bù yī gè jiǎo yìn	"one step, one footprint" — steady, methodical progress — Lit: each step leaves exactly one footprint; nothing rushed, nothing skipped. A modern proverb for diligent, unhurried work that builds on itself. Often used in career advice, study guidance, and praise for craftsmen.
一唱百和	yì chàng bǎi hè	one sings, a hundred answer: a single voice draws a crowd of agreement — One person 唱 starts the note and a hundred others 和 (hè) chime in. Used for an idea or call that instantly wins broad, eager support.
一唱一和	yì chàng yì hè	one sings, the other echoes: to chime in and back each other up — Originally one voice leads and another harmonizes (和 hè, to respond in tune). Now usually mildly negative: two people egging each other on or colluding to push the same line.
一成不变	yī chéng bù biàn	fixed and unchanging; rigidly the same — set in stone; never varying — 成 chéng here carries its classical sense of "established; fixed; accomplished." Lit: "once established, not changing." The phrase carries a critical edge, describing something or someone that has refused all adaptation.
一触即发	yī chù jí fā	touch and it ignites — a situation on the verge of explosion — Lit: one-touch-immediately-fire. A crisis situation where the slightest action will trigger an explosion: political tensions, a fragile negotiation, volatile emotions. Originally describing hair-trigger mechanisms, now widely applied to any situation of extreme tension.
一蹴而就	yí cù ér jiù	to succeed in one step — Literally "one stamp of the foot and it is done," to accomplish something in a single easy stroke. Most often used in the negative, to warn that hard things cannot be done all at once: 学语言不能一蹴而就 ("you can't master a language in one go"). The single-action 一 again, the cousin of 一下子.
一点一滴	yì diǎn yì dī	a dot and a drop: bit by bit, little by little — Lit: one-dot-one-drop. The small increments by which patient effort accumulates. 一点一滴地积累 "to build up bit by bit."
一动不动	yí dòng bú dòng	not moving a muscle: perfectly still, motionless — Lit: one-move-not-move. The everyday phrase for total stillness, a person frozen in place, an animal holding its breath. The doubled 动 frames the stillness as the complete absence of motion.
一而再，再而三	yī ér zài , zài ér sān	once, then again, then a third time — time after time; repeatedly — The fullest expression of Chinese repetition idiomatics. 一而再 (once to twice), 再而三 (twice to three times): the escalating structure conveys frustration or persistence. Almost always used with a negative coloring: someone has done something they shouldn't have, repeatedly. 他一而再，再而三地失约，让人很失望。
一分钱一分货	yī fēn qián yī fēn huò	you get what you pay for — one fen of money, one fen of goods — The Chinese equivalent of "you get what you pay for." 分 fēn is both a fraction of a yuan and a measure of fairness. A practical consumer proverb that endorses quality over cheapness.
一夫当关	yī fū dāng guān	one man guards the pass: a position so strong that a single defender holds off an army — From the line about the road to Shu, 一夫当关，万夫莫开, "one man holding the pass, ten thousand cannot force it open." It praises a place of such natural strength that a lone defender can block a whole host, and by extension any well-held strategic point or a person stubbornly guarding a position.
一概而论	yī gài ér lùn	to lump together and judge as one: to treat distinct cases as if identical — Literally "to discuss everything by one measure." Almost always negated: 不能一概而论 bùnéng yī gài ér lùn "you cannot lump them all together," a standard caution against treating different cases with a single blanket judgement.
一个个	yí ge gè	one by one; one after another — The triple form stresses that things happen or are dealt with individually, in sequence. 学生一个个走进教室 "the students filed into the classroom one by one."
一见如故	yī jiàn rú gù	to feel like old friends at first meeting: instant rapport — 一 (yī, one) + 见 (jiàn, to meet) + 如 (rú, as if, like) + 故 (an old friend, drawing on the 故人 sense). To meet someone for the first time and feel as though you have known them for years.
一见钟情	yí jiàn zhōng qíng	to fall in love at first sight — Lit: one-look-concentrate-feeling. 钟 zhōng here means to gather or focus one's feeling on someone. The standard phrase for instant romantic attraction on a first meeting.
一件不漏	yī jiàn bù lòu	not letting a single item slip: accounting for every piece, leaving nothing out — 漏 lòu = to leak; to omit. A colloquial set phrase built on 件, used when an inventory, a checklist, or a list of tasks is completed in full with no item missed. 他把行李一件不漏地清点了一遍。(He counted every piece of luggage without missing one.)
一件件	yī jiàn jiàn	one item at a time: piece by piece, one matter after another — A reduplicated measure-word phrase rather than a classical chengyu, but extremely common in speech. Doubling 件 turns it into an adverbial sense of taking things one at a time. 我们一件件地处理这些问题。(Let us handle these problems one by one.)
一举两得	yī jǔ liǎng dé	one move, two gains — kill two birds with one stone — Lit: one-raise/move-two-gains. 举 here is a verbal measure word (one lift/movement). A perfect analogue of "kill two birds with one stone." 这样做一举两得 "Doing it this way achieves two goals at once." Among the most common four-character idioms in business and daily speech.
一口气	yī kǒu qì	in one breath; without stopping; in one go — Lit: one-mouth-breath. Describes doing something continuously, without pause, in one uninterrupted exhalation of effort. 他一口气跑了十公里 "He ran ten kilometers without stopping." 一口气读完这本书 "Read the whole book in one sitting." The most common and versatile 气 idiom in everyday speech.
一连串	yī lián chuàn	a string of / a series of — multiple linked events — 一连 = one stretch of consecutive events; 串 chuàn = a string of threaded items (the classifier for strings of things: 一串葡萄 a bunch of grapes). Together: a chain of multiple connected events. 一连串的问题 "a string of problems." 一连串的失败 "a series of failures." Extremely common in news and commentary.
一路顺风	yí lù shùn fēng	"the whole road with following winds": bon voyage, may your trip go smoothly — A maritime image (favorable wind for the sails) generalized to all travel. Ubiquitous farewell phrase, slightly less formal than 一路平安.
一马当先	yī mǎ dāng xiān	one horse takes the lead: to be out front, to take the initiative — The lead horse of the charge. Praises someone who steps forward first and sets the pace for others.
一脉相承	yī mài xiāng chéng	descended from one bloodline: an unbroken line of inheritance — Lit: one-vein-mutually-inherit. Said of ideas, schools, or traditions that pass down through a single connected lineage with nothing broken in between. The image is of a single connecting thread, the same 系 logic of strands held together across generations.
一毛不拔	yī máo bù bá	Not Give Even a Hair — Refuse to give even a single hair from your body. Mencius's phrase for the Yangist philosophy of radical self-preservation, and the word for a miser that it became.
一模一样	yì mú yí yàng	cast from one mould: exactly alike, identical — Lit: one-mould-one-shape. Said of two things so alike they might have come from a single cast: 这对双胞胎长得一模一样 "the twins look exactly alike."
一目了然	yī mù liǎo rán	"one glance makes it clear" — obvious at a single look — 一 (one) + 目 (eye-glance) + 了然 (clearly understood). Describes things immediately comprehensible , a diagram that explains itself, an argument whose logic is visible. The phrase appears in Qing dynasty texts and entered general usage by the early Republic period.
一念之差	yí niàn zhī chā	the difference of a single thought — a momentary lapse that changes everything — 一念 (one thought-moment) + 之差 (the difference of). The idea that a whole fate can turn on a single passing impulse , one wrong thought acted on, one good one suppressed.
一诺千金	yī nuò qiān jīn	one promise is worth a thousand gold — a promise that is absolute — A promise from a person of integrity is as valuable as a thousand pieces of gold. From the story of Ji Bu 季布 in the Shiji: "It is better to have one promise from Ji Bu than a hundred gold pieces from another." Used to praise reliability and personal honor.
一票否决	yí piào fǒu ju é	a single vote vetoes it: one negative vote overrides the rest; absolute veto power — 一票 yí piào = a single vote. 否决 fǒujué = to vote down; to veto. A decision rule in which one opposing vote is enough to block a proposal outright, the power a permanent member holds on the UN Security Council.
一石二鸟	yī shí èr niǎo	one stone, two birds — accomplish two goals with a single action — The Chinese and English idioms are structurally identical. The image of a single stone bringing down two birds appears to have developed independently in both traditions, though the Chinese form likely circulated in literary Chinese before modern contact. In use: 这个方案真是一石二鸟。
一时半会儿	yì shí bàn huì r	in a short time; for a little while — A colloquial set phrase, "one moment, half a spell," meaning a brief span of time, most often in the negative: 这事一时半会儿说不清 ("this can't be explained in a moment"). It builds directly on the 会儿 of 一会儿, stretching it into a fixed expression for "any time soon."
一事无成	yī shì wú chéng	to accomplish nothing: not one thing brought to completion — Lit: one-matter-without-success. Said of a person who, despite time and effort, has nothing finished to show for it. A common note of self-reproach or worry over a life that feels stalled.
一往无前	yì wǎng wú qián	to press forward without turning back — Literally "going straight on, nothing ahead can stop it", an image of fearless forward drive. The 往 here is pure forward motion, the direction-of-travel sense, intensified into dauntless momentum. Said of armies, reformers, and anyone who advances undeterred.
一无所有	yī wú suǒ yǒu	to have nothing at all — Literally "one/whole (一) lack (无) that-which-is-had (所有)": the components of 所有 in their original possessive sense. Cuī Jiàn's 崔健 1986 song 《一无所有》, often called the founding track of Chinese rock, turned the idiom into a generational catchphrase: 我曾经问个不休，你何时跟我走 sung by a narrator who owns nothing.
一心一意	yī xīn yī yì	single-minded; wholeheartedly devoted — one heart, one mind — Lit: one-heart-one-intention. Used for unwavering focus or devotion , to a person, a task, or a cause. 他一心一意地爱着她。(He loves her with his whole heart and mind, without wavering.) The antonym is 三心二意 sān xīn èr yì , "three hearts, two intentions" , indecisive and halfhearted.
一言既出，驷马难追	yī yán jì chū , sì mǎ nán zhuī	once a word is spoken, four horses cannot chase it back — a promise is binding — 驷 sì = a team of four horses (the fastest vehicle in ancient China); 追 zhuī = to chase, to pursue. Once you have spoken, no speed can retrieve the words. Used to impress on someone that speech is irreversible: a commitment made out loud becomes binding.
一言九鼎	yī yán jiǔ dǐng	"a word worth nine cauldrons" — a promise of great weight; a person whose word is binding — 一言 (a single word) is as weighty as 九鼎 (the Nine Cauldrons). The Nine Cauldrons were the bronze vessels cast by Yu the Great, symbols of sovereignty over the nine provinces and among the heaviest objects of state.
一言为定	yì yán wéi dìng	one word and it is settled: a deal is a deal — Lit: one-word-makes-settled. Said to seal an agreement on the spot: a single word given, and the matter is fixed, with no going back. The everyday way to say "deal, it's settled."
一言以蔽之	yī yán yǐ bì zhī	to cover it all in one word — in a word; to sum up — From the Analects II.2, where Confucius summarizes the 300 poems of the Shijing: 诗三百，一言以蔽之，曰思无邪。 — "The three hundred poems can be covered in one phrase: 'no depraved thoughts.'" 以 marks the instrument (one word) used to accomplish the action (cover/sum up).
一眼万年	yī yǎn wàn nián	a single glance, ten thousand years — a look that lasts forever — Lit: one-glance-ten-thousand-years. Modern romantic register, especially in song lyrics and pop fiction: the glance at first meeting that settles a lifetime. Builds on 眼 as the measure word for a single act of looking.
一以贯之	yī yǐ guàn zhī	one thread running through all — a single principle governing everything — Source: Analects 4.15. Confucius tells Zengzi 吾道一以贯之 , "My way is threaded through by one." When Zengzi explains to other disciples, he names that one thing as 忠恕 zhōngshù (loyalty and reciprocity).
一意孤行	yī yì gū xíng	to walk one's own way alone — to push through with one fixed idea, ignoring all advice — Lit: one-intention-alone-walk. Said of someone who refuses to listen, refuses to compromise, refuses to take counsel , and walks straight into the consequences. The 孤 "alone" is what makes it pejorative: not principled persistence (which would be praiseworthy) but stubborn isolation.
一知半解	yì zhī bàn jiě	to know a little, to half-understand: superficial knowledge — Lit: one part 一 known 知, half 半 understood 解. A shallow, fragmentary grasp of something, knowing a bit but not the whole. 对这门学问他只是一知半解 = he has only a superficial grasp of this subject. Usually mildly critical of half-baked understanding.
一字不漏	yī zì bù lòu	not missing a single character — word-for-word; complete and verbatim — 漏 lòu = to leak; to omit; to miss. 他把合同一字不漏地读了一遍。(He read the contract verbatim, not missing a single character.) Used to emphasize thoroughness, total quotation, or painstaking completeness. Related: 一字不差 yī zì bù chā (not one character wrong, absolutely accurate).
一字千金	yī zì qiān jīn	one character, a thousand gold pieces — words of immense value — 字 here is a classifier for characters/words. 金 (gold pieces) is the unit of price. From the story of Lü Buwei's 吕不韦 text 《吕氏春秋》: he challenged anyone to change a single character and offered a thousand gold pieces if they could improve it. Used to praise literary excellence.
一字一句	yī zì yī jù	word by word, line by line: spoken or read with careful deliberation — Lit: one-character-one-sentence. Describes speaking, reading, or copying out so slowly and clearly that each character and each phrase lands on its own. 一字一句地说 "to say it word by word."
贻害无穷	yí hài wú qióng	to leave behind endless harm — 贻 (to bequeath) + 害 + 无穷 (endless): a mistake or evil whose damage runs on without limit. Compare the proverb 害人之心不可有，防人之心不可无 (never hold a heart that harms others, never drop the guard against being harmed), which frames the moral middle ground 害 sits on.
以德报怨	yǐ dé bào yuàn	to repay enmity with virtue — to return kindness for a wrong — Lit: with-virtue-repay-enmity. From the Analects (论语), where Confucius is asked his view of this maxim and pointedly disagrees: "Then how would you repay virtue? Repay enmity with directness (直), repay virtue with virtue (以德报德)." The chengyu remains in common use as a moral ideal, but Confucius's re…
以德服人	yǐ dé fú rén	to win people over by virtue (rather than by force) — Lit: with-virtue-make-people-submit. The Confucian alternative to coercion: a leader whose 德 is genuine attracts willing followers; one who relies on force only gets compliance. The classical contrast is 以力服人 "to make people submit by force" , which produces obedience without loyalty.
以德配天	yǐ dé pèi tiān	to match Heaven through virtue — the moral logic of dynastic legitimacy — The Zhou theological principle: the Mandate of Heaven (天命) is not permanent; it follows virtue. A ruler who loses virtue loses Heaven's backing. This gave Chinese political culture its recurring logic of dynastic rise and fall as moral narrative.
以和为贵	yǐ hé wéi guì	to hold harmony as precious — harmony as the highest value — From the Analects I.12 (有子's saying): 礼之用，和为贵，先王之道，斯为美。 — "In the application of ritual, harmony is what is precious; this is the beauty of the ways of the former kings." Often cited as the Confucian reason why formal rules (礼) exist: they are instruments toward harmony, not ends in themselves.
以礼相待	yǐ lǐ xiāng dài	to treat one another with proper courtesy — 以 yǐ (using; by means of) + 礼 + 相 xiāng (mutually) + 待 dài (to treat). A formal phrase for the reciprocal practice of 礼貌 between parties , between hosts and guests, between rival firms after a difficult negotiation, between countries after a diplomatic strain.
以卵击石	yǐ luǎn jī shí	to throw an egg at a rock: to attempt the hopelessly outmatched — Here the egg is 卵 (luǎn), the classical word for egg, but the image is the same fragile shell shattering on stone. Describes a doomed fight against overwhelming force.
以人为本	yǐ rén wéi běn	to put people first; human-centered governance — Lit: use-person-as-root. A classical Confucian governance principle revived as modern policy language. 本 běn (root; foundation) is the underground portion of a tree, the part everything else rests on. The person, not the state or ideology, is the root of all legitimate policy.
以少胜多	yǐ shǎo shèng duō	"win against many with few" — overcome a larger force; quality over quantity — 以 (by means of) + 少 (few) + 胜 (overcome, win) + 多 (many). The archetype is military: a smaller but better-prepared force defeating a larger one. The Battle of Red Cliffs (208 CE), in which Sun Quan and Liu Bei's combined forces defeated Cao Cao's much larger army, is the classic example.
以身作则	yǐ shēn zuò zé	to set a standard through personal conduct — lead by example — 以 (by means of) + 身 (one whole person; conduct) + 作则 (set a rule/standard). 身 is the entire person understood as embodied conduct , the leader is not separate from the example set. Among the most-cited leadership principles in Chinese management and parenting discourse. 作为领导者，必须以身作则。
以史为鉴	yǐ shǐ wéi jiàn	use history as a mirror — learning from the past to illuminate the present — A classical Chinese phrase with new resonance in the post-Cultural Revolution context. 鉴 (mirror, warning reflection) + 史 (history).
以史为镜	yǐ shǐ wéi jìng	use history as a mirror — learn from the past to govern the present — Taizong's most famous political aphorism: "Using copper as a mirror, one can straighten one's appearance; using history as a mirror, one can understand the rise and fall of dynasties; using people as a mirror, one can perceive one's own gains and losses." The "people as mirror" referred to his minis…
以天为则	yǐ tiān wéi zé	"taking Heaven as the standard" — modeling conduct on the cosmic pattern — 则 zé (standard; rule; model; then). The classical injunction to take Heaven's order as the measure for human conduct. Appears in Mohist and Confucian texts as a basis for ethical argument: if a practice conforms to Heaven's pattern, it is right; if it violates that pattern, it is wrong.
以文会友	yǐ wén huì yǒu	"to make friends through writing" — cultural exchange as the basis of friendship — 以 (by means of) + 文 (writing, culture) + 会 (to meet, to gather) + 友 (friend). From the Analects (Book XII): Zēngzǐ says the exemplary person uses 文 (cultural cultivation) to gather friends. In classical usage, 文 here means poetry, ritual texts, and the cultivated arts.
以小见大	yǐ xiǎo jiàn dà	see the great through the small — the particular reveals the universal — Lit: use-small see-great. A principle of classical aesthetics and moral observation: close attention to a small thing , a grain of sand, a single conversation, a minor act of character , reveals large truths.
以小人之心，度君子之腹	yǐ xiǎo rén zhī xīn , duó jūn zǐ zhī fù	measuring a gentleman's belly with a petty man's heart — projecting one's own baseness — Adapted from a Zuozhuan phrase: assuming others' motives are as small as one's own. The polite deployment is self-accusation: 是我以小人之心度君子之腹了, "I misjudged you by my own petty standard," the graceful way to withdraw a suspicion that proved unfair.
以心传心	yǐ xīn chuán xīn	mind transmitted by mind — the direct transmission of awakening from master to student — The second Chan axiom, paired with 不立文字. Awakening cannot be transferred via words or rituals; only by a direct, living encounter between an awakened mind and a genuinely seeking student.
以怨报德	yǐ yuàn bào dé	to repay virtue with resentment — An inversion of the Confucian ideal: 德 (virtue, kindness) is answered with 怨 (resentment). The phrase appears in the Analects' discussion of how to respond to good and to harm.
倚老卖老	yǐ lǎo mài lǎo	leaning on age to trade on age — exploiting seniority — Lit: lean-on-old-sell-old. The critical idiom for elders who demand deference they have not earned, throwing their age around as a trump card to win arguments or avoid accountability.
义不容辞	yì bù róng cí	duty leaves no room to decline: an obligation one cannot refuse — 义 = duty, righteousness; 不容 = brooks no, leaves no room for; 辞 = to decline, to refuse. A moral duty so clear that refusing it is not an option. Note the 不容 (will brook no) construction: 容 in the negative means "to leave room for." 帮助他是我义不容辞的责任。
义无反顾	yì wú fǎn gù	righteousness admits no looking back — to press forward without hesitation because duty demands it — 义 yì (righteousness) + 无 wú (there is no; without) + 反顾 fǎngù (to look back; to turn back). When 义 demands an action, there can be no hesitation, no reconsidering once the course is set.
义正词严	yì zhèng cí yán	righteous in cause and stern in speech: to speak with upright authority — Lit: principle-upright-words-stern. Said of someone whose argument rests on a just cause and whose wording is firm and severe, leaving no room for doubt that they hold the moral high ground.
异口同声	yì kǒu tóng shēng	different mouths, the same sound — unanimous — Everyone says the same thing at once: the committee that answers in chorus, the witnesses whose accounts match. Neutral to positive in tone; suspicious unanimity would be phrased differently. The mirror image of 众说纷纭, where every mouth says something else.
异想天开	yì xiǎng tiān kāi	wildly fanciful ideas; to have one's head in the clouds — 异 yì (strange; different; fantastical) + 想 xiǎng (thought; imagine) + 天 tiān (sky; heaven) + 开 kāi (to open). Fantastical thoughts that open the sky itself: thinking so far outside reality that heaven itself cracks open.
驿寄梅花	yì jì méi huā	sending plum blossoms by postal relay — a token of remembrance sent across great distance — From a Tang poem, but the Yuan postal relay system (驿站 yìzhàn) was the most elaborate in East Asian history, running thousands of stations across the empire with fresh horses. The phrase evokes distance, longing, and the slender thread of connection maintained across vast space.
意味深长	yì wèi shēn cháng	"meaning runs deep and long" — deeply meaningful; thought-provoking; pregnant with implication — Lit: meaning-flavor-deep-long. Used for words, actions, or expressions that reward reflection , where the surface content is less than what is being communicated. 他的话意味深长，我想了很久。"His words were deeply meaningful , I thought about them for a long time." Common in literary and critical contexts.
因材施教	yīn cái shī jiào	to teach according to aptitude: tailor instruction to each learner — Lit: based-on-talent-apply-teaching. A principle traced to Confucius, who answered the same question differently for different students. The enduring ideal of the teacher who meets each pupil where they are rather than drilling all alike.
因地制宜	yīn dì zhì yí	adapt measures to local conditions: act according to what the place calls for — Lit: follow-the-land, make-it-fitting. 因 here is the older sense, to take an existing ground as one's basis. The phrase counsels suiting your plan to local circumstances rather than forcing one rigid method everywhere.
因陋就简	yīn lòu jiù jiǎn	make do with the crude and the simple: get by with what little there is — 因 to rely on, 陋 crude, 就 to settle for, 简 the simple. Said of working within tight means, building or running something on a shoestring without waiting for better tools.
因时制宜	yīn shí zhì yí	act according to what the time requires — A closely related four-character phrase drawing explicitly on the 时中 tradition. Where 与时俱进 emphasizes forward movement alongside the era, 因时制宜 emphasizes responsive calibration: making decisions that fit the specific circumstances of the moment.
因小失大	yīn xiǎo shī dà	lose much over a trifle: sacrifice the great for the sake of the small — Lit: because-of-the-small, lose-the-big. A warning against penny-wise foolishness: chasing a minor gain or saving while letting something far more valuable slip away.
阴差阳错	yīn chā yáng cuò	yin off, yang astray — a chain of coincidences producing an unexpected result — 阴 yīn + 差 chā (off; awry) + 阳 yáng + 错 cuò (wrong). A tangle of small errors and coincidences, some hidden (阴), some accidental (阳), that combine to produce an outcome nobody intended, often a missed chance or a strange twist of fate. 因为阴差阳错，他们错过了那班火车。
阴错阳差	yīn cuò yáng chā	yin-wrong yang-off — a chain of mishaps and coincidences leading to an unexpected outcome — A series of errors and coincidences (some of a yin nature, hidden and unintended; some of a yang nature, overt and accidental) that together produce an unexpected result, usually unfortunate. 因为阴错阳差，他们错过了相遇的机会。
阴阳怪气	yīn yáng guài qì	yin-yang weird energy — passive-aggressive; sarcastic; speaking in an off-putting, odd manner — A vivid colloquial phrase for someone whose speech or behavior is consistently passive-aggressive, sarcastic, or oddly unsettling. 他说话总是阴阳怪气的，让人不舒服。
阴阳相济	yīn yáng xiāng jì	Yin and Yang complementing and nourishing each other — the ideal of balanced opposition — 济 jì = to aid, to cross over, to benefit. The image is of two forces that are not in conflict but in mutual assistance , each making the other possible. This is the aspirational state, whether in the body, a relationship, a government, or the cosmos.
音容笑貌	yīn róng xiào mào	voice and smiling face: the remembered presence of someone now gone — Lit: sound-face-smile-appearance. The way a person's voice and warm expression linger in memory, used above all of the departed. 音容宛在 "the voice and face seem still present" is a common condolence.
引经据典	yǐn jīng jù diǎn	to cite the classics and quote the canon: to argue from authoritative texts — Lit: draw on classics, rely on canon. Praise for someone whose argument is grounded in scripture and the classic texts, though it can also tease a person for being bookishly pedantic.
引吭高歌	yǐn háng gāo gē	stretch the throat and sing loudly: to sing out at full voice — 吭 is the throat; the image is of someone tipping the head back to let the voice carry. Used warmly for hearty, unrestrained singing.
应接不暇	yìng jiē bù xiá	too busy to cope: more coming in than one can attend to — Lit: responding and receiving without a spare moment. 应接 is "to attend to"; 不暇 is "no leisure." Said when guests, sights, or tasks arrive faster than one can handle them. The yìng reading, "to meet."
应有尽有	yīng yǒu jìn yǒu	everything one could expect is there — 应有 (what ought to be there) + 尽有 (is exhaustively there). The stock phrase for a well-provisioned shop or feature-complete product: 这家超市商品应有尽有 "This supermarket has everything you could want." The structural mirror of 一无所有: total presence against total absence.
迎刃而解	yíng rèn ér jiě	to split apart at the meeting of the blade: solved with ease — Lit: meeting 迎 the blade 刃, it splits 解. Like bamboo that splits cleanly the moment the knife touches it: once the hardest part is cracked, everything else falls apart of its own accord. Used when solving one key difficulty makes all the rest resolve effortlessly.
忧国忧民	yōu guó yōu mín	worried about the country and the people — the Confucian official's moral burden — The phrase encodes the Confucian ideal of public-spirited concern: not personal ambition but sorrow at the state's condition and compassion for the people's suffering.
有备无患	yǒu bèi wú huàn	preparedness prevents disaster — forewarned is forearmed — Lit: have-preparation-lack-disaster. One of the most practical and frequently cited classical Chinese proverbs. The 有/无 binary frames the logic: having preparation eliminates (brings to non-existence) disaster. 出门前要检查好，有备无患。"Check everything before you go , preparedness prevents problems."
有朝一日	yǒu zhāo yī rì	should there come a day: one day, someday — Lit: there-is morning one-day. 朝 here is zhāo, a morning standing for some future day. A set way of saying "one day," usually pointing to a hope or ambition: 有朝一日我会成功 "one day I will succeed."
有口难言	yǒu kǒu nán yán	having a mouth but unable to speak — in a position where one cannot explain oneself — The frustration of having the means to speak but being unable to, because of social constraints, grief, or incriminating circumstances. One of the most vivid expressions for the experience of being misunderstood with no way to clear one's name.
有口无心	yǒu kǒu wú xīn	mouth but no heart — speaking without malice; thoughtless but innocent — Lit: have-mouth-lack-heart. Describes someone who says careless or blunt things but means no harm , the words come from the mouth, not the heart. Used to excuse or explain unintentionally offensive speech. 他说话直，有口无心，别放在心上。"He speaks bluntly , no malice intended."
有来有往	yǒu lái yǒu wǎng	"there is coming and there is going" — mutual exchange; reciprocity — 往 wǎng = to go; toward. 来 and 往 together make up the full back-and-forth of social exchange: gifts, visits, words, favors. A relationship characterized by 有来有往 is balanced and healthy , neither party gives without receiving. Often used to encourage reciprocity in social or diplomatic contexts.
有名无实	yǒu míng wú shí	name without substance — nominal but hollow — Lit: have-name-lack-substance. For positions, titles, or claims that exist in name only , without the actual power, content, or reality they imply. The Chinese equivalent of "all title, no game." 他是经理，但有名无实，什么权力都没有。
有求必应	yǒu qiú bì yìng	every request met with response — to never refuse a reasonable ask — Lit: have-request-must-respond. Said of a generous, responsive person or deity (Guanyin is described this way). 她对学生有求必应，从不拒绝。"She responds to every student's request and never refuses." High praise for helpfulness and generosity.
有始有终	yǒu shǐ yǒu zhōng	to see a thing through to the end — Literally "to have a beginning and have an end", to finish what one starts rather than abandon it midway. The 终 of completion again, valued as a virtue of persistence. The opposite is 有始无终, all start and no finish.
有眼无珠	yǒu yǎn wú zhū	to have eyes but no pupils — to fail to recognize what is right in front of you — Lit: have-eyes-without-pearls (珠 = pearl, here pupil). Said of someone who has missed an obvious quality or opportunity: failed to spot a talent, dismissed a worthy person. Often self-deprecating: 我真是有眼无珠 "I had eyes but couldn't see."
有缘千里来相会	yǒu yuán qiān lǐ lái xiāng huì	"those with fate meet across a thousand miles" — destiny brings people together regardless of distance — The full saying: 有缘千里来相会，无缘对面不相识。"Those with karmic connection will meet across a thousand miles; those without it won't recognize each other face to face." One of the most beloved Chinese sayings about fate and connection.
右文之治	yòu wén zhī zhì	"governance that favors the literary" — an administration that prioritizes civil culture over military force — 右文 (to favor the literary arts: to place the civil over the martial) + 之 (possessive particle) + 治 (governance; rule).
余音绕梁	yú yīn rào liáng	the lingering sound circles the roof-beams — music that haunts after it ends — From the Liezi: the singer Han E, paying for a meal with song, left a melody that circled the beams of the city gate for three days (余音绕梁，三日不绝). The standard praise for a performance that stays with you, extended freely to speeches, films, and any experience with a long afterglow.
鱼和熊掌不可兼得	yú hé xióng zhǎng bù kě jiān dé	you can't have both the fish and the bear's paw — you can't have everything you want — From Mencius: both fish (common) and bear's paw (prized delicacy) are desirable, but you cannot have both. The Chinese equivalent of "you can't have your cake and eat it too." Frequently invoked when someone has to choose between two things they want equally. 鱼和熊掌不可兼得，你只能选一个。"You can't have both.
鱼肉百姓	yú ròu bǎi xìng	to make fish-meat of the common people: to oppress and exploit them — Here 鱼肉 is a verb: to treat people as meat to be carved up. A classical condemnation of tyrannical officials, traceable to the Shǐjì. Still used to denounce abuse of power.
鱼跃龙门	yú yu è lóng mén	fish leaping Dragon Gate — passing a crucial test and transforming one's destiny — 鱼 yú (fish) + 跃 yuè (to leap) + 龙门 lóngmén (Dragon Gate). The legend: a carp that braves the current and clears the great waterfall at Dragon Gate on the Yellow River is transformed into a dragon.
愚公移山	yú gōng yí shān	The Foolish Old Man Moves the Mountains — Two mountains blocked his door. He and his sons began to move them, one basket at a time. A mocker laughed. He said: when I die my sons will continue; when they die, their sons.
与时俱进	yǔ shí jù jìn	to advance together with the times — A classical phrase that became a political slogan in 2001, used to justify the Communist Party accommodating private enterprise, and criticized for justifying whatever the party currently does.
与世无争	yǔ shì wú zhēng	to stand aloof from strife: to live without contending against the world — Lit: with the world, no contention. Describes a person who seeks neither fame nor advantage and stays clear of rivalry, content with a quiet life. Carries a Daoist flavor of withdrawal and unforced ease.
雨后春笋	yǔ hòu chūn sǔn	spring bamboo shoots after rain: springing up everywhere at once — The image of bamboo shoots erupting after spring rain. Modern usage describes new businesses, buildings, or trends multiplying rapidly.
语重心长	yǔ zhòng xīn cháng	words are weighty, feeling is deep — earnest, heartfelt advice — Lit: words-weighty-heart-long. Used to describe sincere, deeply felt words from someone who genuinely cares: a mentor's advice, a parent's warning, a teacher's final lesson before a student departs. The heaviness (重) of the words comes from the depth (长) of the feeling behind them.
欲速则不达	yù sù zé bù dá	Haste Does Not Bring Success — Speed desired, arrival missed: Confucius on why rushing produces the opposite of what you intend.
寓兵于农	yù bīng yú nóng	to lodge soldiers among farmers: keep a militia by having peasants farm in peacetime and fight in war — A classical statecraft principle: soldiers feed themselves from the land in quiet years, so the army costs little until it is needed. Used today of any scheme that hides one function inside another.
原封不动	yuán fēng bù dòng	the original seal unmoved: left exactly as it was, untouched — 原封 is the original seal on a package. To leave something 原封不动 is to return or keep it intact, never opened or altered. Everyday modern usage.
原形毕现	yuán xíng bì xiàn	the original form is fully revealed: a true nature laid completely bare — Lit: original-shape-completely-appears. Said when a disguise drops and someone's real, usually unflattering, character or identity becomes plain for all to see.
原原本本	yuán yuán běn běn	from source and root: in full and exact detail, from start to finish — The doubled 原 (source) and 本 (root). To tell something 原原本本 is to give the whole account faithfully, leaving nothing out and adding nothing.
缘木求鱼	yuán mù qiú yú	"climb a tree to look for fish" — to seek something by completely wrong means; a futile approach — Lit: climb-tree-seek-fish. Here 缘 means "to climb along" rather than "karmic connection" , a completely different sense of the character (the edge-clinging, tree-climbing meaning). A cautionary idiom from Mencius. Used when someone's method is fundamentally unsuited to their goal.
远亲不如近邻	yuǎn qīn bù rú jìn lín	"a distant relative is no match for a close neighbor" — proximity creates community — 远亲 (distant kin) + 不如 (not as good as) + 近邻 (near neighbor). A proverb rather than a classical chengyu with a single attributed source, but documented in Song dynasty collections and widely cited since.
远水救不了近火	yuǎn shuǐ jiù bù liǎo jìn huǒ	distant water cannot put out a nearby fire — From the Hán Fēizǐ. Help too far away is useless against an urgent crisis; a homely proverb on the gap between resources and immediate need.
远走高飞	yuǎn zǒu gāo fēi	walk far and fly high — to go far away; to escape and seek freedom — Lit: far-walk-high-fly. The image of a bird launching into open sky. Used when someone leaves a constraining situation (a bad job, a difficult relationship, a suffocating hometown) to seek a better life elsewhere. Carries a tone of liberation and sometimes wistfulness.
约法三章	yu ē fǎ sān zhāng	a covenant of three clauses — simple, clear rules agreed upon in advance — Liu Bang's proclamation upon entering Qin territory: abolishing Qin's thousands of regulations in favor of just three (no murder, no assault, no theft). Now: any simple, clear agreement or set of rules established upfront between parties. 我们约法三章：不准迟到，不准说谎，不准逃课.
月黑风高	yu è hēi fēng gāo	moonless and windy — a dark night fit for crime or treachery — 月黑 (the moon is black, that is, no moon) + 风高 (the wind is high). A set scene-setting phrase for a night when something sinister is afoot. The full classical line is 月黑风高杀人夜 (a moonless, windy night, a night for killing). Storytellers use it to signal that the next thing to happen will be dark.
越来越好	yu è lái yu è hǎo	"better and better" — a wish or observation of continuous improvement — Not classical 成语 but a near-fixed conversational formula and a cultural mantra of optimism. The opening line of a famous song by Sun Yue (孙悦) used at the 2000 Lunar New Year gala, 越来越好 ("Better and Better"), fixed it in popular memory.
越陷越深	yu è xiàn yu è shēn	"the more one sinks, the deeper one falls" — to become increasingly trapped — A 越…越… frame applied to 陷 (xiàn, to sink, to become trapped). Used for any situation where each step makes escape harder: debt, addiction, scandal, a bad relationship.
越俎代庖	yu è zǔ dài páo	"to overstep the sacrificial vessel and take the cook's place" — to do someone else's job, to overstep one's role — From the Zhuangzi (庄子). 俎 zǔ is the sacrificial chopping block , the priest's tool , and 庖 páo is the kitchen's domain. The original image is of a priest abandoning the altar to do the cook's work.
晕头转向	yūn tóu zhuàn xiàng	"dizzy head, spinning direction" — disoriented; thrown off; bewildered — 晕 (yūn, dizzy) + 头 (tóu, head) + 转 (zhuàn, to spin) + 向 (xiàng, direction). The character 向 alone , not 方向 , is doing the directional work in the chengyu. Used when someone is overwhelmed, confused, or has lost track of what is going on.
再接再厉	zài jiē zài lì	to make further efforts; to keep working hard; to do even better next time — 再接 (take it up again) + 再厉 (sharpen again; work harder again). Used as encouragement after success or after failure: "keep it up" or "do even better." Common in school settings, performance reviews, and sports. 你这次考得很好，希望你再接再厉。
载歌载舞	zài gē zài wǔ	both singing and dancing: to celebrate with song and dance — 载…载… is a classical frame meaning doing two things at once. Standard description of festive crowds at a 春节 (chūnjié) gala or village celebration.
造反有理	zào fǎn yǒu lǐ	rebellion is justified — Mao's most radical formulation — Mao Zedong's phrase, originally from a 1939 speech, given new prominence and murderous application during the Cultural Revolution. "马克思主义的道理千条万绪，归根结底，就是一句话：造反有理。
责无旁贷	zé wú páng dài	a duty one cannot shirk — Literally "the responsibility cannot be passed to another," a duty that falls squarely on you and that you ought to shoulder. Used when one accepts an obligation as rightfully one's own, the firm sense of "should" hardened into "must."
瞻前顾后	zhān qián gù hòu	"look ahead and glance behind" — to be overly cautious; to hesitate by considering every angle — 瞻 zhān (to look ahead; to gaze forward) + 前 qián (front) + 顾 gù (to look back; to attend to) + 后 hòu (back). Looking anxiously in both temporal directions , toward the past and the future , before acting. Used critically of someone who deliberates so carefully they become paralyzed.
斩草除根	zhǎn cǎo chú gēn	cut the grass and pull the root: to eliminate a problem at its source — Lit: cut-grass-remove-root. Weeds cut at the surface grow back; only by tearing out the roots are they truly gone. The idiom urges finishing a job completely so trouble cannot return, often with a ruthless edge.
崭露头角	zhǎn lù tóu jiǎo	to show one's emerging talent — horns beginning to protrude — The image is a young animal whose horns are just breaking through the hide. Used for a young talent beginning to stand out. Very common in Chinese writing about emerging professionals or artists.
站不住脚	zhàn bù zhù jiǎo	cannot stand on its feet: untenable — Literally "the feet cannot hold their stand." Used of an argument, excuse, or theory that collapses under scrutiny. Colloquial and very frequent.
站稳脚跟	zhàn wěn jiǎo gēn	to stand firm; to gain a foothold — Literally "to stand steady on one's heels." A common set phrase, not a classical four-character idiom: to establish oneself securely in a place, job, or market before making a move. Everyday modern usage.
站在风口浪尖	zhàn zài fēng kǒu làng jiān	to stand where the wind and waves meet: at the eye of the storm — To be exposed at the most dangerous, contested forefront of events, where pressure and scrutiny are fiercest. Modern journalistic register, common in commentary.
张灯结彩	zhāng dēng jié cǎi	hang lanterns and tie up silks: to decorate festively for a celebration — Lit: hang-lanterns-tie-colored-silks. The classic picture of a place dressed up for a wedding, a festival, or New Year, with lanterns strung and bright silk streamers tied everywhere. Here 结 is the literal tying of decorations.
长此以往	cháng cǐ yǐ wǎng	if this goes on for long — a warning about sustained bad behavior — Lit: long-this-by-going. Used to warn that if a current (usually bad) situation continues indefinitely, serious consequences will follow. 长此以往，身体会垮掉的 "If this keeps up, your health will collapse." Almost always negative; rarely used for positive sustained trends.
长风破浪	cháng fēng pò làng	a long wind breaking through the waves — bold ambition and perseverance — From the Tang poet Li Bai: 长风破浪会有时，直挂云帆济沧海. "There will come a time when the long wind breaks through the waves; I shall set my cloud-sail straight across the vast sea." The image is unstoppable ambition riding the great winds, no obstacle too large to overcome.
长篇大论	cháng piān dà lùn	a long-winded discourse: a lengthy, overdrawn speech or piece of writing — Literally "long chapters, big discoursing." A speech or text that goes on at excessive length. Usually mildly critical: the listener or reader feels the argument could have been made in a fraction of the words.
长生不老	cháng shēng bù lǎo	long life without ageing — immortality — The obsession that drove the First Emperor, who sent expeditions in search of the elixir of immortality and is said to have died from mercury pills meant to grant it. The chengyu names the dream of eternal life free from ageing, a recurring theme in Daoist alchemy and in the legends around 秦始皇.
长吁短叹	cháng xū duǎn tàn	long sighs and short groans: to sigh repeatedly in distress — Describes a person worn down by worry, audibly lamenting their troubles. Literary and slightly old-fashioned in tone.
着手	zháo shǒu	to set about; to begin tackling (a task) — 着 zháo (second tone, resultative) + 手 hand. Literally "to have the hands land on something" , to get a grip on a task and begin. The image is of hands making contact with work.
着眼	zháo yǎn	to focus on; to have one's eye on; to consider from the angle of — 着 zháo + 眼 eye. "To land the eye on" a target or consideration. Most commonly found as 着眼于 (focused on, with an eye to) or 着眼点 (focal point, angle of concern). Common in political and analytical writing: 着眼长远 "with an eye to the long term." A formal way to name what frame or priority is operative.
贞观之治	Zhēng uān zhī Zhì	the Well-Governed Era of Zhenguan — the Confucian ideal of enlightened imperial rule — Taizong's reign era (627–649 CE), celebrated as the model of good governance in Chinese political tradition. The formula "[reign-era name] 之治" became the standard way to name historical periods of exceptional governance, as in 文景之治 and 开元盛世.
真命天子	zhēn mìng tiān zǐ	the true Son of Heaven, destined to rule — The legitimate ruler chosen by Heaven, as opposed to a usurper or pretender. Used in historical fiction and now, loosely and often jokingly, for "the one true destined person" in any field. It rests on the idea that the emperor's authority comes from the 天命 (Mandate of Heaven), not from force alone.
真相大白	zhēn xiàng dà bái	the true face comes fully to light — 真相 (the true state of affairs) + 大白 (made fully plain, the white of 明白). The headline phrase when a mystery resolves or a cover-up collapses. Its verb form 水落石出 ("the water recedes and the stones emerge") describes the same moment hydrologically.
真心实意	zhēn xīn shí yì	with sincere heart and genuine intent — utterly in earnest — Lit: real-heart-real-intent. The standard four-character emphatic for sincerity. 我真心实意地感谢你 "I sincerely thank you with my whole heart."
真知灼见	zhēn zhī zhuó jiàn	true knowledge and penetrating insight — genuinely wise judgment — Lit: real-knowing-burning-seeing. 灼 = scorching, here "piercing." High praise for someone whose understanding cuts through to the essential.
振兴中华	zhèn xīng Zhōng huá	revitalize China — the rallying cry of national renewal — Attributed to Sun Yat-sen and the Revive China Society (兴中会). One of the most durable slogans in modern Chinese political history, used by the Nationalist government, the Communist government, and by Xi Jinping's "China Dream" (中国梦 Zhōngguó Mèng) rhetoric.
振振有词	zhèn zhèn yǒu cí	to argue with apparent conviction: to speak plausibly while in the wrong — Lit: assured-and-having-words. Describes someone who defends a weak or unjustified position with a confident flow of arguments, sounding righteous though the case does not hold. Mildly critical in tone.
争论不休	zhēng lùn bù xiū	to argue without end: an endless, unresolved dispute — Literally "dispute and discuss without ceasing." Describes a debate that drags on with no side yielding and no resolution in sight. 不休 bù xiū "without stopping" stresses the wearisome, going-nowhere quality of the argument.
蒸蒸日上	zhēng zhēng rì shàng	"rising like steam, day by day" — prospering and flourishing continuously — 蒸 zhēng = steam; to rise in vapor. The image of steam rising without ceasing, day after day. Used of businesses, careers, nations, or any enterprise that is consistently growing and thriving. A very positive set phrase, commonly used in well-wishes and assessments of success.
正经八百	zhèng jīng bā bǎi	"upright and eight hundred" — perfectly serious; genuinely proper — 正经 (proper, serious) intensified by 八百 (eight hundred), where the large number simply amplifies the quality. The phrase insists that something is done in earnest, no joking, the real and proper thing: 正经八百地谈 (to discuss in all seriousness).
正中下怀	zhèng zhòng xià huái	hitting exactly what I hoped for — exactly what I wanted — Lit: exactly-hit-one's-heart/intention. Note: 中 here is zhòng (tone 4, to hit). The expression describes something that lands exactly where you hoped (a proposal, a result, a turn of events) as if it aimed directly at your wishes. 这个方案真是正中下怀 "This plan is exactly what I had in mind."
郑和下西洋	Zhèng Hé xià Xī yáng	Zheng He's expeditions to the Western Oceans — shorthand for Chinese maritime greatness — Used as a historical reference point in modern discussions of Chinese global engagement, maritime strategy, and the "peaceful rise" narrative. The voyages are cited as evidence that Chinese power projection has historically been tributary rather than colonial.
政通人和	zhèng tōng rén hé	government flowing smoothly, people in harmony — the ideal of good governance — From Fan Zhongyan's (范仲淹) "Yueyang Tower Preface" (岳阳楼记, 1046 CE): 政通人和，百废具兴 , when governance flows and the people are in harmony, all that was ruined can be restored. The four-character condensation became a standard formula for describing a well-governed state.
支离破碎	zhī lí pò suì	limbs apart and shattered to bits: fragmented, in pieces — Here 离 means scattered or come apart. Describes something broken into incoherent fragments, a wrecked argument, a shattered country, a disjointed text.
枝连叶合	zhī lián yè hé	branches linked, leaves joined — close-knit family or unity — Lit: branches-connect-leaves-join. A literary phrase for family solidarity or any close-knit organic unity, like branches of a tree that are all connected at the root. Uses 连 in its original botanical/linking sense.
知错就改	zhī cuò jiù gǎi	recognize a fault and at once correct it — Praise for the rare person who, the moment they see their error, fixes it without excuse. Echoes the Confucian ideal of 过则勿惮改, do not fear to mend a fault.
知恩图报	zhī ēn tú bào	knowing a kindness and planning to repay it — grateful; not forgetting a debt of gratitude — 知 zhī (to know; to be aware of) + 恩 ēn (kindness; grace; favor) + 图 tú (to plan; to intend) + 报 bào (to repay; to respond). The compound 知恩 , knowing that a kindness has been done to you , is the first act; 图报, planning how to return it, is the second.
知法犯法	zhī fǎ fàn fǎ	to know the law and break it anyway: to offend with full awareness — Lit: know-law-violate-law. Said of someone who understands exactly what the law forbids and breaks it regardless, which makes the offense worse, not more excusable.
知己知彼	zhī jǐ zhī bǐ	know yourself and know your opponent — thorough strategic understanding — From Sun Tzu's Art of War (孙子兵法·谋攻篇): 知彼知己，百战不殆 (zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài) , "Know your opponent and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will not be imperiled." The fuller phrase is often compressed to 知己知彼.
知己知彼，百战不殆。	zhī jǐ zhī bǐ , bǎi zhàn bù dài .	Know yourself and know the enemy, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril. — The single most quoted line in the Art of War and one of the best-known Chinese sayings worldwide. The full passage continues that one who knows only himself will win some and lose some, and one who knows neither will lose every time.
知难而退	zhī nán ér tuì	to retreat on seeing the difficulty: to back off when the odds are clearly against you — Lit: know-hard-and-withdraw. On recognizing how hard a thing is (知难), one 而 wisely pulls back (退). It can praise prudent judgment or, more pointedly, chide a lack of nerve.
知人者智，自知者明。	zhī rén zhě zhì , zì zhī zhě míng .	To know others is wisdom; to know oneself is enlightenment. — From chapter 33. The Daodejing consistently ranks inward mastery above outward conquest: knowing others is mere cleverness, but knowing oneself is true clarity (明 míng, the brightness of genuine insight); overcoming others takes force, but overcoming oneself takes real strength.
知书达礼	zhī shū dá lǐ	to know books and understand rites — educated and well-mannered; the Confucian ideal — 知书 zhī shū = to know books; to be literate and learned. 达礼 dá lǐ = to have arrived at an understanding of 礼; to know and practice proper conduct. Together: the classical ideal of the cultivated person, academically educated and socially formed.
知天命	zhī tiān mìng	to know heaven's decree — Confucius at fifty; the age of understanding one's place in the order — From Analects 2.4: 五十而知天命 (wǔshí ér zhī tiānmìng , at fifty, I understood heaven's decree). The phrase is not about political legitimacy here but about a different kind of knowing: what heaven put you on earth to do, what your capacities and limits are, what it is pointless to resist.
知行合一	zhī xíng hé yī	Unity of knowing and acting. — Wang Yangming's most cited formulation. The argument is conceptual, not motivational: genuine moral knowing is not a cognitive state that precedes action but an orientation that is already action-shaped. The person who "knows" something is wrong but consistently does it does not truly know it.
知之为知之，不知为不知。	zhī zhī wéi zhī zhī , bù zhī wéi bù zhī .	To know what you know and know what you don't know — that is real knowledge. — From the Analects of Confucius. The full saying ends 是知也 ("this is wisdom"). It teaches intellectual honesty: genuine knowledge includes a clear sense of the limits of one's knowledge.
知足常乐	zhī zú cháng lè	knowing sufficiency brings lasting happiness — contentment is the source of joy — From Laozi (老子·道德经, Chapter 33): 知足者富 (zhī zú zhě fù) , "Those who know sufficiency are wealthy." The fuller proverb 知足常乐 is not directly from the Daodejing text but is a Taoist-derived commonplace built on that chapter's logic.
知足者富。	zhī zú zhě fù .	Those who know sufficiency are wealthy. — Chapter 33. The full passage offers four paired contrasts: knowing others is wisdom (智 zhì), knowing oneself is enlightenment (明 míng); overcoming others requires force (力 lì), overcoming oneself requires strength (强 qiáng); knowing sufficiency is wealth (富 fù), acting with determination is will (志…
执法如山	zhí fǎ rú shān	to enforce the law like a mountain: to uphold it firmly and without bending — Lit: enforce-law-like-mountain. Praise for an official or judge who applies the law unshakably, immovable as a mountain, favoring no one and yielding to no pressure.
纸上谈兵	zhǐ shàng tán bīng	strategize on paper — armchair theorizing without practical ability — From the Battle of Changping (260 BCE): Zhao Kuo (赵括) could discuss military theory fluently but had no battlefield experience. His appointment as Zhao's commander, reversing the caution of the veteran Lian Po, led to the encirclement and massacre of 400,000 Zhao troops.
指鹿为马	zhǐ lù wéi mǎ	point at a deer and call it a horse — deliberate falsification to identify loyalists — Zhao Gao presented a deer to the court and declared it a horse, watching who agreed and who dared contradict him. Those who said "deer" were later executed.
指手画脚	zhǐ shǒu huà jiǎo	pointing with hands and gesturing with feet — bossing others around with showy gestures — Lit: point-hand-draw-foot. Said of someone who criticises and orders others about while making theatrical gestures. Carries a strong note of irritation: the speaker is performing authority rather than exercising it.
指指点点	zhǐ zhǐ diǎn diǎn	to point and gesture: to criticize or gossip about others behind their backs — The reduplicated 指点 zhǐdiǎn (to point out, to instruct) turns sour here: to keep pointing fingers and passing judgment on what is not one's business.
志同道合	zhì tóng dào hé	sharing the same goals and ideals — kindred spirits — Describes friends or partners who share the same ambitions (志 zhì) and follow the same path (道 dào). The classical ideal of friendship: not mere companionship but a meeting of values and direction. Used for close friends, allies, and collaborators who are truly aligned in what they want and believe.
志在必得	zhì zài bì dé	determined to get it; fully committed to winning — 志 zhì (will; ambition) + 在 (located in) + 必 bì (certainly) + 得 dé (to obtain). The ambition is so fixed that obtaining the goal is taken as given, not from arrogance but from total commitment. Used to describe someone who has made a full decision and will not waver. 他对这个项目志在必得，不成功不罢休。
制礼作乐	zhì lǐ zuò yu è	to codify ritual and compose music — founding a cultural order — The achievement credited to the Duke of Zhou during his regency. Used as a compound phrase to describe the founding moment of Zhou cultural civilization, and by extension any act of creating the formal cultural infrastructure of a new order.
制天命而用之	zhì tiān mìng ér yòng zhī	Master the decrees of Heaven and use them — human agency as the response to natural necessity — From 天论 (On Heaven). Contrasted with the alternative: 大天而思之, "exalting Heaven and longing for it." Xunzi argues that the latter is passive and futile; the former is the correct response to a world governed by regular, impersonal natural processes.
治国安邦	zhì guó ān bāng	"govern the state, pacify the realm" — the task of statecraft — 治国 (govern the state) + 安邦 (stabilize the realm; 邦 bāng, polity, domain). The paired formulation for the ruler's task: governing the state and maintaining peace across the whole domain. A classical political phrase that appears in pre-Qin texts.
治世之能臣，乱世之奸雄	zhì shì zhī néng chén , luàn shì zhī jiān xióng	a capable minister in peace, a villainous hero in chaos — The famous double-edged appraisal of Cao Cao, conceding his talent while condemning his ambition. The phrase is quoted as a character type in itself: the gifted person whose abilities turn dangerous when the rules break down. 奸雄 jiānxióng, "villain-hero," is the role Cao Cao defines.
致良知	zhì liáng zhī	Extending innate moral knowledge. — The core practice of Wang Yangming's philosophy. 致 means "to extend" or "to bring to bear fully." The practice is not the construction of moral knowledge through study but the removal of whatever obstructs the 良知 that is always already present.
智者千虑，必有一失	zhì zhě qiān lǜ , bì yǒu yī shī	even a wise person's thousand deliberations will have one mistake — From the Shiji (史记, Records of the Grand Historian), the strategist Li Zuoche (李左车) speaking to Han Xin: "The wise person's thousand deliberations will have one mistake; the fool's thousand deliberations will have one success." Often quoted in its truncated form 智者千虑，必有一失 as a reminder that no one i…
置身事外	zhì shēn shì wài	to place oneself outside the matter: to stay aloof, keep clear of it — Lit: place-body-affair-outside. To keep oneself out of an affair, neither helping nor interfering. Often mildly critical, of someone who stands apart when they ought to be involved.
中流砥柱	zhōng liú dǐ zhù	a pillar standing firm in the middle of the current — a mainstay; steadfast support — Lit: mid-current-firm-pillar. The image of a rocky pillar in the middle of a fast-moving river, standing unmoved while the water rushes past. Used to describe a person, organization, or principle that holds firm and provides stability amid turmoil.
众口铄金	zhòng kǒu shuò jīn	many mouths melt gold — From the Guoyu and other classical texts: collective speech is so powerful it can melt metal. A more extreme formulation of the same principle as 三人成虎: the force of accumulated voices is overwhelming, even against something as solid as reputation or fact.
众所周知	zhòng suǒ zhōu zhī	as everyone knows; it is common knowledge — A formal phrase, literally "what the crowd all knows," used to introduce a widely accepted fact. 众 (the masses) + 周知 (universally known). Common in writing and speeches as a way of appealing to shared knowledge, the Chinese equivalent of "as is well known."
众志成城	zhòng zhì chéng chéng	"when wills unite, a city wall is formed" — collective will is an impregnable defense — From the Guoyu (国语 Guóyǔ), a pre-Qin historical text. 众 (the many; the people) + 志 (will; resolve) + 成 (form; become) + 城 (city wall). When a people are of one mind, they become as strong as a city's walls. Used in political speeches, team motivation, and times of national crisis. 面对困难，我们众志成城，一定能克服。
重蹈覆辙	chóng dǎo fù zhé	to follow the overturned cart's tracks again: to repeat a past disaster — Lit: again-tread-overturned-ruts. The chóng reading. To make the same ruinous mistake that wrecked others before, having failed to learn from it.
重于泰山	zhòng yú tài shān	weightier than Mount Tai: of the gravest possible significance — From Sima Qian: a death may be 重于泰山 (weightier than Mt Tai) or 轻于鸿毛 (lighter than a goose feather), depending on what it is given for. The zhòng reading, weight as worth.
周公吐哺	Zhōu Gōng tǔ bǔ	the Duke of Zhou spits out his food — a ruler's eagerness to receive talent — From a passage in the Shiji: the Duke of Zhou was so eager to receive visiting scholars and advisors that when eating he would stop mid-meal, spit out his food, and go to meet them, lest a talented man leave without an audience.
助人为乐	zhù rén wéi lè	to take joy in helping others — Literally "to help others as one's joy," to find genuine pleasure in aiding people. A prized social virtue, often used to praise the selflessly helpful. Built on 助 (to aid), the same character at the heart of 帮助.
转危为安	zhuǎn wēi wéi ān	turn danger into safety: pull through a crisis — A four-character mirror of 居安思危, read in the other direction. The relief phrase after a patient stabilizes or a company survives. Common in news and speeches.
装模作样	zhuāng mú zuò yàng	to fake a shape and put on a show: to playact, to put on airs — Lit: feign-mould-make-shape. To strike a false pose, going through the motions of sincerity or effort while meaning none of it. A pointed way to call out pretense.
追本溯源	zhuī běn sù yuán	trace back to the root and seek the source — 追 (pursue) + 本 (root) + 溯 (go upstream) + 源 (source). Used for rigorous investigation of origins: of a word, a practice, a family line, a historical claim. The metaphor of going upstream to find the source of a river runs through classical Chinese thought about genealogy and textual scholarship.
子承父业	zǐ chéng fù yè	the son carries on the father's trade: inheriting the family calling — Said when a child takes up the parent's profession or business, from a craftsman's shop to a family firm. Neutral to approving, depending on whether the inheritance is seen as continuity or constraint.
子非鱼，安知鱼之乐	zǐ fēi yú , ān zhī yú zhī lè	You are not a fish — how can you know the happiness of fish? — From the 秋水 chapter. Used in modern Chinese as a rhetorical challenge when someone claims to understand an experience or perspective that is not their own: "You haven't been through what I've been through; how can you know how I feel?" The exchange in the original is a philosophical puzzle about per…
字里行间	zì lǐ háng jiān	within the words and between the lines: the meaning an author implies but does not state — Lit: inside-the-characters, between-the-lines. The unspoken sense that lives in the spaces of a text. 字里行间流露出真情 "true feeling shows between the lines."
字斟句酌	zì zhēn jù zhuó	weighing every character, deliberating every sentence — writing with extreme care and precision — 斟酌 zhēnzhuó = to deliberate; to weigh carefully. Used for careful writing, diplomatic language, or painstaking editing. A compliment to someone who writes with rigor. 这份合同是字斟句酌写成的。(This contract was written with extreme care.)
自得其乐	zì dé qí lè	to find one's own pleasure: content in one's own way — Lit: self-obtain-its-joy. Said of someone happily absorbed in a quiet pursuit of their own, needing no audience or approval, perfectly content alone.
自食其力	zì shí qí lì	to support oneself by one's own labor: to earn one's own keep — Lit: self-eat-one's-strength. To live on what one's own effort earns rather than leaning on others, high praise for honest self-reliance.
自我感觉良好	zì wǒ gǎn ju é liáng hǎo	to feel good about oneself — often wryly, overly self-satisfied — A common modern expression using 感觉 gǎnjué (feeling), a close relative of 觉得. Literally "self-feeling is good," it describes someone with a high (often too high) opinion of themselves. Usually said with a touch of irony about another person's unearned confidence.
自相矛盾	zì xiāng máo dùn	to contradict oneself: spear against one's own shield — Lit: self-mutually-spear-shield. From the fable of a peddler who swore his spear (矛) could pierce anything and his shield (盾) could stop anything, until a bystander asked what would happen if he used the one on the other.
自行其是	zì xíng qí shì	to act on one's own judgment; to go one's own way regardless of others — 自 zì (self) + 行 xíng (to act; carry out) + 其是 qí shì (what one considers right). Doing what one believes to be correct without consulting or deferring to others.
自言自语	zì yán zì yǔ	to talk to oneself: to mutter under one's breath — Lit: self-speak-self-say. The 自 repeats to stress that both the speaking and the listening are oneself, used of someone murmuring aloud with no one else there.
自由自在	zì yóu zì zài	free and at ease: unhurried, answerable to no one — Lit: self-free-self-present. A doubled 自 that paints a life lived on one's own terms, comfortable and unconstrained, like a bird with the whole sky to itself.
自作自受	zì zuò zì shòu	what you make, you suffer: to reap the consequences of your own actions — Lit: self-do-self-bear. The Chinese counterpart of "you made your bed, now lie in it." Said of trouble that a person has brought entirely upon themselves.
走马观花	zǒu mǎ guān huā	"look at flowers from a galloping horse" — a superficial, rushing view — 走马 (galloping horse) + 观花 (observe flowers). The mounted rider moves too fast to see the flowers properly , their gaze skims the surface without stopping to appreciate what is there. A criticism of rushed, inattentive engagement with a subject.
足智多谋	zú zhì duō móu	full of wisdom and many stratagems — highly resourceful and clever — 足 zú (sufficient; full of) + 智 zhì (wisdom; intelligence) + 多 duō (many; much) + 谋 móu (stratagem; scheme; counsel; 谋 contains 言, speech, over 某, a certain person, suggesting deliberate planning). The ideal military or political advisor: smart and strategically inventive, always with another plan.
罪魁祸首	zuì kuí huò shǒu	the ringleader of the crime and the chief of the disaster: the main culprit — Lit: crime-chief-disaster-head. The principal wrongdoer, the one most to blame for an offense or calamity. Here 首 is the head, the ringleader. 他是这场事故的罪魁祸首 "He is the chief culprit behind this accident."
左顾右盼	zuǒ gù yòu pàn	"look left, glance right" — looking around hesitantly or alertly; distracted attention — 左 (left) + 顾 (to look back; to turn and look) + 右 (right) + 盼 (to look; to gaze with expectation). The eyes move ceaselessly left and right , taking in everything around, unable or unwilling to settle on a single point.
左思右想	zuǒ sī yòu xiǎng	thinking left and right — to turn something over and over in the mind; to deliberate from all angles — 左 zuǒ (left) + 思 sī (to think) + 右 yòu (right) + 想 xiǎng (to think). The spatial metaphor makes tangible what overthinking feels like: the mind moving left, then right, finding no ground to rest on.
左右逢源	zuǒ yòu féng yuán	"meet a spring on the left and on the right" — resourceful; successful in every direction — 左右 (left and right) + 逢 (to encounter; to meet with) + 源 (a spring, source of water). Wherever you turn, you find a source of nourishment or support. Originally from Mencius (孟子·离娄下): a scholar who has deeply internalized principle will find it arising naturally from every direction.
左右为难	zuǒ yòu wéi nán	"left and right both difficult" — caught in a dilemma; no good option in either direction — 左右 (left and right) + 为 (to be; causing) + 难 (difficult). Whichever direction you move , left or right , you face difficulty. The idiom captures the specific kind of dilemma where the problem is bilateral: pleasing one side offends the other, taking one path closes the other.
作茧自缚	zuò jiǎn zì fù	to spin a cocoon and bind oneself: to trap yourself by your own doing — Lit: make-cocoon-self-bind. As a silkworm spins the cocoon that encloses it, a person can create rules, habits, or schemes that end up trapping them.
